Bill Oddie: Comedian who found nature a welcome refuge from mental illness

BBC News Mon, 27 Jul 2026 16:11:20 GMT

Bill Oddie, who has died at the age of 85, was one of Britain's best known comedians and naturalists.

A product of the Cambridge Footlights, the cradle of so much post-war British comedy, he shot to fame in the 1970s as a member of the anarchic Goodies.

Bird watching was a lifelong passion and he moved into presenting nature programmes, including the BBC's Springwatch.

But his life was plagued by bouts of acute depression which caused repeated admissions to psychiatric hospitals - where Oddie suffered from severe lithium poisoning as a result of his treatment.

William Edgar Oddie was born near Rochdale, Lancashire on 7 July 1941.

His ancestors on both sides were mill workers. However, his father Harry had made good, moved to Birmingham and worked as an accountant at the Midlands Electricity Board.

The comedian later said his father's work ethic greatly influenced his approach to his own career. But Bill saw little of his mother Lillian during his childhood.

She had been diagnosed with schizophrenia and spent much of her time in hospital. Oddie later discovered that her depression had followed the premature deaths of his two older siblings.

As a child, he became interested in bird watching - a record of one of his first observations was even preserved in a West Midlands Bird Club publication in 1956.

After leaving King Edward's School, where he was an enthusiastic rugby player, he went to Pembroke College, Cambridge to read English.

There he became involved with the Footlights Club, which numbered Graeme Garden and Tim Brooke-Taylor among its members.

Oddie wrote for and appeared in the famous 1964 review, A Clump of Plinths, which, having taken the Edinburgh Festival by storm, travelled to London's West End as well as New Zealand and the United States.

While still at Cambridge, Oddie wrote material for David Frost's satirical BBC TV show That Was the Week That Was.

He fondly recalled a poem he wrote for fellow comedian Lance Percival in the style of The Ballad of Eskimo Nell about Camberley Kate who seduced dustbin men in Kent.

Having left university, he went on to join the cast of the BBC radio show I'm Sorry I'll Read That Again, which featured many of the Footlights performers.

He was also developing as a composer, writing many of the show's songs, some of which appeared on an album Distinctly Oddie in 1967.

While some of the old Footlights team went off to form Monty Python, Oddie - together with Graeme Garden and Tim Brooke-Taylor - created The Goodies.

It featured three characters on their "trandem" who pedalled about offering themselves for hire with the tagline "We Do Anything, Anywhere, Anytime".

This spawned a series of comical situations, much slapstick and the use of fairly primitive special effects, mainly sped-up film.

One of the memorable episodes was Kitten Kong, in which a giant feline toppled the Post Office Tower. A version of this episode won the Silver Rose at Montreux TV Festival in 1972.

Oddie composed a number of comic songs for the series, often parodies of contemporary pop music. The most successful, Funky Gibbon, reached number four in the UK charts and the trio performed it on Top of the Pops.

Forty years later, the track was re-released and the profits given to a campaign to preserve the primate's habitat.

The Goodies ran on BBC Television for most of the 1970s, eventually transferring to ITV for a short - and less than successful - period.

The show became cult viewing in Australia - and the team reformed to tour the country in 2005 - but the BBC never repeated it in the UK, something that annoyed the three performers.

Garden eventually went on record to suggest that the lack of repeats was punishment for the trio's "disloyalty", saying in 2020: "It seems they've held that grudge ever since."

Oddie and Garden also co-wrote the scripts for many of ITV's Doctor in the House comedy series. But Oddie's childhood interest in ornithology had never waned and, by the mid 1970s, he was developing a career as a naturalist.

He made guest appearances on several programmes including Animal Magic. And the humorous style of his Little Black Bird Book, published in 1980, made it a bestseller.

"Bird-watchers are tense, competitive, selfish, shifty, dishonest, distrusting, boorish, pedantic, unsentimental, arrogant and - above all, envious" he wrote.

It also heralded a flowering of his career as a TV presenter and he seemed to be rarely off our screens.

The Great Bird Race, for Channel 4 in 1983, was followed by a number of programmes for the BBC including The Great Kenyan Bird Safari and Oddie in Paradise.

In 1985, the BBC ran a 50-minute Nature Watch special: Bill Oddie - Bird Watcher, in which he travelled to many of the areas where he loved to watch birds.

By the beginning of the new century, he was one of the BBC's best-loved presenters with shows like Birding with Bill Oddie and Bill Oddie Goes Wild, which took birdwatching to new audiences.

Northumberland Wildlife Trust chief Mike Pratt paid tribute to Oddie's "influential" and entertaining presence as a naturalist, serving as the charity's patron for nearly 30 years.

"Bill was a fantastic inspiration to my generation of young conservationists from the 1970s onwards," said Pratt.

"He made being a naturalist fun and exciting, and led me and many of my counterparts into campaigning and taking action to save wildlife.

"We will miss his support for what he genuinely cared about - life in all its forms."

In 2004, Britain Goes Wild pulled in a record audience when it aired on BBC Two. A year later it returned as Springwatch, with Autumnwatch following a year later.

When he wasn't fronting wildlife programmes, Oddie popped up on a string of quiz shows, had a part in a Doctor Who episode and, a memorable and poignant appearance in the BBC's genealogy series, Who Do You Think You Are?

He also carved out a career as a voice-over artist.

He was the cat in a Thompson Directory advert and made a series of spots for the DIY chain B&Q. He later described this aspect of his life as one of the most financially lucrative.

He lent his celebrity to the campaign against the illegal trade in ivory, warning that poachers kill thousands of elephants a year.

But Oddie had always been prone to bouts of depression and he was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder - which he occasionally blamed on his remote relationship with his mother.

Oddie parted company with Springwatch in 2008.

The star told the Daily Mirror in 2018: "I never had a proper explanation.

"I was called in and told: 'We won't be asking you to make any more programmes.'"

Oddie added: "Unfortunately, my bipolar element had come into it and I could be very tetchy."

The Mirror reported that the BBC did not know at the time he had a conditon, but later issued a statement saying: "We wish Mr Oddie a speedy recovery."

"At the time I was flabbergasted, " he said in a 2015 interview with the Independent.

"But a year later, I was diagnosed as bipolar. I thought back. If I knew then what I know now, I'd have accepted that I was going through a manic phase."

The audience missed him. Before he left, the show had averaged 3.19 million. After he left, that figure fell to 2.55 million.

Oddie later revealed his condition caused him to try and take his own life.

In 2020, he announced that he had been severely ill as a result of lithium poisoning: a treatment aimed at stabilising his moods.

He later posted on social media that "the past few years have been grim for me.

"Lost enthusiasm, but I am still here."

His outside interests included music. He once did a spell as a radio DJ playing jazz and his house contained his collection of thousands of CDs.

Oddie was also a passionate supporter of the Green Party and gave his time, and fame, to bolster wildlife charities such as the RSPB.

His 1967 marriage to the musician, Jean Hart, ended in divorce. In 1983, he married Laura Beaumont, who had previously worked with him on a number of projects.

Oddie was a true polymath, a man who seemed to make a success of everything to which he turned his hand.

But it was his conservation work that gave him the most satisfaction. "Wildlife," he said, "has long been a refuge - probably more than I realise."

Devastating European wildfires in maps - and how they're being tackled

BBC News Mon, 27 Jul 2026 15:59:27 GMT

Wildfires are tearing through France and Spain, forcing more than 300,000 people to evacuate their homes.

France has seen its worst fires in two decades, while officials in the Spanish capital Madrid say they are the worst the region has ever experienced.

It follows a sweltering summer of heatwaves across Europe that have seen temperatures soar above 40C (104F) in many places.

Separate wildfires in the regions outside Madrid have together burned about 297 sq miles (770 sq km), authorities estimate - an area larger than Madrid itself.

In France, the worst affected area is Gironde, around the city of Bordeaux, where more than 200,000 people have been forced from their homes.

The blaze has spread rapidly, tearing through forests and fields in France's famous wine region, and burning more than 162 sq miles (420 sq km) in less than four days - an area roughly four times the size of Paris.

It is now just nine miles (15km) from the south of Bordeaux.

The fires have also threatened a number of sensitive military and industrial sites in the area, including facilities that work on French ballistic missiles, rocket motors, and the processing of hazardous chemicals.

Satellite imagery above Gironde shows vast areas of scorched, blackened earth, with smoke drifting inland to the east.

The fires have become so extreme they have created their own giant fire thunderstorm.

A rare weather event, storms like these are formed when heat from the wildfires makes the air above the fire rise rapidly, carrying smoke, ash and water vapour high into the atmosphere.

As the air rises, it cools, and the water vapour condenses into a cloud. If the fire is powerful enough and the atmosphere is unstable, that cloud can grow into a cumulonimbus - the same type of cloud associated with thunderstorms.

If these clouds then become large enough, they can produce their own lightning, which can then start new fires. They can also occasionally bring hail and rain.

These extreme and unpredictable conditions make the fires all the more difficult to stop.

To combat them, French firefighters have been using planes loaded with fire retardant, as well as planes like the Canadair, which can scoop 6,000 litres of water from lakes or the sea in 12 seconds and drop it directly on the fires.

On dangerous days, loaded aircraft patrol high-risk areas before any fires have been reported, so they can drop within minutes of a sighting. Planes often fly in a continuous shuttle while retardant is laid along the edges of the fire and ground crews attack the flames directly.

In Gironde, about 2,500 firefighters, 1,500 military personnel, and 1,200 police officers and gendarmes have been involved in tackling the blaze.

But even with these numbers, Gironde official Jean Luc Gleyze told the BBC that authorities don't have enough people to combat the fires.

"We don't have enough people and enough trucks and even I think France don't have enough," he said.

Around the town of Lacanau, bulldozers, diggers and mechanical shovels have been used to carve a firebreak that is 100m (328ft) wide at points, according to French media.

A firebreak is essentially a stretch of land that has been stripped of all vegetation to stop the fire from spreading - removing any potential fuel before the fire has a chance to reach it.

Spanish teams have been using many of the same techniques to tackle their wildfires, which are on course to become the worst the country has seen in two decades.

Francisco Martin, a government delegate in Madrid, described the fires as "undoubtedly the largest fire in the history of the Madrid region".

This summer's fires have been aided by the hotter, drier conditions caused by climate change, which allow fires to spread faster and burn more fiercely.

Many on the ground - in both Spain and France - are fearful that the coming week could see worsening conditions, with high pressure forecast to bring dry, settled and increasingly hot temperatures.

Andy Burnham has said the UK is "with Ukraine 100%" as Volodymyr Zelensky became the prime minister's first international visitor since entering No 10.

Burnham said the visit of the Ukrainian president was designed to "send a very clear message" about the UK's continued support.

"To put it simply, Volodymyr, I want you to know that we've got your back, you can count on me and you can count on us. You can count on the UK for as long as it takes," he said at a naval base in Portsmouth on Monday.

Zelensky, meanwhile, said Ukraine's relationship with the UK was "stronger than ever".

Addressing Zelensky, Burnham said: "I am personally with you 100%, Mr President, and I will honour every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full."

Burnham added that he intended to visit Ukraine "soon" following the "very warm meeting" between the pair.

The PM also announced the sharing of the intellectual property behind the UK's new "Stone Cloak" electronic warfare system, enabling Ukraine to produce the technology at scale.

Burnham said: "It will help them to hit their targets and help save Ukrainian lives."

The Stone Cloak jammers are the size of a tablet computer and are designed to block the detection of any drones they are fitted to.

The Ministry of Defence has already given thousands of the devices to Ukrainian forces to bolster their drone operations.

Downing Street said that following its deployment in Ukraine, the technology will be built into the UK's next generation of long-range weapons.

It said this would include Project Brakestop, a government programme to develop low-cost cruise missiles - self-propelled guided weapons that fly like normal aircraft for much of their flight.

During Monday's visit, the two leaders also met more than 200 Ukrainian military personnel who have spent the last three weeks taking part in a maritime exercise in the UK.

Exercise Sea Breeze is aimed at strengthening warfighting capabilities and counter-mine measures in the Black Sea.

Burnham also said the UK would support Ukraine to get a "full and unconditional ceasefire".

"We will keep up the pressure, pushing for a ceasefire and a resumption of negotiations which must have Ukraine at the table and include a strong voice for Europe too."

Britain's backing of Ukraine has been constant since Russia's invasion four years ago, and the UK has committed £25bn in funding for the country's warfighting efforts.

In one of his first calls after becoming prime minister last Monday, Burnham spoke to Zelensky and invited him to visit the UK "at the earliest opportunity".

Zelensky wrote on X shortly afterwards: "I truly appreciate that the support for Ukraine and our people will remain steadfast."

Burnham's predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, visited Kyiv on his final full day as Labour leader.

During that trip, he announced fresh funding worth £255m (€300m) for Ukraine's fight against Russia and was awarded Ukraine's Order of Freedom.

Asked if he was concerned about changes of leadership in Britain, and in France next year, Zelensky said: "Of course I'm afraid of changes, of course we are afraid because we are in the war each day.

"But again the priority is the relation between nations, not just between just people. I'm sure that these relations will not change, or we have to do our best not to lose such very good relations."

He added: "I hope we will never lose strong relations with the UK during or after the war." Sir Keir replied: "You won't."

Teen denies endangering 165 lives on migrant boat

BBC News Mon, 27 Jul 2026 15:03:24 GMT

A teenager accused of endangering the lives of 165 migrants by allegedly piloting a record-breaking dinghy crossing of the English Channel is to stand trial.

Chan Mathok Atak, 19, originally of Sudan, appeared at Margate Magistrates Court earlier, where he denied endangering lives at sea during the attempt which set off from France last Thursday.

He appeared with the aid of an Arabic interpreter and when asked how he wished to plea, denied having piloted the dinghy.

Atak was then remanded into custody and will next appear at Canterbury Crown Court on 24 August.

Prosecutor Lucie Fish told the court that, on Thursday, a rigid hulled inflatable boat departed the French coast headed towards Dover carrying the migrants.

The vessel was intercepted by Border Force and Atak is alleged to be one of two people controlling its speed and travel.

The boat was poor quality, overcrowded and "appeared to be deflating upon interception", the prosecutor added.

Pictures of Border Security Command towing the dinghy into Dover showed to be about the same size as a standard bus, at 13m (42ft) long.

During the hearing, the court heard that the French authorities had recovered the body of a man who had suffered head injuries - but there was no indication in court whether his death was related to the record-breaking dinghy.

A spokesman for the National Crime Agency told BBC News: "We are aware of an incident on Thursday 23 July in which an individual died in French waters. French partners are leading the investigation into the circumstances".

Endangerment at sea is a new offence that was created by the government under Sir Keir Starmer to target those alleged to have steered small boats over the English Channel.

In June, two men were the first to be jailed for the crime, each receiving sentences of more than two years.

The previous record arrival in a single vessel was 128 people.

Home Office figures show that while the overall number of arrivals this year is down by about 45% on 2025, the number of migrants per boat has gone up.

Four options for tackling social care

BBC News Mon, 27 Jul 2026 14:45:01 GMT

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he would not want to leave office without bringing in "substantial change" to the social care system in England which provides support for older people and working-age adults with disabilities.

The social care system - which is mostly provided by companies rather than directly by the state - is widely perceived as underfunded and unfair.

It is estimated by Age UK there are two million older people in England now living with some unmet need for social care.

At the moment funding for somebody getting care in their own home is means tested - so they may qualify for local council funding based on their income and savings. The value of their home is not taken into account.

For residential care though the value of a person's home is generally part of the means test. People with assets above £23,250 are normally expected to pay the full cost of their care.

There have been multiple attempts by governments to reform the system over the past 16 years - none of which have come to fruition because of arguments about how they will be paid for.

BBC Verify has looked at four options for approaching reform and how much they could cost.

Some people face extremely high costs for care at the end of their life.

It has been estimated that around one in seven people aged 65 and over face lifetime care costs of more than £100,000.

One proposal is to cap these costs with the government picking up the bill above a certain cash threshold.

In 2011 a commission headed by the economist Andrew Dilnot proposed a lifetime cap of £35,000.

Dilnot estimated his proposed reforms would cost between £1.3bn and £2.2bn a year. The cost today would be higher due to inflation and the ageing population.

The Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government, led by David Cameron, accepted Dilnot's recommendations.

But after the 2015 general election, which delivered a Conservative majority, Cameron delayed the implementation of the cap to 2020 over what he said were pressures on the public finances.

In 2017, when Theresa May was in No 10, the Conservatives' general election manifesto proposed a different way to reform social care.

This would have included the value of an individual's home in the means test used to decide what state funding they could get for care in their own homes.

It did not, initially, include any cap on lifetime care costs, with the manifesto saying this was more "equitable" than the Dilnot plan.

The May plan was branded a "dementia tax" by opponents and eventually dropped.

In England people can currently qualify for local authority financial support in a residential care home if all their assets - including their home - are worth less than £23,250.

This is known as a means test - where the level of financial support a person gets is based on the value of their assets and savings.

Some have suggested this threshold should be raised significantly so that many more people would qualify for means-tested support.

Boris Johnson's Conservative government in 2021 planned to raise the means test threshold to £100,000.

The annual cost of Johnson's reforms would have been £1.8bn a year over three years - although this was expected to rise over time as more people qualified.

The Johnson government planned a new Health and Social Care levy to pay for the package, but this was eventually scrapped by his Conservative successors as prime minister, because they wanted to keep taxes down.

An alternative approach is to ensure that everyone who is eligible, based on their needs, should get state-funded personal care that is free at the point of use.

This would be provided free regardless of an individual's means and whether it was received by an elderly person in their own house or a residential care home.

Scotland has implemented such a system.

However, it's important to note that personal care takes in things like helping frail elderly people wash and dress and go to the toilet.

But it does not include accommodation, food and everyday living costs which are subject to means testing.

The Health Foundation think tank estimates that implementing a Scottish-style system in England would cost £7.5bn a year by 2036.

Like Scotland, Japan and Germany have systems which base entitlement to personal social care mainly on people's care needs rather than their ability to pay.

Japan and Germany though have a mandatory long-term care insurance system which is funded through contributions from workers and employers.

Both countries also do not usually cover the full cost of personal care so individuals are responsible for some of the expenses.

Some have suggested that the government should set up a national care service in England, similar in ambition to the NHS.

This would mean all personal care would be free at the point of use while establishing national standards and care entitlement criteria.

The Health Foundation has estimated the cost of creating a universal and comprehensive social care system in England would be around £19bn a year extra by 2036.

When Andy Burnham was health secretary in Gordon Brown's Labour government in 2010 he produced a plan for a national care service.

It was suggested this would be paid for through a compulsory contribution from people's estates after they'd died.

But the idea was branded a "death tax" by Labour's opponents. The party lost the 2010 general election and its proposals went no further.

In the 2024 general election Labour again proposed a "national care service" without providing details or how it would be funded.

And after the election then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer effectively kicked the issue into the long grass by commissioning Louise Casey to investigate social care reform and report back in 2028.

It's worth bearing in mind that these four approaches above are not mutually exclusive.

Previous reform proposals have often combined more than one of them - such as a cap on lifetime costs and a more generous means test.

'Give him his passport' - Hearn backs British champion's citizenship fight

BBC News Mon, 27 Jul 2026 14:07:32 GMT

This video can not be played

'I feel pain' - the British champion with no British passport

The UK government should be "embarrassed" that boxing champion Bilal Fawaz does not have a British passport after living in the country for more than 20 years, says his promoter Eddie Hearn.

Fawaz, 38, was trafficked to the United Kingdom at the age of 14 and has not travelled outside the country since.

The London-based light-middleweight represented England as an amateur before turning professional after receiving a work permit.

He has since become British and Commonwealth champion, but his immigration status prevents him from fighting abroad - or taking his family on holiday.

"What on earth is the hold-up?" asked Hearn.

"You want to go down to Number 10 [Downing Street] and bang on the door and say: 'Any chance of dealing with this?' It's the most ridiculous thing I've ever heard.

"If you were them, you'd almost be embarrassed. Someone should look at it and go, 'What are you guys doing? Give him his passport.'"

A Home Office spokesperson told BBC Sport it does not routinely comment on individual cases.

Fawaz's remarkable story is explored in the new BBC documentary Fighting for Freedom, which followed him as he prepared to defend his British title against Ryan Kelly in Wolverhampton in May.

Bilal Fawaz (right) beat Ryan Kelly in Wolverhampton in May to defend his British and Commonwealth titles

Fighting For Freedom - Bilal Fawaz

Fawaz was trafficked to the United Kingdom aged 14 and held in conditions that amounted to modern slavery

Born in Nigeria to a Beninese mother and Lebanese father, Fawaz says his childhood was shaped by abuse, neglect and a persistent feeling he did not belong.

He was sent to live with relatives before being taken to London, believing he would be reunited with his father. Instead, he claims he was confined in a house, forced to work and prevented from attending school or mixing with other children.

"My best friend was the window," he says. "I could see people walking and kids outside playing, but I wasn't allowed to play with them."

After escaping, he entered the care system and received convictions for minor offences - including cannabis possession and graffiti - during his youth. Fawaz says he was a vulnerable teenager who needed guidance rather than punishment.

"I've never robbed anything," he says. "I've never beaten anyone up. I've never done anything that's atrocious.

"I was just a kid who needed guidance and I never had that. Somebody should have taken care of me and fixed my whole life before I turned 18."

Fawaz found stability at the All Stars Boxing Club in west London. He became an English amateur champion and represented England six times, but was unable to pursue Olympic qualification or accept professional contracts because he did not have permission to work or travel.

He was twice held in immigration detention and threatened with deportation before a judge ruled there were no lawful grounds to detain him. He was released and found himself effectively stateless.

Fawaz has won 12 fights, with one defeat and one draw, since turning professional in 2022

Fawaz received a work permit at the age of 33, by which point many professional fighters are approaching retirement.

After turning professional he made up for lost time by beating Junaid Bostan to win the English light-middleweight title, then defeating Ishmael Davis to become British and Commonwealth champion.

"Boxing saved me," he says. "It's my addiction. Boxing gave me the feeling that I deserve more. I've worked hard. When will I get the dues and respect that I deserve?"

The documentary follows Fawaz inside the gym and at home with his family, as well as on the dancefloor during one of his regular salsa sessions.

It also explores how his childhood has shaped him as a father.

"The only way I can fill the void is by being there for my family and my sons," he says. "That's healing."

Fawaz has a British partner and British children, but says he continues to feel as though the authorities do not recognise his contribution to the country.

"I am in prison," he says. "I've been in this country for 24 beautiful years and I've never travelled. I was being used. 'Fight for us... but you're not British'. I fought for them six times as an amateur. I was bleeding in the ring.

"They don't view me as important or someone who is trying to make an honest living. I am a Commonwealth champion who can never take my belt to another country."

Fawaz is not able to travel abroad for lucrative fights or sparring opportunities

Fawaz is on a 10-year 'route to settlement' and will be 43 before becoming eligible for British citizenship.

Under this route, people must complete 10 years of lawful residence before applying for indefinite leave to remain. The granting of that status allows them to stay in the UK without immigration restrictions.

British citizenship can then be applied for - if relevant requirements are met.

The UK has shorter settlement routes, including five-year routes available to people who meet the requirements of certain immigration categories.

The route someone follows depends on the basis of their immigration status and their individual circumstances, including factors such as family life, work, length of residence and private life in the UK.

It is not clear whether the 10-year route was the only option available to Fawaz or why that route applied in his case.

The Home Office previously said the decision to place Fawaz on a 10-year route to settlement was not made by the department.

Without a passport, Fawaz cannot accept potentially lucrative fights in countries such as Saudi Arabia or the United States. He can, however, take up such opportunities in the UK.

He believes he could already have become a world champion had he received a passport in his early 20s.

"The government are denying him that opportunity, which is so wrong," says Hearn, who would also stand to benefit from being able to get Fawaz fights overseas.

"I could get him a big fight in America. I could get him a fight in Saudi. This is a story that resonates in any part of the world. How can you not be allowed to travel?"

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, you can visit BBC Action Line.

Carly Simon reveals Parkinson's diagnosis

BBC News Mon, 27 Jul 2026 14:04:01 GMT

The singer-songwriter Carly Simon says she has been diagnosed with Parkinson's and is "learning how to live" with the "sometimes frightening" condition.

In a statement provided to the BBC, the 83-year-old described the "unpredictable" progress of the disease, saying: "Some days I'm so tired I can't get the day moving at all. On others, it gives me a little more room to move, think, work, and feel like myself.

"But I have not stopped living, and I have not stopped working," said the singer, best known for songs like You're So Vain, Why, and Coming Around Again.

Simon added that she had recently received surgery to remove a cancerous growth on her face that had "affected my appearance".

The surgery "made me more self-conscious about being seen in public," she added.

"I have always been more critical of my appearance than anyone else could possibly imagine (check out the irony of having written You're So Vain), and this gave my inner critic quite a lot of new material."

Parkinson's is a progressive disorder that affects the brain, nervous system, and muscle control.

It is the fastest growing neurological condition in the world, with about 153,000 people in the UK living with the condition.

Simon said her problems began with arthritis in both knees and one of her hips. However, her mobility failed to improve after three replacement surgeries.

"I had trouble standing up from low chairs and deep couches without someone offering me an arm," she said.

"Overstuffed furniture became my enemy. Once seated, I could feel as though I had been swallowed by the chair and might remain there permanently, like a guest who had badly overstayed her welcome.

"Eventually, there were periods when I could not walk without considerable help. My family and I knew that something more was going on. After an extensive evaluation at the Mayo Clinic, I was diagnosed with Parkinson's."

The musician has been receiving medication and treatment; but says the condition also comes with episodes of anxiety, depression, and apathy.

"The apathy is particularly strange," she observed.

"You can find yourself lying there like a starfish drying in the sun, arms pointing in all directions, while nothing inside is telling you to get up, read, watch, write, sing, call someone, or do much of anything at all.

"That has been one of the hardest things to explain. It is not simply sadness or laziness. It is as though the part of the brain that sends out invitations to participate in life has temporarily misplaced the guest list."

Simon said she had decided to speak about her diagnosis after she received letters, "kindly wondering about my relative silence, asking how I am and what I have been doing."

Despite her health condition, the musician recently announced a new album - Comes In Waves - which will be released in August 2026.

The first single, Howl, was released last month. It finds the singer consoling a friend who has just been through a break-up.

"Howl like the wind, roar like the river / Wail like the rain, cry, shout, and shiver," she advises, her tawny, contralto voice instantly recognisable.

A press release said the album would see Simon revisiting familiar themes such as "love, memory, family, self-reckoning, and forgiveness, while allowing space for contradiction, ambiguity, and emotional evolution."

One of the most recognisable singer-songwriters of the 1970s, Simon was known for her emotionally honest, piano-led pop anthems, and intricate character studies.

Among her most beloved songs are the Bond theme Nobody Does It Better and Legend In Your Own Time, a withering portrait of an arrogant man.

The latter was something of a dry run for the scathing You're So Vain - written about actor Warren Beatty (and two other men) .

In 2003, she auctioned off the subjects' true identity for $50,000 (£38,000) - on the condition that the winner continued to keep the secret.

In the statement confirming her Parkinson's diagnosis, Simon said she did not consider the condition "a gift or a blessing".

"It is neither," she wrote. "It is difficult, frustrating, and sometimes frightening. I am still learning how to live with it and how to accept it without feeling that I have surrendered something essential.

"I am still writing, singing, imagining, laughing, worrying, remembering, and occasionally getting trapped in an overstuffed chair.

She continued: "I am deeply grateful to my children, my family, my friends, my caregivers, and the medical professionals who have helped me through this. Their love and patience have carried me through days when my own reserves were not enough.

"These days I move more slowly, I lean on others more than I once did, and I have learned to accept that every day will look a little different.

"But I am still very much here."

How wildfires in France and Spain might affect your travel plans

BBC News Mon, 27 Jul 2026 13:21:49 GMT

Wildfires in Spain and France have caused mass evacuation and disruption, with more than 300,000 people forced to leave their homes and many sleeping in sports halls and other temporary shelters.

An official from one of the French departments affected by the fires has pleaded with visitors to stay away.

On Sunday, Sophie Brocas, prefect of the French department of Gironde, said, "I urge tourists not to come," while advising those already there to consider an alternative destination.

For those who have upcoming holidays to the affected regions, here is what you should know about how it might impact your plans.

The UK government has not specifically warned against travel to anywhere in France or Spain, but it does advise caution.

In France, it says access to affected areas may be restricted and roads may close at short notice. It adds that further evacuations may take place.

It has also issued a general warning about the high risk of wildfires in France during the summer season from April to October.

For those in an affected area in France or Spain or planning to travel there, the UK government recommends following instructions and updates from local authorities and emergency services at all times.

Those needing emergency help in France or Spain can call 112.

Travellers should also bear in mind the UK government's advice can and does change in response to moving events.

Anna-Marie Duthie, travel insurance expert at financial rating firm Defaqto, says that if this happens after you have booked your trip, "you may be covered for cancellation or curtailment".

"You may also be covered for additional travel and accommodation costs should your trip be disrupted due to a catastrophic event, if your insurer offers this cover or you've paid to include it," she adds.

To know if this applies to you, check your policy.

The UK government says parts of Gironde and Landes in the south west of France are affected.

The official French wildfire map gives Gironde and Pyrénées-Orientales its highest fire alert level. Meanwhile, Aude and Var have its second highest alert level.

As of Monday, the map says there are more than 20 fires burning across the country, including on Corsica.

In Spain, authorities have declared a national emergency because of wildfires in parts of Madrid and Ávila. The UK government says there are also reports of wildfires in other inland areas of Spain.

Once again, the answer depends on your policy.

"If your travel plans are disrupted by a wildfire and your policy includes trip disruption cover then travel insurance may cover some of the resulting costs," says Chris Bose, director of general insurance policy at the Association of British Insurers (ABI).

However, only half of travel insurance policies have "catastrophe" cover, according to analysis from Defaqto.

This means that, in many cases, travellers might not be covered by their insurance in the case of wildfires.

To know if this does or does not apply to you, speak to your insurer or check the wording of your policy.

In the case of cancelled flights or accommodation, Bose recommends seeking refunds from your airline, tour operator or accommodation provider in the first instance.

Duthie says if your airline cancels your flight due to wildfires then "they should offer you the chance to rebook, or provide a full refund".

She says if your holiday was booked as a package then this refund should cover "all elements", including flights, accommodation and transfers.

"But if you've booked everything separately, you'll need to deal with each provider independently. Your airline may refund your flight, but your accommodation provider may not if the property is unaffected."

Check what your insurance policy says about flights, accommodation or trip bookings first.

Rory Boland, editor of Which? Travel, says this is especially true for those not due to travel in the next week or two.

"Travellers who cancel now will likely forfeit their right to a refund or rebooking," he says.

As the UK government has not warned against travel to anywhere in the two countries, he says travellers are "unlikely to be able to claim on their travel insurance".

"As a rule, insurance firms won't make allowances for 'disinclination to travel'," Boland says.

"Instead, holidaymakers should wait until closer to the departure date to see if the holiday can go ahead or what flexible booking options are offered from the tour operator or airline.

"Travel companies will be prioritising anyone due to depart in the next couple of days."

The amount of land burned by wildfires across Europe has increased by 57% since summer 2022, according to the World Health Organization.

It adds that climate change is intensifying wildfires and increasing their frequency.

Duthie says insurance firms are adapting to "potential new and increasing risks involved in travel as a result".

In the near term, she says it is unlikely insurance providers will change their policies.

"Current clauses may refer to 'severe' or 'extreme' weather, but the definitions for these can vary and currently no providers go as far as to specify criteria such as maximum temperatures."

However, she says that "longer term there is a chance that we may end up seeing less insurable destinations and increased premiums".

TV presenter and comedian Bill Oddie dies at 85

BBC News Mon, 27 Jul 2026 12:47:47 GMT

TV presenter and comedian Bill Oddie has died at the age of 85, his agent has said.

Oddie became a household name in the 1970s as part of zany TV comedy trio The Goodies, before concentrating on his love of wildlife, as one of the original hosts of BBC TV's Springwatch and other shows about birdwatching.

In a statement, David Foster said: "It is with deep sadness that I announce the passing of Bill Oddie, the country's best-loved birder.

"Bill was a multi-talented celebrity – wildlife presenter, broadcaster, comedian, writer, songwriter, musician and conservationist. Yet it was never fame that he valued. Instead he encouraged us to respect and protect the environment."

Foster continued that Oddie "taught us the wonder of" the environment. "He protested, lobbied and campaigned for it.

"He led the way and people of all ages and backgrounds responded to his call. And such a massive contribution to conservation will never be forgotten.

"As Bill's agent I witnessed close hand his intelligence and wit. He was my friend and it was an honour and a privilege to represent him for so many years. I will miss him terribly."

Paying tribute, Oddie's former Springwatch co-host Kate Humble told BBC Radio 4's The World At One: "No-one could tell a story like Bill. No-one could make me laugh like Bill. No-one could enthuse anyone, whoever they were, to go outside and get excited about a robin.

"He just had that way of just making the natural world everybody's world, and I think that's what we all loved about him."

Oddie had many other interests and talents, she said. "He was so interested in so many things. He wasn't just the nerdy birder, or the funny, slightly irascible comedian, or the brilliant musician. He was all of those things. And he was always interested in everything."

She added: "Sometimes he'd be fantastically grumpy and would be the last person I'd want to see first thing in the morning, and other times he would just be the best company in the world, and he talked very openly about his struggles with mental health."

Chris Packham, Oddie's successor on Springwatch, wrote on social media: "Sadly we've not only lost a goodie, we've lost one of the besties."

In his tribute, Packham said: "A renegade polymath with binoculars and a beard, Bill was invariably funny and occasionally furious. He loved birds and loathed those who harmed them. He was delightfully unpredictable, sparky, smart and at times a bit spiky.

"Critically he really knew his stuff, and his passion was true - he didn't just pick up his binoculars on telly, he went birding whenever he could. So he was genuine and that's why we loved him."

Oddie was born in Rochdale, near Manchester, and grew up in Birmingham before attending Cambridge University, where he was a member of the illustrious Footlights comedy troupe.

Before graduating, he was already writing for shows like satirical TV series That Was The Week That Was in the early 1960s.

He went on to write and appear on programmes including I'm Sorry I'll Read That Again, At Last the 1948 Show, Twice a Fortnight and Doctor in The House.

Often, he starred and wrote alongside other up-and-coming comedy names like Monty Python's John Cleese, Michael Palin and Terry Jones, and his fellow future Goodies - Tim Brooke-Taylor and Graeme Garden.

Python star Eric Idle said he was "very sad" about the loss of Oddie.

"We watched England win the World Cup together at Wembley in '66. He was a very fine songwriter and I learned a lot from him," he wrote on X.

The Goodies got their own series in 1970, and the trio's slapstick comedy and madcap songs entertained millions of viewers for 12 years.

Oddie was "known as the hairy, cynical, anarchist member" of the group, the BFI said, and his contribution also included writing novelty songs like The Funky Gibbon and The Inbetweenies, which both reached the UK top 10.

The Goodies also worked together in the 80s on sci-fi comedy Astronauts and children's TV show Bananaman, and Oddie also appeared in popular kids' shows Tickle on the Tum, From the Top and The Bubblegum Brigade.

He turned his attention to his other great love, wildlife and ornithology, in BBC series including Birding with Bill Oddie, Britain Goes Wild with Bill Oddie, and Bill Oddie's How to Watch Wildlife.

Oddie was made an OBE in 2003 for services to wildlife conservation.

He co-presented the first four series of the BBC's annual Springwatch from 2005, as well as spin-off Autumnwatch.

But after being dropped in 2009, he said he suffered "probably the worst 12 months of my life" due to his struggle with depression and bipolar disorder.

Humble praised Oddie for being one of the first celebrities to speak openly in public about his mental health struggles.

"He was one of the earliest, bravest people to say, 'No, this is something that I have, and this is something that I have to deal with, and my family has to deal with,' and it was really tough for him," she said.

"I was witness to that, but he was always very honest and straightforward and in the end, as I say, there was no-one who could make me laugh like Bill."

Others paying tribute included actor and avid birdwatcher Samuel West, who wrote on X about the impact of watching Birding With Bill Oddie.

"Bill Oddie wore a great learning lightly, but he could never hide his enthusiasm," West said.

"His captivated, always improvised narration made that show the platonic ideal of natural history for me, and introduced a whole generation to the fascination of birds."

Naturalist and author Stephen Moss posted that Oddie "did more than anyone to popularise birding".

"Very sad news of the death of Bill Oddie: birder, comedian, musician, artist and environmental campaigner, and dear friend and colleague to me and many others," Moss wrote.

Oddie was a former vice president of the RSPCA, and the animal charity's current chief executive Jo Rowland said: "I know many of our wildlife rescuers were inspired into animal welfare by Bill's groundbreaking broadcasting work and incredible knowledge of British birds, which brought the wonders of nature into millions of homes across the country.

"Nature has lost one of its best friends, fiercest champions and most iconic defenders.

"Our thoughts are with his family, friends, and the countless people he inspired to spend time birdwatching, to cherish nature, and to build a kinder world for animals."

Reading FC also posted a tribute: "A guest of honour at many matches down the years, he became a much-loved figure at the club.

"Bill's legacy will live on through his iconic chant among Royals supporters at the SCL Stadium and around the country for many years to come."

Oddie was married to children's TV writer and artist Laura Beaumont. They have a daughter, Rosie, while Oddie and his first wife - singer and actress Jean Hart - had two daughters, Bonnie and Kate.

Anger as Berlin Pride attacker revealed to have been freed weeks earlier

BBC News Mon, 27 Jul 2026 12:33:31 GMT

In Germany there is grief, shock and, increasingly, anger about the attack at Berlin Pride on Saturday night which left one Polish woman dead and injured at least 29 others.

The main suspect, Abdul Ballout, a 21-year-old German citizen with Lebanese heritage, was shot and killed by police on Sunday.

Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Ballout "had previously drawn attention to himself through a high volume of criminal offences, radicalisation and affiliation with the Islamist scene."

As details emerge about his criminal convictions, many are asking why Ballout was not in prison.

Prosecutors say that in 2025, Ballout decided to try to join Islamic State group's armed struggle in Syria, travelling via Turkey to Lebanon. In Lebanon, they say, he met several people he believed were members of IS.

He was arrested in Lebanon in July 2025 and sentenced to three months in prison for incitement to religious and sectarian conflict.

Then in November 2025 he returned to Germany, where he was arrested at Berlin Brandenburg Airport and held in pre-trial detention.

In May this year, a Berlin court sentenced Ballout to a juvenile sentence of one year and ten months, for "preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state".

The sentence was suspended while prosecutors appealed against the verdict, calling for a longer sentence.

Ballout was released and placed under the supervision of a probation officer.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told RTL that the decision to impose a suspended sentence was "certainly incomprehensible... given the level of danger involved in this case".

He said the authorities were investigating how that happened.

Berlin's Governing Mayor, Kai Wegner from the centre-right Christian Democrat party (CDU), said he was dumbstruck at the way the Berlin judiciary had handled Ballout's case.

"He was sentenced... under juvenile criminal law," he told RBB TV. "And then, unfortunately, the court handed down a suspended sentence. I don't want to pass judgement on that – that's the independence of the judiciary – but I'm really at a loss for words."

The opposition far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party described the attack as a total failure of security policy.

"If an Islamist threat known to the police was able to carry out such an act, a thorough investigation must be carried out to establish why he was still able to move about freely in the first place," said Martin Hess, the AfD's home affairs spokesperson.

According to Der Spiegel, Ballout told the Berlin court this spring that he had distanced himself from extremist ideology and violence.

Thomas Mücke, an extremism expert at the Violence Prevention Network VPN, told ARD television that he had met the suspect.

He said Ballout had given social workers "a very composed, very cautious, very controlled and very friendly impression".

"And those are precisely the criteria where we realise we can't really get to know the person," he continued.

Some have called for Germany's laws against terrorism to be made stricter.

Peter Neumann at King's College London told ZDF that Germany's criminal law on terrorism is "too lenient," and sentences too short by European standards.

He also called for a rethink of Germany's juvenile justice system, which he said prioritises education rather than the protection of the public.

The home affairs spokesperson for the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD), Sebastian Fiedler, told Deutschlandfunk radio that criminal law was not the problem, but the way it was applied.

"We need to look more closely at why [Ballout] still at large. Another key question is: 'What actually happened after his release from prison? Who was he still in contact with?' Although he was under surveillance, there was clearly a gap in the system."

Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz said it was too early to say what political consequences will be drawn from the attack, but promised there would be action: "We will have to respond with prudence, but also with determination."

He said if individuals classified as threats could not be detained, their freedom of movement should be restricted "as much as possible."

"I cannot understand how I can track my mobile phone from anywhere in the world... yet it is supposedly impossible, or technically unfeasible, for security authorities in Germany to determine the whereabouts of individuals classified as security threats to that same extent."

He said he had asked the interior ministry to review the law regarding monitoring jurisdiction.

BBC News Mon, 27 Jul 2026 12:04:15 GMT

What began as a chance encounter on a flight to Las Vegas could soon be heading to the big screen, as a group of grandmothers and a pro-wrestler discuss a film based on their story.

Lynn Crawford, 71, Susie Matthews, 73, Rose Sulley, 74, and Christine Goodwin, 80, met DeReiss Gordon - known in the ring as Man Like DeReiss - on the flight in April.

They were travelling to the city to scatter the ashes of Rose's late husband, Pete. Upon boarding the flight, there was confusion - with Gordon in one of the seats they mistakenly believed they had booked - before a friendship was formed, and the nans took Gordon up on his offer to watch him at WrestleMania.

Film producer Nick Barton said he believes this "extraordinary story could make a really brilliant and successful movie".

"When I first heard about this story in May, it reminded me of Calendar Girls and Kinky Boots, which Harbour Pictures and I produced for Disney and Buena Vista.

People were holding banners with their photos chanting "Nanas! Nanas!".

This unlikely friendship has created something of a fan base in the wrestling world.

"It was absolutely hilarious", Sulley said.

The four women admitted they knew "nothing" about wrestling before meeting Gordon earlier this year.

Recalling what it was like to meet the group for the first time, Gordon said he was "completely outnumbered" by the nans from Cardiff.

As well as getting the nans into the ring, the group took an open-top bus tour of Cardiff, and had a night of bingo.

Going forward, Gordon said he hopes to keep any "angry Welsh nana's" on his side of the wrestling ring, adding that the group of four were "natural performers".

Reflecting on the friendship, Goodwin said "all of this goes to show if something comes your way just grab it with both hands".

Matthews said: "I worked in an old people's home and I used to say then, that's not gonna be me sat in that chair thinking I wished I'd have done this and wished I'd have done that.

"Thank God I'm lucky enough to say I did it, and I'm hopefully gonna do a lot more."

Gordon added: "We're all human, we all have blood inside us and if you speak to the person next to you, you never know what you have in common, what you might share."

UK's iconic Jodrell Bank telescope faces axe in science cuts

BBC News Mon, 27 Jul 2026 11:50:13 GMT

The Jodrell Bank Observatory, which has housed the UK's largest telescope for nearly 70 years, has lost its funding and could now close, the BBC understands.

The observatory and its network of telescopes have been pivotal to the country's study of distant galaxies and training future astronomers. Scientists have described the decision as "heartbreaking" and "scientifically misguided".

All scientific observations at Jodrell are expected to cease on the 1 April 2028 unless alternative funding can be found.

The funding body, the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) agency, said it had to focus investment on projects that deliver "the greatest long-term impact".

Prof Brian Cox, professor of particle physics at the University of Manchester - which hosts Jodrell Bank Observatory - described the cuts as "hasty and ill-considered".

"The damage to the UK's science base has already been substantial. I am astonished that UKRI are still ploughing ahead and not working with the Burnham government to find a solution," he said.

In response, Jonathan Reynolds, who is the new Secretary of State in the expanded business department that now has responsibility for science, told BBC News that the UK's world class research was "absolutely central to creating a better future for the UK".

"I am committed to working with UKRI to ensure the UK remains able not only to sustain its world-leading research capabilities, but also to invest in the next generation of scientific facilities and infrastructure that will underpin discovery, innovation and growth in the years ahead."

The Jodrell Bank site was first established in 1945 and pioneered radio astronomy and the study of galaxies beyond our own.

It was also pivotal during the Cold War, when it was used to monitor Soviet missiles during the height of nuclear tensions between the USSR and Nato powers.

Its contribution to global scientific efforts earned it Unesco World Heritage status in 2019.

But the UKRI, which has an annual budget of just under £10bn, says it has had to cut the observatory's annual £2.8m budget because planned research costs for physics and the running of its labs had escalated.

The announcement is part of broader cuts to astronomy, nuclear and particle physics research over the next four years which will also impact on other projects.

The UK will no longer participate in research at the James Clark Maxwell Telescope in Hawaii, which scientists are using to image supermassive black holes at the centre of galaxies.

UKRI has also cut funding for the UK's involvement in two instruments on the Extremely Large Telescope which is being built in Chile to search for signs of life on other Earth-like worlds.

And a number of upgrades to improve experiments at the Large Hadron Collider will not be paid for by the agency.

Twenty-eight jobs are at risk at the Jodrell Bank site in Cheshire, but its closure would also affect the work of nearly 3,000 scientists who use it in their research.

Prof Simon Garrington, associate director of the Jodrell Bank Observatory, told BBC News that everyone at Jodrell Bank was "devastated" by the decision.

"It's not just because of the fantastic science that we do, but Jodrell Bank and its telescope network [have been] a national capability for nearly 70 years and a beacon for science in the north-west [of England], attracting young people into science and engineering careers," he said.

The importance of the site to science and the community has seen it immortalised in popular science fiction works from the Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy to Doctor Who.

Prof Garrington said the UKRI's decision would be challenged, but added that if those discussions failed the leadership team would do all it could to find alternative funding to keep the iconic Lovell Telescope, which is at the heart of the observatory and the network of telescopes it supports, continuing in some form.

"It is a huge hill to climb to try to establish a new way to fund this if UKRI will not fund any of it," he said.

Scotland's Astronomer Royal, Prof Catherine Heymans, who was speaking for the UK's community of astronomers, described the decision by UKRI as "a real act of national self-harm".

Despite its age, continuous upgrades have kept the Lovell telescope at the cutting edge of astronomical research.

It is the third largest steerable radio telescope in the world, and its science was supercharged when it was connected to six other telescopes across central England, to create the e-Merlin network.

Joined together these UK telescopes can zoom into objects in deep space and see them in incredible detail - with similar resolution to the Hubble space telescope.

The e-Merlin network is being used for research into:

The e-Merlin network is part of a pan-European network of telescopes - without it, images of distant stars and galaxies will be less clear.

Prof Michael Kramer, is executive director of the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy in Bonn, and a highly respected scientist at the University of Manchester.

He told BBC News that he believed the decision by UKRI to be "scientifically, technologically as well as economically short-sighted".

But another important role of Jodrell Bank Observatory is training UK astronomers in the science of radio astronomy. Astronomers have claimed that the closure of Lovell and the e-Merlin network will mean that Britain will fall behind in a field that was pioneered at Jodrell Bank.

"Internationally, people will look at that and will hardly believe it. You're cutting off the radio astronomy capability in the country," Prof Kramer said.

The cut comes at a time when other countries are investing in their own national observatories to prepare for, what many astronomers believe will be, the dawn of a golden age in radio astronomy. This is because of the construction of a new super radio telescope in South Africa and Australia called the Square Kilometre Array (SKA).

SKA is due to start to come online in five years and in 10 years begin to answer some of the biggest questions in astronomy.

But having been one of the leaders in the field for decades, the UK now risks missing out on this scientific bonanza, according to Prof Philip Diamond, a former head of Jodrell Bank as well as the SKA organisation.

"It's removing the science capability which is essential for the long-term health of UK radio astronomy and the SKA, so it would have severe impact on the training and career of young researchers."

A portrait of the pop star Charli XCX has been added to the National Portrait Gallery's collection - the same week she is aiming for her second number one album of the year.

If its sales hold up, it would become Charli's fourth UK number one overall, and her second this year, after the soundtrack to Wuthering Heights topped the chart in February.

"I made b-sides for each of the songs released ahead of Music, Fashion, Film because it felt natural to pair each songs with a fitting counterpart – something that's adjacent to the album but not entirely part of it," she wrote on Instagram.

"Traditionally, b sides often become fan favourites… and I guess in the case of some of the b sides for this album, that has proven to be true.

"I felt adamant I wouldn't put them on streaming because it sort of felt counter intuitive to the whole ethos of those songs, but I know you all really wanted them so I've begrudgingly put them on iTunes lol."

Fans will get to hear the new material live when Charli headlines the Reading & Leeds festival next month.

Amber heat health alerts have been issued for much of eastern England for later this week as temperatures rise again.

But southern parts of the country - where the least amount of rain has fallen - are set to see temperatures climb once again, with more dry and sunny weather in the forecast.

It comes as parts of Wales have officially entered drought status, while parts of southern, central and eastern England remain in "prolonged dry weather", the final stage before drought is declared.

The coming days will only exacerbate dry conditions as another heatwave is expected to be declared, with temperatures peaking around 34-35C (93-95F) in south-east England or the East of England.

How 'fire-generated thunderstorms' make wildfires more deadly

BBC News Mon, 27 Jul 2026 11:11:07 GMT

Tens of thousands of people have been evacuated from Bordeaux's surrounding region of Gironde, as France continues to fight against wildfires being stoked by an unprecedented "pyrocumulonimbus" or fire clouds.

Scientists sometimes describe these clouds as a fire-generated thunderstorm because the fire itself provides the energy needed to build the cloud.

The huge amount of heat generated by wildfires makes the air above the fire rise rapidly, carrying smoke, ash and water vapour high into the atmosphere.

As the air rises, it cools and the water vapour condenses into a cloud.

If the fire is powerful enough and the atmosphere is unstable, that cloud can grow into a towering cumulonimbus - the same type of cloud associated with thunderstorms.

Turbulent winds created by the fire clouds can send embers shooting off in all directions, making wildfires unpredictable and harder to fight. Lightning strikes can also spark more blazes.

French firefighting authorities have blamed the phenomenon for the blazes near Bordeaux, adding that it had never before been seen in the country.

Across Europe, the summer months have sweltered through intense, record-breaking heatwaves with minimal rain. This has meant regions have become dry and susceptible to wildfires which have been sparked in France, Spain and the UK.

On Monday the Gironde prefecture said the situation remained "broadly stable" overnight.

But efforts to tackle the blaze could get further complicated with another heatwave forecast later this week with highs of up to 40C (104F) predicted in France this week.

The wildfire in Gironde will likely burn "for many weeks" and could take months to fully extinguish, a senior official involved in the response has warned.

Pyrocumulonimbus are more likely when there are extremely dangerous conditions such as high temperatures, strong winds and little moisture.

Scientists have predicted that climate change is likely to increase the chances of such events.

While once seen as fairly rare events, a similar example was seen during the 2019-2020 Black Summer bushfires in Australia, which created extreme "firestorms" that made its own weather.

The event was one of the most intense and catastrophic fire seasons for the country, with at least 33 people killed - including four firefighters - and more than 11 million hectares (110,000 sq km or 27.2 million acres) of bush, forest and parks across Australia burnt.

Fire officials in New South Wales reported that embers from the storm were landing 18 miles (30km) ahead of the front which was three times more than the usual distance.

At the time, Nasa described pyrocumulonimbus as "the fire-breathing dragon of clouds" as they funnelled a smoke-like chimney into the earth's atmosphere while hurling thunderbolts, wind and rain.

Similarly in California through the summer of 2021, the intense fires raging across the western United States generated pyrocumulonimbus.

Smoky clouds towered a mile (1.6km) and rose over the blaze in California and surrounding states.

California firefighting officials said at the time the season saw more than 7,300 wildfires burning across 1 million hectares (2.5 million acres) and at least three firefighters killed.

Why budding birders are flocking to Shazam-like apps to identify avians

BBC News Mon, 27 Jul 2026 07:53:30 GMT

Megan Szostak, 26, was always a "bird kid".

The urge to watch and appreciate the world around her - and avians flitting in and out of it - has been ingrained in her since childhood, when she was given her grandfather's binoculars after he died.

Armed with this and a field guide in her home of San Francisco, she set about identifying birds from an early age.

But in recent years, her birding toolbelt has expanded to include something far more modern - an app.

"I had friends who probably wouldn't describe themselves as birders, but more just curious about nature and the world around them, recommend it to me," Megan said.

She is one of many millions of people who have downloaded Merlin Bird ID, which claims to be able to identify almost any bird by its look, song or call.

"I think that it's been a really great tool that I've integrated into my birding routine," she said.

And whether down to heatwaves sending more people outdoors, or younger people delving into birding, these apps are booming in popularity.

Chief among them is Merlin Bird ID, which was developed by Cornell University's Lab of Ornithology.

It has been downloaded 12 million times in 2026 alone, according to director Jessie Barry - who says it has had 42 million downloads overall.

She says the app has come a long way since it first launched in the US in 2014, with machine learning systems which could identify 285 common bird species from photos.

A real feather in its cap at the time, but a decade or so on, and it can now identify 11,000 species of birds - around as many as exist in the world.

Barry put the development down to AI, as well as "an amazing community of global bird watchers who are able to submit their recordings" - meaning more data to train the tech.

Seasoned birdwatchers would be quick to say the app doesn't always get it right.

Some experts and charities have urged not to rely too much on Merlin, or other apps like it, especially to record official sightings.

Nonetheless, Cornell says its Sound ID tool has been used for 4.4 billion identifications.

Market intelligence firm Sensor Tower said other Bird ID apps have also been used more - such as Birda, which it says has had 31% more downloads this year.

These recent surges may in turn reflect the growing popularity of birdwatching among young people, with reports Gen Z birders have flocked to nature reserves.

"We have minimal demographic information, but we can definitely see the shift to younger audiences," said Barry.

"The folks who are sharing their experiences with Merlin, talking how they're just getting started birding for the first time, might be making references like 'well now that I'm 30, I'm a bird watcher'.

"It's been really fun to see younger folks jump in."

For Megan, having both audio and visual methods to ID birds in Merlin reflects the "inclusive and accessible" nature of birdwatching.

"A lot of people out there bird using their ears or their eyes," Megan said.

"You don't need to use all of your senses while you're birding, which is really amazing."

And while noting "fair" criticism that the app gets it wrong sometimes, Megan said it helped open up a hobby "people once thought was reserved for a very specific type of person with a specific set of knowledge".

As part of a Gen Z contingent whose appreciation for birding has surfaced on social media, Megan also shares her sightings on TikTok and Instagram.

"I honestly really enjoyed seeing those memories and creating these little videos, and I'm by no means a master videographer, but I do think my biggest strength with it is slowing down and noticing," Megan adds.

"I think that creating the videos honestly encourages me to do that more."

Merlin has often been called a "Shazam for birds" - likening it to Apple's app letting users identify a song playing using a phone's microphone.

But some fans felt it left room for more.

Sam Lewis, a 32-year-old software engineer living in Stockport, used Merlin for several years before he was inspired to build his own bird ID app, Lifer.

It lets people collect virtual cards for their catches, with backgrounds illustrated in hand-drawn watercolours by his partner Emily.

It borrows ideas from other games, with the cards changing based on the quality of the image or sound recording used to ID the bird - as well as its rarity.

Sam hopes to attract those who, like himself, felt the pangs of an infamous monster collecting game when using Merlin to ID and save their bird sightings.

"They are real-life Pokémon, really, if you think about it," he said.

Pokémon Go, still popular a decade on, prompted people to venture out to catch 'em all, with the added perk of it helping them stay fit - something Sam thinks this lends itself naturally to birding.

"I think it's getting out and about, but still having that gamified technical side to it," he said.

"People love the rarity and scarcity of stuff, like Pokémon cards, and there's rare birds out there that you can see and hear right now."

Sam hopes his idea can contribute more broadly to conservation efforts.

To combat fears using such apps may drive people to seek out some species when they shouldn't, Lifer hides precise locations of rare breeding birds on maps during sensitive periods.

Qualifying catches are also sent to the Global Biodiversity Information Facility, an international network which provides open access to data about all types of life.

And Barry tells the BBC the future plan for Merlin is to continue keeping it simple.

"We really want Merlin to be fun and easy to use, first and foremost, and have it be a place where you can jump in and think about your world of birds," she said.

"It's trying to be the best experience with the technology of a mobile device in your hand, but really encourage you to get outside, look at those birds and enjoy that experience with them."
