Let him roam, owner says: Chase the Christchurch celebrity cat

New Zealand Herald July 27, 2026

Chase is world famous in Christchurch, with his owner Nick White and fans keeping a Facebook page of the feline's escapades updated with sightings. Photo / Facebook

By RNZ Checkpoint

Wanted posters have sprung up around Christchurch for an explorer named Chase. But unlike your traditional “wanted” poster, this one is to tell people that it is okay for Chase to roam.

Chase is a cat.

With Chase attracting regular attention – and occasionally going missing – his owner Nick White resorted to posting the messages about town and starting a Facebook group for Chase, hoping to teach people how to look after the wandering cat’s best interests, with messages such as: “If I tell you I am hungry, do not believe me. If you meet me, please pat me and tell me to go home.”

The Facebook page Has Anybody Seen Chase? now attracts regular updates with paparazzi-like shots of the celebrity cat on his latest exploits. Sometimes in quite unexpected places.

White told Checkpoint: “About six months ago he all of a sudden hit his teenage years, and just left. And now he comes home exhausted and doesn’t really have any time for us anymore.”

“He disappeared about 10 o’clock this morning and we haven’t seen him all day. He comes and goes.”

Chase’s visits include a Mexican restaurant, Te Pae Christchurch Convention Centre, he has been seen trying to get into a hotel by Victoria Square, and wandering up and down the Bridge of Remembrance.

“I’m not sure if he’s actually aware of his fame,” White says. “He’s gained weight – he’s definitely gained fame weight, because I think his fans – despite the posters mentioned – have been feeding him, and he hangs around a lot of ice-cream shops.

“He sleeps upstairs in a whisky bar, apparently, which has been great – on Regent St.

“He likes to hit the streets on big rugby weekends or Saturday nights, and wander round getting pats and dropped kebabs, I think.”

While Chase “tends to go in one direction, toward the central city”, videos of black cats wandering through houses and yards, that do look like Chase, have also been sent in.

“Because he’s a pretty generic black cat, it’s difficult to tell,” White says.

But problems have arisen when, about seven or eight times, people have found Chase, thought he was lost and taken him with them.

The cat is now equipped with a distinctive orange high-vis collar, with the URL for his Facebook page embroidered on it: “We’re just trying to use the Facebook page as a GPS, so we know where he’s actually been,” White says.

“The longest he’s been away for is about 13 days, and we thought he’d been kidnapped or something.”

He once got stuck between two buildings in Cathedral Square, he’s been taken as far as Ferrymead and his owners have had to pick him up from vets.

Local vets know who Chase is, and regularly advise people who call them about the cat to leave him be. But sometimes people insist on delivering the cat to the vets’ care, White says, and he gets another call to pick him up.

“Which is terribly annoying – he just wants to go adventuring.”

If Chase can be left to his own devices – apart from pats and scratches – he’ll be fine wandering, and will keep bringing joy to those he meets, White says.

“He’s absolutely hanging out with some of the unhoused members of the community, and there are people who see him regularly on the way to work. We get a lot of people that just go into town to find him.”

Waiuku murder trial: Man denies murdering Judith Cunniffe in rural South Auckland

New Zealand Herald July 27, 2026

A man with name suppression appears in the High Court at Auckland after Judith Cunniffe was found dead inside a vehicle in Waiuku in April 2025. Photo / Michael Craig

Chicken hoarding and methamphetamine abuse appeared to have played roles in a rural South Auckland homicide in which a woman’s battered body was found doused in bleach and stuffed upside down in her abandoned vehicle.

Details of the bizarre case have been made public for the first time as the trial began in the High Court at Auckland yesterday for Judith Rose Cunniffe’s alleged murderer, a 51-year-old man who continues to have interim name suppression.

Cunniffe, a poultry enthusiast who was known to friends and family as Judy, was found dead on April 11 last year - one day after the 53-year-old had called 111 to report the defendant visiting her boarding house with his chicken-chasing dog when he wasn’t supposed to be there.

Police went out to the property that same evening, deciding to conduct a brief search after a flatmate falsely claimed the defendant was no longer there. But they were unable to find him hiding under a bed in one of the seven bedrooms because of the filthy state of the rubbish-strewn residence, Crown prosecutor Jay Tausi told jurors during his opening address.

The defendant beat Cunniffe to death during a confrontation at the residence later that evening, both sides agreed.

In a phone call some time after the incident, the defendant explained to an associate that Cunniffe had “come out of the bushes” and started arguing with him about his dog, revealing that she had gone to police.

“That’s when I started to nail her out, you know?” he said on the call, which was recorded. “I just smashed her.”

But that didn’t mean prosecutors could prove murder, defence lawyer Sacha Norrie said during her opening statement, describing the Crown’s murder accusation as based on “theories, guesses and lies”.

“He did not mean to kill her,” Norrie said of her client. “He says [that] he says sorry to her every day.”

If jurors decline to find the defendant guilty of murder, they will also have the option of manslaughter, which is a homicide without murderous intent.

Both sides described the scene of the killing as one that jurors might find confronting due to the conditions the residents were living in and the drug abuse that took place there.

The 17-hectare property, about 2km from the main town centre, saw a steady turnover of tenants - most of whom were in their 50s and 60s and “lived complex and complicated lives” that included addiction, prosecutors said. The defence described the living conditions as “frankly horrifying”.

“By all accounts, Ms Cunniffe was an animal lover with a particular propensity for collecting chickens,” Tausi said. “Over time, the chickens started to venture into the main body of the house and into some of the bedrooms.”

By the time of her death, he added, her “love of chickens had gotten out of control” - probably fuelled in part by her methamphetamine addiction - to the point where she had “dozens and dozens” of the birds at the property. She made a habit of sleeping outside the home in her gold Toyota Corona, which she nicknamed “Coronavirus”, while the chickens stayed in two bedrooms of the house.

On the day of Cunniffe’s death, the defendant had been visiting the address with another tenant after drinking with him in town that morning and early afternoon, authorities allege. Cunniffe returned home to find the defendant’s dog off his leash and chasing her chickens.

“She said she would ring the police and get [the dog] put down,” Tausi said, explaining that she then made good on the threat - first driving to the police station then, after realising it was closed, calling 111 around 4.18pm.

Staff at a nearby op-shop would later describe her demeanour as “anxious, walking back and forth and shaking”.

Police searched the home around 5pm, looking for the defendant. Cunniffe returned home afterwards but stayed in her car, suspecting the defendant might still be there, prosecutors said.

No witnesses saw the assault that happened several hours later, but another resident said he heard the defendant and Cunniffe arguing, with the defendant yelling, “F*** off.” A post-mortem exam would later reveal Cunniffe suffered fractures to her head, jaw, nasal wall and eye socket as well as cuts and bruises on various parts of her body, including what were characterised by authorities as “defensive wounds”.

Although he then took steps to clean the scene, stuffing Cunniffe head-first into the footwell of her car and dousing her in bleach so that her floral-print dress was significantly faded, he was strangely upfront with her roommates about what had happened as they smoked methamphetamine together that same night.

“[He] was telling them he had killed Ms Cunniffe,” Tausi told jurors. “They were all confused by the casual manner of [his] revelation, so much so that they were unsure if he was being serious.”

The next morning, the defendant drove Cunniffe’s Toyota towards town during the morning rush hour and abandoned the vehicle between some bushes and tennis courts. A short time later, a woman with two young children in her car saw him trying to hitchhike and picked him up, concerned because he was stumbling.

The motorist is expected to give evidence later in the trial stating that the defendant smelled strongly of alcohol and cleaning products, and he had mud and twigs on him.

“He was also putting on an obviously fake European accent,” Tausi said.

Word of the defendant’s alleged admissions to his acquaintances travelled quickly in the small town and police were alerted later that day. Cunniffe’s body was discovered, and he was arrested.

During a subsequent search of Cunniffe’s home, police found a blue torch outside that was smeared in Cunniffe’s blood, with the defendant’s palm print on it. Police also recovered the defendant’s jacket, which was stained with bleach spots, and found Cunniffe’s blood on the knee of his trousers.

The case is certainly not a “whodunit”, the defendant’s lawyers acknowledged. They told jurors they would agree with most of the evidence prosecutors presented at the trial so that jurors could narrow their focus to the few parts that are in dispute.

One area of disagreement is the Crown’s suggestion that the defendant used the torch to beat Cunniffe, Norrie said, noting that her client is “crystal clear” he only touched the implement after realising Cunniffe had died.

“He accepts that aspects of his behaviour in Waiuku that day you could well feel [could] be described as unusual,” she said, adding that there “is no excuse” for the attack on Cunniffe.

“But the Crown have got it wrong when they say it is murder,” she said, urging jurors to “stay laser focused on the charge at hand” rather than letting emotion taint their judgement.

Cunniffe’s cause of death was determined by a pathologist to have been blunt force head trauma, but her own methamphetamine use was found to be a contributing factor because of the strain it put on her heart.

The trial is expected to continue today before Justice Simon Mount and the jury.

Craig Kapitan is an Auckland-based journalist covering courts and justice. He joined the Herald in 2021 and has reported on courts since 2002 in three newsrooms in the US and New Zealand.

Burnham to tell schools in England to adapt teaching to local business needs

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 21:30:20 GMT

PM wants curriculums for students aged 14 and above to be more responsive to local jobs market

Andy Burnham will tell schools across England to adapt their curriculums to the needs of local businesses as part of a devolution drive aimed at tackling the jobs crisis for young people.

By moving decision-making to local areas, the PM hopes the plan will make technical and vocational skills as valued as academic qualifications – and help cut the benefits bill.

Based in part on the Greater Manchester baccalaureate that Burnham introduced as the region’s mayor, it will task schools with making their curriculums for students aged 14 and above more responsive to the local jobs market, teaching technical skills alongside traditional academic subjects.

It would, Burnham said, mean the country could “value the hard hat every bit as much as the graduation cap”.

Described by No 10 as “a fundamental change to the education system”, the announcement kicks off a week of policy initiatives by Burnham, expected to also cover adult social care, defence and devolution.

After last week’s succession of rapid, consumer-focused policies such as help with electricity bills, Burnham’s team aim to use the coming days to present him as a leader willing to tackle more intractable and complex political problems.

Under the plan, intended to begin operating from September 2028, mayors and other local leaders would work with schools, colleges and employers to devise technical training built around local jobs.

In combination, there will be prioritised funding for such technical and vocational qualifications, plus guidance to Ofsted to recognise the value of these as well as more traditional qualifications.

In addition to giving local areas more control over education for the 14-16 age group, Burnham said the intention was to redress what he said was an over-simplified focus on academic routes.

He said: “For too long in this country, students have been told that you must take the academic path to do well and to be respected. The whole school system has been built around it and that has let down young people seeking technical qualifications.

“I want an education system based on parity between academic and technical which gives all young people a clear path in life. From today, Britain will value the hard hat every bit as much as the graduation cap.”

The intention is also to help address the worsening problem of young people not in education, employment or training, which was the subject of a report published in May by Alan Milburn, the former Labour cabinet minister.

The first part of an ongoing review, Milburn’s report said the issue now affected 1 million young people across the UK, with the numbers rising fast. It cited a number of factors, including a changing job market, inequality and health problems, but also blamed a lack of focus on employability skills and non-academic qualifications.

Milburn said in a statement that he welcomed the plans to overhaul and devolve education for 14-plus pupils, calling it “a big step in the right direction and consistent with the findings of my review”.

Moves to get more young people into work will also be a key element of wider efforts to tackle the benefits system, due to be guided by both Milburn’s findings and a separate review by Stephen Timms, the minister for social security, into the personal independence payment disability system.

Sign up to First Edition

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

In an interview with the BBC broadcast on Monday night, Burnham said he believed that many young people had been failed by a system that “pays for failure” rather than “sets people up for success”.

Asked if he believed some people received benefits they did not need, he replied: “I wouldn’t necessarily go straight to blaming those people. What I would say is that there are people in the benefit system, young people in their 20s, who have been, I would say, quite seriously let down because the support wasn’t there for them when it should have been there.”

This failure included, he said, “an education system that for a very long time has been obsessed on the university route but hasn’t done enough for young people who want technical qualifications and in many ways has treated them as second class students”.

The new initiative is firmly based on Burnham’s flagship education policy as Greater Manchester mayor, introduced in September 2024.

Known as the Greater Manchester baccalaureate, or MBacc, it was designed to offer courses and work experience for children aged 14 and over in key sectors in the regional economy.

Alongside the traditional subjects of English, maths and sciences, schools in Greater Manchester can now offer technical lessons tailored towards employment in industries including financial services, engineering and manufacturing, construction and the green economy. There are also new routes into public services such as health and social care, education and transport.

Experts say it is too soon to properly evaluate whether the MBacc has been a success – it was piloted in only 10 schools in its first academic year. However, several other of England’s regional mayors have called for greater power over the school curriculum to link it more closely with their local economy.

Some mayors complain that the Department for Education has been one of the most stubborn government bodies when it comes to devolving powers outside Whitehall.

Green party leader shared picture of man wearing T-shirt with words ‘we’re only making plans for Nigel’ alongside a guillotine

Police are “conducting inquiries” into an image shared by Green party leader Zack Polanski on Instagram after Reform UK reported it for “inciting murder”.

The image showed a man wearing a black T-shirt with the words “we’re only making plans for Nigel”, alongside a photograph of a guillotine.

A Green party spokesperson said that Polanski “condemns the image on the T-shirt” and accepted being tagged in a post with 20 images “without realising there was more to it than he had seen”.

Nigel Farage shared a screenshot of the image on X and wrote: “This is what Zack Polanski has just posted on his Instagram.

“If I was to post anything as inciteful then I would expect to be arrested, and so should Polanski.”

Reform UK’s spokesperson for home affairs, Zia Yusuf, said Polanski was “inciting murder”, and that sharing the image weeks after the death of former Conservative MP Ann Widdecombe, who was murdered in her home in Devon, was “staggering”.

Last week, prosecutors told a court that a man allegedly hit Widdecombe 21 times over the head with a hammer in a “planned and targeted” attack.

A Green party spokesperson said: “The T-shirt is clearly in poor taste, especially at a time of heightened fears for the security of public figures, having experienced multiple threats himself [Polanski].

“He [Polanski] and the Green party call on everyone involved in public discourse to show kindness and not encourage more division.”

A spokesperson for the Metropolitan police said: “Earlier today, we received a third-party report relating to an image shared on social media.

“We take reports of this nature extremely seriously, and officers are conducting inquiries into the matter.”

Yusuf wrote on social media: “Zack Polanski has posted to his 713k Instagram followers a photo of a man in a T-shirt calling for the beheading of Nigel Farage.

“Polanski is inciting murder. It must be treated as such by the police.”

The image, which has since been removed from Polanski’s Instagram account, was shared in a collaborative post with other accounts, as part of a carousel of images from a Green party event on Sunday.

The words on the T-shirt come from Making Plans for Nigel, a song by English rock band XTC, which was released as the lead single from the 1979 album Drums and Wires.

A post on a website that appeared to sell the T-shirt for £20 stated: “Whether it’s a nod to old punk music or a sharper bit of political satire, this design is for those who prefer their statements with a side of mystery.”

Earlier this month, Andy Burnham said that a serious review is needed into MP security after the murder of Ann Widdecombe. Jess Phillips previously told the Guardian that the threat to MPs must be tackled at source, amid an ongoing refusal by social media platforms to take responsibility for what’s published on their platforms.

According to the BBC, Polanski has not been contacted by the police.

Ndevelo seizes chance to try again in pursuit of breakthrough Commonwealth Games medal

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 21:00:41 GMT

Tryagain Morning Ndevelo through to 60kg quarter-finals

Namibia boxer taking inspiration from name given to him

Every boxer has a story. Few have one written into their name. For Namibia’s Tryagain Morning Ndevelo, every trip into the ring is a reminder of the lesson his mother taught him growing up: if today does not go your way, there is always another chance tomorrow.

That philosophy is now carrying him towards the Commonwealth Games medals after the 60kg contender booked his place in the quarter-finals with a unanimous points victory against Bangladesh’s Md Ruhin Reza in Glasgow.

After receiving a walkover in the opening round when Trinidad and Tobago’s Anthony Joseph failed to make the call time, Ndevelo finally got the opportunity he had been craving, and seized it in style. All five judges awarded him 10 points in each of the three rounds as he completed a 5-0 victory to move within one win of a Commonwealth medal.

The performance showed the bizarre scenes of his opening contest had done little to derail his focus. On Sunday, Ndevelo had completed his ring walk through the smoke before discovering he was the only boxer inside the ropes. Joseph never answered the call to the ring, leaving the Namibian warming up alone before the opening bell sounded with just one fighter present. Officials eventually declared a walkover victory before cameras caught the dejected Trinidadian arriving too late to compete.

For a boxer chasing a breakthrough at his third Commonwealth Games, it was hardly ideal preparation. Ndevelo said after his fight against Reza that he simply wanted the chance to test himself. “It was nice,” he said. “I’m glad that I got to go into the ring. Got to face somebody. I can see my level.

“A lot of hard work has gone into this. So at least I finally got a chance to practise what I have been learning. I was thinking: ‘Am I really fine?’ and ‘Am I ready?’ because I didn’t get a taste. At least now I know. I don’t feel tired. I have an extra level I can get to. I was excited to have him [Reza] at least show up.”

This is Ndevelo’s third Commonwealth Games appearance, having exited in the last 16 on the Gold Coast before reaching the quarter-finals in Birmingham four years later.

Now, in Glasgow, he has matched that achievement and has another opportunity to take the next step and his remarkable first name has become one of the stories of these Games.

“My mother is my whole world,” he said. “[Growing up], whenever I missed training or I was feeling down, I would be told: ‘You don’t have to miss training. Just show up. Even if you are not good, just show up.’ She has always been behind me and that itself is the definition of my name.

“Every day you wake up in the morning and you have the chance to do what you didn’t do yesterday. That is why my middle name is Morning. Tuesday, Wednesday, whenever I fight again, I have the chance to better what I did here today. That’s all from her, for giving me this name. Every time I feel low, I get up and try again.”

The story behind his name has garnered much fanfare and the 27‑year‑old could not quite believe he was signing autographs in Glasgow after his victory. “It feels nice that there are children inspired by me. It is probably their first time seeing me in person and something about me interested them. It’s nice that I can leave a mark on somebody even when I am so far away from home. I am so overwhelmed.”

That refreshing attitude came to mind as Scotland’s Archie Goodburn received the biggest roar of the night in the same race despite finishing tied last. And no wonder, given the 25‑year‑old was competing here having been diagnosed with terminal brain cancer two years ago.

“The reception was monumental,” said Goodburn, who was strikingly positive afterwards. “I tried to prepare myself for it. But that was the next level.”

Doctors have diagnosed oligodendrogliomas, which accounts for roughly 3% of all primary brain tumours, and means he may have only a decade to live. But Goodburn has made it his mission to raise as much awareness as possible about the condition.

“Every athlete talks about tough times, but there’s been some really tough times,” he said. “And the shoes I was in, or the position I was in this time last year, it was a dark spot.

“So looking back on where I am now 12 months later, and everything we’ve managed to achieve over the year, thanks to the support of my friends, family and the University of Edinburgh. I can’t say a big enough thank you. And long may that continue.”

Last year, Goodburn started using Vorasidenib – a breakthrough new treatment designed to slow the spread of cancer. That has delayed the prospect of chemotherapy. But there are plenty of tough times ahead.

When asked how he remained positive, he was powerful and direct. “I advocate because I believe that my own advocacy can make a difference to my own life. And the best way I can do that is to be positive about the situation and positive for change.

“But I also advocate for the future Archies. I swim for future Archies that want to succeed on an international level. But also young patients and people with brain cancer under the age of 40.

“Brain cancer is the biggest killer of all cancers for people under the age of 40 in the UK. And I do believe that our advocacy groups are making a difference to that. That we’ll hopefully see over the next few years.”

In a Sunday letter, Raskin wrote to Infantino and called for Fifa to provide any documents and communications related to gifts, payments or benefits provided to Trump and his associates, as well as the visitor logs for Fifa’s office space in Trump Tower, which it acquired last year. The committee also requested that Infantino sit for a transcribed interview.

Infantino’s relationship with Trump came under scrutiny in the lead-up to this summer’s World Cup. In December, at the World Cup draw in Washington, Trump was awarded a newly created “Fifa peace prize” at the Kennedy Center, where renovations were allegedly “rushed” on the administration’s orders to prepare for the event. Fifa opened its office in Trump Tower in midtown Manhattan last July.

Such scrutiny intensified during the World Cup. Trump made several calls to Infantino to lobby for a review of US striker Folarin Balogun’s controversial red-card suspension before the Americans’ last-16 match against Belgium. Fifa did reverse Balogun’s ban, but the political circus cast a pall over the US team and drew the ire of other teams and associations from around the world.

Alongside the leaders of Canada and Mexico, Trump joined Infantino for the World Cup trophy presentation after Spain beat Argentina in the final. The pair, who watched the final together in a glassed-in section of luxury seats, were met with boos from the New York New Jersey Stadium crowd when they took the field.

Raskin’s letter references the Department of Justice’s decision to “dismiss the indictments” of defendants in US government investigations into corruption in global soccer, including the 2015 prosecution of more than 20 high-level Fifa officials and sports-marketing executives.

“[Y]our election as Fifa president was supposed to mark a red-card break from a decades-long culture of corruption and scandals that dressed down world soccer’s reputation,” Raskin wrote to Infantino in the letter. “Instead, at the start of your tenure, you dismantled Fifa’s ethical guardrails and disabled the organization’s ethics committee by pushing out most of its members. This lack of transparency and oversight has since paved the way for you to ingratiate yourself with the Trump administration via tactics that a New York University law professor and one of your former ethics committeemen described as ‘legal bribery’.”

The letter also addresses Fifa’s World Cup ticketing policy, which is already the subject of investigations by several attorneys general in the United States. The use of dynamic pricing drew much criticism during the tournament, leading to massive surges and pricing out many fans from attending games.

“The most recent quid pro quo that Fifa and President Trump orchestrated is not a victimless crime. It hurts Americans. Fifa has taken its newfound favored status in the Trump administration as a sign that it may rip off its consumers, most notably, by employing illegal price-gouging and fraudulent sales tactics for the World Cup,” Raskin said in the letter.

The letter gives a deadline of 9 August to provide the requested documents and schedule the interview. Raskin does not have the power to compel Infantino to appear, given that Democrats do not hold the majority in the House, unless he garners Republican support.

Fifa’s interactions with the US government did not end with this summer’s World Cup. The US is expected to be the primary host of the Women’s World Cup in 2031, and the success of this year’s tournament has led many to speculate that the 2038 men’s World Cup could be hosted by the US. Fifa has been approached for comment.

More than 200 Fifa members have endorsed Infantino ahead of the presidential election in March, but some associations have stood in opposition. Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate will remain in jail at least two more weeks until their next hearing as they fight extradition to the United Kingdom, where the brothers are accused of rape and sex trafficking, a federal judge said on Monday.

US magistrate Lauren Louis set a detention hearing for 13 August to determine whether the Tates should stay in jail or be released during what could be a months-long extradition process.

The brothers were not in court on Monday or required to be there and have remained in jail since making a brief court appearance two days after their 18 July arrest.

The Tates have become among the world’s most polarizing internet personalities with their promotion of wealth, male dominance and misogyny through their social media empire. The new allegations are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the Tates that has spanned the US, Britain and Romania. The brothers have repeatedly denied wrongdoing.

Attorneys for the brothers said on Monday that they want the US government to turn over documents that UK officials submitted to secure their arrest.

“They don’t have anything but the accusations,” Joseph McBride, an attorney, said after the hearing. “It’s just their word against our word right now.”

The UK has until mid-September to turn over all of its materials to the state department, Alejandra Lopez, a US attorney, said in court.

The brothers have long claimed that their violent and misogynistic statements have been taken out of context or were intended as jokes.

Jackie Perczek, another one of their attorneys, said the Tates have shown they are not a flight risk by returning to Romania every month after they were accused there of luring women for sexual exploitation.

“For three years they have not fled,” she said. “They’ve traveled the world and every month they return to Romania.”

The former professional kickboxers, who have dual US and UK citizenship, have millions of social media followers and are vocal supporters of Donald Trump. The White House has said the brothers shouldn’t expect any help from the president.

McBride said shortly after the Tates were arrested that “they’ve never done nothing wrong. They shouldn’t be extradited for crimes they did not commit,” he said.

McBride said the extradition attempt was politically motivated, though he provided no details.

Prosecutors in Britain said the new charges relate to four new accusers and were brought after authorities received evidence from police in Bedfordshire, in south-eastern England. The allegations, which span from 2010 to 2017, include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography”.

The brothers are already charged with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other accusers in the UK between 2012 and 2015.

The brothers moved to Romania in 2016 and were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations, and the Romanian case has not gone forward because of legal and procedural problems.

Andrew Tate, 39, became known a decade ago when he was a contestant on the UK reality television show Big Brother. He was booted from the show when a video appeared to show him assaulting a woman.

He has amassed more than 10 million followers on X but has been banned from other platforms, including YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, for violating hate speech guidelines. He has made widely condemned comments, such as saying women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for the attacks and sharing graphic descriptions of how he might attack women.

Industrial chicken farming accelerating spread of diarrhoea bacteria, study finds

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 19:00:17 GMT

Intensive nature of modern chicken farming creates ideal conditions for campylobacter, allowing bacteria to evolve

Industrial chicken farming is accelerating the spread of the world’s most common bacterial cause of diarrhoea, scientists have found.

The study found a dramatic increase in the exchange of campylobacter strains between wild birds and chickens as farming has intensified, creating the ideal conditions for the bacteria to mix, spread and acquire new traits. There has also been a rise in antimicrobial resistance traits in circulating strains, raising concerns that serious illness in people will be more difficult to treat.

“As the chicken population has exploded, they’ve increasingly picked up strains from different wild birds and become a cauldron of bacterial evolution,” said Prof Sam Sheppard of the University of Oxford and senior author of the paper. “Lots of strains come together and hybridise. We do not want that, because that’s where new Frankenstein monster bugs emerge.”

Campylobacter is the most common bacterial cause of diarrhoea worldwide, causing more than three times as many gastroenteritis cases in the UK each year as all other monitored foodborne bacteria combined. An estimated 60-80% of campylobacter infections are caught from raw chicken.

“Cooking kills pathogens, but just a tiny splash and it’s on your lettuce leaves or your hands or your knife,” said Sheppard.

Most people will get better without treatment, but sometimes antibiotics are required and infection also raises the risk of irritable bowel syndrome. Rising rates of antimicrobial resistance, which occurs when bacteria resist drugs designed to kill them, mean that some antibiotics that were previously used to treat campylobacter infections are no longer effective.

The latest work suggests that the evolution of the infection is being fuelled by the unprecedented scale of chicken production.

Since the 1960s, global chicken numbers have increased seven-fold to approximately 27 billion birds, accounting for about 70% of all bird biomass on Earth. Intensive breeding has led to “super growing” chickens that reach adult size and are slaughtered at around five weeks old. The industrialisation of chicken farming has led to affordable animal protein at scale, but also presents new health risks.

The latest work, published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, analysed nearly 2,800 bacterial genomes collected from chickens and wild birds in 30 countries, including the UK, US and China, between 1979 and 2024.

The dataset allowed the scientists to reconstruct the evolutionary trees of the diverse strains, including the rate of exchange between hosts. Prior to domestication of the chicken 5,000 years ago, strains of campylobacter tended to be tightly linked to individual species of birds, with little cross-infection. But as chicken numbers increased, this picture changed, with an estimated 100-fold increase in transitions of strains between chickens and wild birds since 1900 compared with pre-domestication – a trend that appears to have continued steeply in recent decades.

“The scale is what’s bad,” said Sheppard. “By adjusting the world’s ecosystems in this dramatic way, it leads to the evolution of pathogens within those birds. That’s a massive risk to us. We can’t continue to produce chickens at this huge capacity.”

The researchers also identified genetic changes in campylobacter that were associated with adaptation to the chicken environment. These included genes involved in antimicrobial resistance, which can help bacteria survive and thrive in modern poultry production systems, where antibiotics are routinely given to encourage rapid growth or to keep disease under control in densely packed sheds.

Maya Pardo, legal coordinator at Communities Against Factory Farming (CAFF), said: “Intensive chicken farming has spread out of control in the UK, and the 100-fold increase in the movement of campylobacter is the latest in a long list of devastating consequences. While communities are desperately calling for no more factory farms, the government is absurdly looking to relax planning rules to build yet more of these disease-ridden industrial facilities.”

Mind the ever-growing gap: the Premier League keeps spending big

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 19:00:17 GMT

English clubs have spent more on players this summer than the other four major European leagues combined

The financial power of the Premier League is unmatched. The teams in England’s top division have collectively invested more than £1.4bn in new players already this summer (through disclosed fees alone), around £303m more than the 76 clubs from the Bundesliga, La Liga, Ligue 1 and Serie A combined.

These figures are the gross spend, so take no account of players sold to help balance the books. Factoring this in only increases the divide. The clubs of Ligue 1 and the Bundesliga are £203.4m and £72.2m in credit from their transfer dealings respectively. While La Liga (£163.1m) and Serie A (£124.1m) have spent more than they have earned, they are an ocean adrift of the Premier League’s net spend of £523.6m.

None of this is new; it has been the trend for many years. The worrying aspect for teams across the continent is that the gap between the Premier League and the rest may grow wider before the summer is out.

Despite their enormous outlay, top-flight English teams have spent about £230m less than Premier League clubs of 2025-26 had at this point last year. But only 25 deals were completed by the end of 1 July (which is when new contracts usually start, explaining why pre-arranged moves are often finalised then). It’s roughly half as many as the 47 that occurred by that date last summer. The expanded World Cup will probably have delayed some deals, creating a potential backlog of transfer spending that will soon hit the books.

Assessing clubs individually highlights why most might continue spending. Aston Villa, Brighton and Tottenham have already spent more in gross terms than in the entirety of the summer 2025 transfer window. Unai Emery has a net £109.6m burning a hole in his pocket following business which includes the departures of Morgan Rogers and Youri Tielemans. Brighton will need a larger squad as they have a Conference League campaign on the horizon while Tottenham are hoping to improve upon consecutive 17th-place finishes. Their trading may not be complete even though they’ve already outspent their efforts from last summer, with Spurs’ net spend of £149.7m the highest in Europe’s big five leagues.

Chelsea also have a higher net spend than last year, even before their reportedly agreed deal for Crystal Palace’s Maxence Lacroix goes through. Even if that transfer is not completed, would you bet against BlueCo throwing more money around, especially with a new manager to back? Danny Welbeck is the latest to emerge on the Stamford Bridge radar. Either way, Chelsea have already invested more in new talent than they had on this day last year. The same is true for Everton, Fulham, Manchester City and Newcastle, all of whom may have further incomings in the pipeline, too.

There are other clubs with work to do. The three promoted teams have only spent £8m more between them than Sunderland alone had at this point in 2025. Régis Le Bris added a total of 18 new players to his squad last summer, with fellow promoted sides Burnley (15) and Leeds (11) also hitting double figures for incomings. By these standards, Ipswich (with seven new players), Hull (four) and Coventry (three) must recruit further.

At the opposite end of the Premier League scale, Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United have collectively spent two-thirds of a billion less on new talent than they did last summer. The latest rumour mill gossip says the champions may make a move for Vinícius Júnior. If not the Brazilian then perhaps Bradley Barcola, though Liverpool are also said to be pursuing the Paris Saint-Germain winger. Neither player will be remotely cheap. United are believed to be targeting Ollie Watkins – he wouldn’t cost Vinícius or Barcola money, but neither would Villa sell to a rival at a reduced fee.

The Premier League also has clubs who have yet to make an outlay. It is unlikely Crystal Palace, Nottingham Forest and Sunderland end the summer without spending a transfer fee as is now the case. It would be remiss of Palace and Sunderland not to invest when they are in European competition this season. As for Forest, like Chelsea they have had an insatiable thirst for player turnover in recent times. With Elliot Anderson having left for an enormous fee, replacements will surely arrive soon.

It is remarkable to think the Premier League may not be halfway through its summer outlay when £1.4bn has already been used for recruitment. The top-flight English clubs collectively spent £3.1bn on players last summer, with over £600m in the final week of dealing alone. That figure may be blown away by the time the transfer window closes on 3 September.

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 18:32:00 GMT

It took just seven days in office for Andy Burnham to meet his first world leader. As he welcomed Volodymyr Zelenskyy to a naval base in Portsmouth on Monday, the new prime minister told the Ukrainian president it was “no accident” he was his first international visitor since entering No 10.

“It is intended to send a very clear message,” Burnham told him. “We are with Ukraine 100%, I am personally with you 100%, and I will honour every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full.” In short, the UK’s support for Kyiv would continue despite the change in leadership.

For Keir Starmer, the relationship with Zelenskyy became one of the defining ones of his premiership. He visited Ukraine four times over his two years in office, inviting the Ukrainian president back to the UK on another four occasions. They also met regularly at international summits.

In a symbolic move, Starmer travelled to Ukraine during his final week in office, receiving the order of freedom medal for his role leading the coalition of the willing and helping to persuade Donald Trump back to the table on Ukraine after he flirted with siding with Putin.

But over the course of his premiership, the former Labour leader faced accusations of spending too much time on international issues instead of domestic ones, with his critics nicknaming him “never here Keir” and even his own Downing Street team complaining that he “needs to get off a plane”.

Burnham, in contrast, has always been clear he would prioritise what was happening at home, reflecting his own political instincts as well as his wariness of not falling into the same trap as his predecessor. But it led some in the Labour party to worry that he would be unprepared for the global stage.

“It’s a frustrating characterisation because not many incoming prime ministers, including Keir, have any experience of international affairs,” one of his inner circle said. “Andy has said that his priority will be domestic, but of course there will be moments where he’ll need to be more outward facing.”

Day to day, Burnham’s allies have suggested that he will rely on delegating responsibility to his team – including his foreign secretary in Ed Miliband and senior diplomatic adviser in Jonathan Powell, whom he persuaded to stay on in No 10 from the Starmer administration.

Labour MPs point out that Yvette Cooper, Miliband’s predecessor, was often left fighting for influence as there were so many other senior figures who saw themselves as the de facto foreign secretary, including the deputy prime minister, David Lammy, Powell, and Starmer himself.

One senior MP said: “I suspect that Ed may be in a fortunate position where he is actually given more freedom than other foreign secretaries in the past. As long as Ed is known to have the authority of the PM and to be trusted to speak for him, then this may be his moment.”

Other Labour figures suggested that strong prime ministers should be able to delegate and rely on their teams. One said: “I don’t think Andy is particularly interested in foreign affairs. He’ll need to front some things up, but as long as he’s well briefed and charming, he doesn’t need to make the day-to-day decisions like Keir did.”

But they warned there would inevitably be moments where complex international issues “crash land” on UK domestic policy – as Starmer found to his cost when dealing with Trump – and he would have no choice but to intervene.

Burnham has already indicated he will not shy away from standing up to the US president. “Obviously, the relationship is important to the UK, but not to the point where we just go along with anything that they say,” he told the Guardian last month.

There are some with experience of foreign affairs in government who believe that Starmer has already done the hard yards on foreign policy – on Ukraine, the European Union and the US in particular – so Burnham just has to stick to the same course.

In his final interview in office, Starmer told his successor that he should not spend less time focusing on international affairs, in order to prioritise the situation at home. “It’s not sensible to think you can just separate these two things out,” he said.

“If you’re PM and you care what bills are going to be like in any household around the country, you have to care about finding a lasting solution to the situation in Ukraine, you have to care about what happens in the strait of Hormuz.”

But those around Burnham believe he can better balance them. At least for now. They have been watching events in Iran closely, mindful of the potential to cause yet more global economic upheaval should Trump take further action.

“Andy has a bit of space now to prioritise policy at home – but it could all be blown off course by Iran,” one Foreign Office insider said. “He has to seize this moment to talk about the domestic, because this window might not come again.”

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 17:30:24 GMT

Robert Bush, owner of Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, left bodies ‘rotting away’, family members say

A fraudulent funeral director broke the trust of families on an “almost industrial scale” as their loved ones’ bodies were left “rotting away”, a court has heard.

Robert Bush, owner of Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull, appeared at Hull crown court on Monday for a five-day sentencing hearing. He previously pleaded guilty to 67 offences, including 30 counts of preventing lawful and decent burial.

Several family members read out their victim impact statements to the court, recounting nightmares and PTSD from Bush’s offending, with some breaking down in tears and struggling to speak.

On his way into court, Bush, 48, from Otley, West Yorkshire, told reporters he was sorry to the families affected.

Several family members recalled Bush “smiling” as he handed them the wrong ashes, while their loved ones remained secretly uncremated. When Jayne Rimmington came to collect the ashes of her 86-year-old mother, Shirley Wright, in October 2023, she was surprised by how heavy they were. Bush claimed this was due to her “bone density”.

The body of Wright was recovered on the Legacy premises five months after her death. “I trusted him,” said Rimmington. “He stood there smiling, handed me the box, when she was still laying there, rotting away. It’s a purely evil thing to do.”

Vicky Mitchell received the ashes of her father, Colin Wainman, in a navy blue box inside a Hobbycraft bag, with Bush apologising at the time for not having any gift bags at hand. The 69-year-old’s body was recovered on 8 March 2024, 198 days after his death.

“My opinion is he is a charlatan,” Mitchell told the court. “A gravedigger from the 1800s. He didn’t care.”

Prosecutor Chris Paxton KC said Bush “operated within the heart of the community for around 14 years, entrusted by hundreds of bereaved families in their time of need”. However, Bush “breached that trust on an almost industrial scale in a myriad of ways”.

In a search of the Legacy premises in March 2024, Humberside police found many bodies left uncovered and in varying states of decomposition, stored on racks on both sides of the room. One naked body still lay on a stretcher on the floor. Flowers, rings, teddy bears and cards with messages, intended to be placed with loved ones, had been swept under the floor.

The removal of bodies took two days and several officers, including a disaster identification team. Bodies had to be identified by dental records, DNA examination or fingerprints.

Police also uncovered the remains of an 18-week stillborn boy, identified as Sunny Beverley-Conlin, on the floor of the premises, inside what appeared to be a police evidence bag. His mother, Jasmine Beverley, believed he had been given a funeral and cremated.

Rea Burton, granddaughter of David Burton, attended the Legacy funeral home to collect his ashes in December 2023. Bush asked Burton what the family intended to do with the ashes, to which Burton replied they would be put in necklace charms for the family and her uncle would put some into the ink for a tattoo. Bush told her this was a “brilliant idea”.

“In reality, Rob had deceived us,” said Burton. “He had abandoned and hidden our loved one for months and had given us a stranger’s ashes with a smile on his face.”

After the funeral service of 94-year-old Norman Bridger, his daughter, Karen King, placed what she believed to be her father’s ashes into lockets worn by her and her mother. “I now feel violated [that] I had some unknown person’s ashes so close to me,” King said.

To thank him for his work on the funeral, King had also given Bush a bottle of port. “The smile on his face as he accepted it will always haunt me,” she told the court.

David Gorbutt visited Bush to collect what he believed were the ashes of his wife, Susan, in September 2023. He was handed a paper bag containing a small cardboard box with her name. When Gorbutt told Bush he “hope[d] they’re the right ones”, Bush replied: “Yes, they are definitely the right ones.”

Gorbutt scattered the ashes at the same site as her son’s in a local country park, as per Susan’s wishes. Her body was recovered at the Legacy premises six months after her death.

In his statement, Gorbutt said he felt guilty for being “unable to fulfil my wife’s last request, that I deal with her death quickly” as she wanted, recalling that “Susan would say: ‘You know I do not like the cold.’”

Like many families, Gorbutt also called for stronger regulation of the funeral industry. “It is hard to believe a person needs more permits to sell burgers than to deal with the dead,” he said.

The Guardian view on Europe’s wildfires: politics must catch up with the new reality

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 17:30:15 GMT

At a time when the quickening pace of global heating has never been clearer, climate policies are being deprioritised

A new and ominous word has entered the vocabulary of firefighters struggling to cope with the vast wildfire sweeping through south-west France. A pyrocumulonimbus is a fire-generated thunderstorm that can whip up winds in unpredictable ways, making the containment of a blaze and assessment of its likely course far more difficult. A known phenomenon in North America and Australia, firefighters believe France is suffering its first in the Bordeaux region, as the country endures the consequences of the third major heatwave of the summer and prepares for a fourth.

The dire statistics of the ongoing fires in France and Spain tell a story of deepening devastation and human misery. A far greater expanse of French land has already been burnt this year, compared with the 30,000 hectares during the whole of 2025, while 220,000 people have been evacuated from their homes in the Gironde. In Spain, the environment ministry has calculated that over 170,000 hectares have been affected, compared with 29,000 last year. Over 100,000 people have been forced to flee.

As climate scientists long warned would be the case, Europe’s wildfires are worsening in intensity, scale and duration as the planet heats up. When the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, attributed the current crisis to the effects of the climate emergency, he was stating the obvious. But to his great credit, Mr Sánchez has been among the few leaders to argue that the European Union’s green transition should be accelerated accordingly. Whether on funding adaptation efforts, or driving the macro changes needed to slow the rate of global heating, far too many others appear happy to fiddle while the continent burns.

In June, for example, with spectacularly bad timing, Emmanuel Macron’s government sought savings by announcing steep cuts to a Green Fund designed to help local authorities address climate and environmental challenges. Across Europe more generally, amid persistent low growth and the fallout from Donald Trump’s war on Iran, a false dichotomy is increasingly being drawn between green ambition and competitiveness. This month, under pressure from countries such as Giorgia Meloni’s Italy, the European Commission unveiled proposals to weaken the EU’s emissions trading system, its flagship climate policy. If adopted, heavy industry would receive free polluting permits for longer and at lower cost.

Calls for the dilution of green measures are generally accompanied by the assertion that Europe needs to take a more pragmatic approach, at a time of geopolitical uncertainty and aggressive economic competition. The argument is wrong twice over: the faster the EU moves towards net zero, the better it will consolidate Europe’s position in the global markets of the future. More fundamentally, as the appalling impact of this summer’s wildfires vividly illustrates, the notion that climate measures are a kind of optional add-on, appropriate only when times are good, is wildly at odds with the developing reality.

As a fourth heatwave hits Europe, temperatures in south-west France are predicted to hit 40C on Wednesday. According to a recent study, if the warming rate of the last decade continues, the 1.5C limit set by the Paris agreement will be redundant by 2030. Yet, far from seeking to catch up with the pace of change, too many governments and leaders are seeking to put their foot on the policy brake. That is not realism; it is a dereliction of duty.

The Guardian view on ancient DNA: a female shaman exposes our flawed assumptions about the past

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 17:25:15 GMT

Thanks to new technology we are are acquiring insights into earlier times, and realising how little we truly know

Archaeologists believe the Upton Lovell Shaman, who lived in what is now Wiltshire 4,000 years ago, was an important religious leader and metalworker because of the artefacts and tools buried with the body. Until very recently it was also believed, on considerably slimmer evidence, that this shaman was a man: it was simply assumed that someone of such status must be male, and the view was barely questioned over the years. Now ancient DNA analysis performed at the Francis Crick Institute has revealed that the body, held by the Wiltshire Museum, is in fact a woman.

That should cause a stir in bronze-age studies. But it is also yet another example of how many of our assumptions about human history have been upended by the rise of ancient DNA analysis over the past two decades. Others include the revelation that there were (frequent) liaisons between humans and Neanderthals just 50,000 years ago, a reconstruction suggesting that the first modern Britons had “dark to black” skin, and the closing of longstanding mysteries such as what really killed two members of Italy’s powerful Medici family in the 16th century (probably malaria, not murder as was often believed). Every time we widen our keyhole view of the past even slightly, we are confronted by how many of our seemingly grounded assumptions are, in fact, wrong.

These insights have emerged because the technology to extract and read DNA from ancient, poorly preserved samples has improved exponentially since around 2010. DNA analysis hardly provides a total picture of the past, but it has been useful for mapping migrations, sexual relations and family structures, as well as tracking plagues and diseases. For instance, it has told us that groups of ancient humans moved around and intermixed with each other far more often than previously thought, allowing us to imagine a more dynamic, less lonely ancient world.

It also suggests that the replacement of one group with another, such as evidence of the near-total disappearance of the Stonehenge-building Neolithic Britons, just a few centuries after the arrival of the Bell Beaker people around 2400BC, was relatively common. But it cannot answer why or how that replacement took place. These are big questions that will keep scientists, anthropologists and archaeologists busy for decades.

Alongside a deeper and richer view of the past, we should take a lesson from the constant stream of debunking and myth-busting emerging from this research. The politics behind assuming a shaman is male are obvious, but last year a study took on more subtle biases by proving that famous plaster casts of citizens of Pompeii long believed to show a mother and child locked in a final embrace were in fact two people who were not related, and the adult was male. The authors note that there was no published evidence suggesting the sex or family relations of these bodies, but both scholars and the public found the romantic (and very modern) interpretation irresistible.

We will probably always try to see something of ourselves in our ancestors. But the past is more interesting when we consider it on its own, often bracingly foreign, terms. DNA evidence will not conveniently overturn every one of our biased judgments about the ancient world, but each case does make it easier to recognise how readily it happens, and to be humble about how little we really understand.

Ronnie Le Drew, puppeteer behind Zippy and David Bowie’s goblins, dies aged 78

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 17:21:11 GMT

Canadian-born British operator, president of the British Puppet Guild, died after a ‘short illness’

Ronnie Le Drew, best known for operating the puppet Zippy on the classic children’s television programme Rainbow, has died aged 78 after a short illness. The news was confirmed by the British Puppet Guild, of which Le Drew was president.

The Canadian-born British puppeteer was also known for working on 1986’s Labyrinth alongside David Bowie as well as 1986’s Little Shop of Horrors and various Muppet movies including in 1992’s The Muppet Christmas Carol. He worked on various iterations of Sooty, alongside Harry and Matthew Corbett, usually as Sweep, Sooty’s sidekick.

He trained at London’s award-winning puppet theatre the Little Angel Theatre, with which he enjoyed a long association, eventually teaching there. He also co-founded the London School of Puppetry with his partner Caroline Astell-Burt.

In the statement announcing his death, the British Puppet Guild said: “We are saddened to announce the death of our president and friend Ronnie Le Drew, following a short illness. Ronnie has been our president for 10 years, possibly the most active and supportive president we have ever had or will have. Attending nearly every event whether it be online or in person, often performing when asked and always willing to chat, tell stories and entertain in whatever way he could.”

Le Drew’s son, John, wrote via his father’s social media channels: “We’re devastated to announce that dad passed away this morning, after a brief illness. We’re all grieving and sorry for our loss of such a sweet beautiful man.”

The puppet duo of Zippy and George were initially voiced by Roy Skelton, who also voiced Doctor Who’s Daleks between 1967 and 1988. He died in 2011, aged 79, and contributed to the enduring popularity of brash mouthy know-it-all orange Zippy, and the rather more shy and retiring pink hippopotamus George.

The programme launched in 1972 and was made by Thames Television continuously until 1992, with David Cook as the original presenter, and Geoffrey Hayes taking over in 1974. A revival by Tetra Films from 1994 to 1997 featured Le Drew also performing as the voice of Zippy, as well as operating the puppet.

Rainbow was conceived as a British equivalent of Sesame Street, with a bunch of friends exploring different educational topics together – often via the medium of conflict between Zippy, George or Bungle the bear, which Hayes, who died in 2018, would reconcile.

Le Drew was working until recently, having just appeared on YouTube channel My 70s TV Childhood, talking about his career and the job as Zippy, which he described as “a six-week contract that lasted 20 years”.

Private equity finds soft takeover targets in London – yet again

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 17:11:31 GMT

Offer for DCC Energy leaves total of completed or agreed deals within FTSE 100 this year at five, but has Westminster noticed?

DCC, one of FTSE 100’s biggest energy firms, agrees £5.75bn takeover

And another one goes. Dublin-based DCC Energy is a lower-profile member of the FTSE 100, but they all count. We’re now at five completed or agreed takeovers within London’s leading index this year – and it’s still only July.

The subplot at DCC was vocal opposition from a few shareholders who thought the private equity groups KKR and Energy Capital Partners, a unit of Bridgepoint, should be paying more than the £5.75bn, or £65.25 a share, at which the board has rolled over. Fidelity International and Aviva Investors were to the fore, as well as DCC’s founder.

The resistance movement had good points. DCC seems to be executing, roughly on time and on budget, the eight-year strategy it adopted in 2022 to double operating profits to £830m by 2030 by slimming down to its core energy operations.

The core comprises old-school petrol stations and liquid gas distribution networks across Europe, plus a growing clean energy services division that installs solar panels and suchlike. DCC, in other words, is an energy transition play with a mix of old and reliable cash earners and newer growth assets – the sort of thing the market, in theory, ought to like. About 35% of the required growth in operating profits has been achieved, and the board says it “remains confident” in the 2030 ambition.

So why sell at anything less than top dollar? Neither the 24% premium on the pre-action share price, nor the 36% cited as the boost to the 12-month rolling average, scream unmissable value.

Fidelity International’s Alex Wright said at the start of this month he wouldn’t accept less than £70 a share and laid out his reasons: DCC’s attractive returns on capital; the scope for growth through acquisitions; pricing power in a consolidating market; share buybacks to boost earnings per share; overdone fears about the structural decline of the fossil fuel distribution business; and the potential to scale up the renewable energy activities.

DCC management’s explanation for acceptance was the standard one about “a compelling and certain opportunity for DCC Energy shareholders to realise value in cash today”. Well, yes, there is always “execution risk” in any strategy. But the revealing bit was the long grumble about the difficulty of finding new investors.

“The DCC Energy shareholder register has become more concentrated in recent years and the number of market participants that have engaged in the story has reduced over time,” the company said. Feedback suggested “exposure to low-volume growth end markets” – in other words, petrol stations and gas distribution – “weighs on perceived terminal value and, in turn, DCC Energy’s trading multiple”.

DCC managed to tickle up the bidders in stages from £58 a share initially to £65.25 (or almost £68 if one includes an already paid dividend plus a contingent 125p that depends on a remaining technology business being sold at a good price), so one can’t say the board has not negotiated hard. The chief executive, Donal Murphy, is almost certainly correct when he predicts the majority of shareholders will vote in favour.

But the basic plot here is yet another bad advert for London in terms of risk-taking and depth of capital. In short, a couple of private equity firms, via their infrastructure funds, are willing to take a far longer-term view of DCC’s prospects than public market investors (with honourable exceptions) will.

The story isn’t new – most all-cash bids succeed – but a newly depressing feature is the regularity. Last week it was Segro, the warehouse landlord, falling to a bigger US rival for £14bn. The broker Peel Hunt calculated 154 bids for UK companies with a market value of more than £100m, equating to £165bn of stock market capitalisation, since the start of 2023. They’re not all private equity deals, of course – but London is the buyout brigade’s happiest hunting ground. In the meantime, arrivals on the London market have dried to a trickle.

In a different world, the shrinking of the UK stock market, and thus soft political power on a global stage, would be causing alarm in Westminster. Sadly, the political class either haven’t noticed or aren’t bothered. They’ll regret it one day.

Trump warns of return to ‘strong military action’ if Iran diplomacy fails

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 17:02:56 GMT

Washington and Tehran issue conflicting messages over the status of talks to end Middle East crisis

Donald Trump has once again warned that the US will return to “strong military action” against Iran if diplomatic efforts do not bring a rapid resolution to the crisis in the Middle East.

“We are in very deep talks with Iran. If they don’t work out, we will go back to very strong military action,” the US president told Axios on Monday. Asked for how long he would allow the talks to proceed, he answered: “Not much time. Either it goes fast or not at all.”

He reiterated the line to reporters later the same day on Air Force One. “They want to meet, and we’re meeting. Without what we did, they wouldn’t even be talking to us … They would not have requested the meeting if we were doing poorly. The only reason they want to meet is because we’ve been hitting them very hard.”

He doubled down at a rally in Michigan soon after. “You ⁠can’t bribe them. ​You’ve ‌got ‌to beat them, ‌and we’ll beat the hell out of them. But we’ll ‌see how it turns out,” ​he said . “Right now, ⁠there are very ​friendly negotiations going ​on.”

Earlier, Tehran said there were no direct talks with the US to end the conflict, which began in late February with a wave of US-Israeli strikes and has rocked the region and the global economy.

“Mediators may convey messages from the American side to us regarding current developments in the region. But at present we are not engaged in any negotiations with the United States,” said the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei.

The diplomatic back and forth came as Oman and Iran drew closer to an agreement in principle on the future management of the strait of Hormuz, but remained unable to resolve Tehran’s demand that all ships passing through the strategic waterway must pay some type of transit fee or toll to a consortium led by the two countries.

Oman and Iran met for technical talks in Tehran on Friday and Saturday that may hold the key to preventing a further round of fighting.

Perceived progress in the talks – backed by China, Qatar and Pakistan – was understood to have fed into the US decision to pause its attacks on Iran after nearly two weeks.

Senior US officials are also reported to have warned Trump over dwindling US munitions stockpiles and the impact of Iranian reprisals on US bases in the region, including Kuwait and Jordan.

The top US military commander in the Middle East, Adm Brad Cooper, reportedly recommended stopping the bombing campaign around the strait because it had reached the limit of its effectiveness.

The US attacks have been described by Washington as a response to repeated Iranian breaches of the memorandum of understanding signed in June, including by trying to prevent commercial shipping from transiting the strait through a southern route overseen by the US.

Iran argues the southern route breaks the ceasefire agreement, which it insists left the country in sole charge of how the strait was reopened.

A diplomat said: “The aim of the Tehran talks is to marry the Iran and Oman proposals so what emerges is clearly compliant with the law of the sea, and internationally acceptable.”

At a Tehran press conference, Baqaei denied that the pause in US fighting amounted to an informal ceasefire.

Oman has been trying since May to persuade Tehran that any plan for charging fees in the strait must be voluntary, to comply with the law of the sea. It has proposed a model similar to that which governs the strait of Malacca: countries that use it voluntarily contribute to a fund that provides for environmental and safety services to shipping.

Oman argues that a similar entity could be set up in the strait of Hormuz with the agreement of the UN and the International Maritime Organization. The IMO secretary general, Arsenio Dominguez, has told the Guardian that the Malacca strait model is worth considering for the strait of Hormuz.

Iran’s department of environment has drafted its own plan, under which “the annual passage of over 50,000 ships and oil tankers through the strait of Hormuz and their role in polluting the Persian Gulf” must be compensated for. Under the plan, Iran would be able to collect “fees” from passing vessels proportional to the type of ship, cargo volume, navigation history and history of pollution.

The comparison between the straits of Malacca and Hormuz is imperfect since fewer ships see ports in the Malacca strait as a destination point. But the Iranian media appear increasingly drawn to the Malacca model. The Khabaronline news agency argued such an agreement would be “a win-win situation for Iran”.

Baqaei described the talks with Oman as useful and constructive but said they had nothing to do with the US. “The goal is for Iran and Oman, as two coastal states, to develop mechanisms to ensure safe shipping in the strait of Hormuz, while respecting the sovereign rights of the two coastal states and also preserving Iran’s security and national interests,” he said.

Oman is in a tight spot since it knows the US is opposed to the introduction of tolls, but it may accept a very clearly delineated system of fees for specific services.

The talks come as the US continues to encourage commercial shipping to test the strength of the Iranian blockade of the strait.

Iranian officials reported that six vessels with their navigation systems switched off attempted to pass through the southern route of the strait on Sunday. One of them was fired upon and the others were turned back to the Persian Gulf. The US has reimposed a blockade of Iranian oil exports and ended a sanctions waiver on its oil exports.

The United Nations Office for Project Services said on Monday that transits through the strait of Hormuz had fallen to an average of approximately five ships a day over the past week, compared with nearly 130 a day before the war.

How Andy Burnham can make his devolution agenda work

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 16:48:15 GMT

Rabbi Jeff Newman, David Williams and Tom Carr respond to an editorial on the new prime minister’s plans to decentralise power

Your editorial (22 July) rightly identifies the structural paradox at the heart of Andy Burnham’s devolution agenda – that it takes a confident assertion of central power to give real power away. But one institutional mechanism that goes some way to resolving this paradox operationally deserves mention: the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority (Nista), which has sat jointly between the Treasury and the Cabinet Office since April 2025.

Inherited from Keir Starmer’s government, Nista (with about 250 civil servants) merges what were the National Infrastructure Commission and the Infrastructure and Projects Authority into a single body reporting simultaneously to both departments. Under Starmer, the Cabinet Office side of that dual accountability was relatively weak. Under Louise Haigh’s new Office of the Prime Minister and Cabinet – explicitly endorsed by the Institute for Government as implementing long-called-for structural reforms – that balance may shift.

Nista becomes, potentially, the operational expression of the relationship between Haigh and John Healey, the new chancellor, that your editorial identifies as central to whether Burnham’s ambitions survive contact with Treasury orthodoxy.

Whether it works will depend significantly on Healey. Your editorial frames him as “not a big beast of the species likely to build a power base to rival Mr Burnham”, which may be accurate. But it understates the more interesting question of his formation. Before entering parliament, Healey spent years in disability rights and trade union work – at Mind and the Trades Union Congress, where he helped design the national minimum wage.

That pre-parliamentary biography suggests a chancellor whose instincts may align more naturally with the “preventive state” agenda than his Brown-era Treasury service implies. His predecessor Denis Healey’s capitulation to Treasury orthodoxy in 1976 shaped British politics for 50 years – the stakes of getting this relationship right are that high.

The paradox that your editorial identifies is real. Nista, under a genuinely strengthened Cabinet Office, is at least an attempt to resolve it institutionally rather than just rhetorically. Rabbi Jeff NewmanFinchley, London

Andy Burnham’s determination to make regional devolution a reality rather than a catchphrase (remember the “northern powerhouse”?) is laudable and potentially gamechanging, but it depends so much on the ability, altruism, efficiency and drive of the regional mayors and civic leaders whose job it will be to deliver it. How many of them have the capability that Andy Burnham has shown in Manchester?

I suspect the truth is that we don’t really know. How many of us even know the names of these people, never mind what their particular strengths and proclivities are? And if that is true of those in our own region, how much more so of those we entrust to deliver in their part of the country, within the context of the national interest? Who are they, what is their motivation and what got them into the positions they occupy?

If Burnham’s policy is to be carried out properly, our expectations of these representatives have now become much wider. They are potentially champions of us all. I for one would be interested in a Guardian profile of these key regional ambassadors.

Having been in regional development in a past role myself, I have seen both good and bad, and I recognise how crucial these roles can, and must, be if they are to be the engineers of growth for us all. David WilliamsHexham, Northumberland

It is certainly refreshing to hear that our new prime minister is trying to decentralise our London-centric government by opening a No 10 North in Manchester. However, reading his comments, it appears that he identifies Manchester as “the north”. He must realise that the north of England is much more than just the Manchester conurbation, and that replacing a single-centre approach with a double-centre one will not in itself achieve his aims of improving every postcode in the country. Tom CarrNewcastle upon Tyne

After the 1981 English House Condition Survey, which showed the high rate of disrepair in the housing stock, the government introduced generous repair grants, and contributed £1bn through subsidies. The decision to discontinue funding for the private sector housing renewal programme, which had been reduced to £376m in 2009‑10, was a result of austerity. Perhaps Andy Burnham and Angela Rayner need to revisit the past to learn what can be done. Dr Stephen Battersby Environmental health and housing consultant (retired)
