France and Spain race to contain huge wildfires before fresh heatwave begins

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 16:36:30 GMT

Coming days are ‘absolutely critical’ for firefighters before temperatures rise again this week, officials say

Firefighters in France and Spain are racing to bring huge wildfires under control before another heatwave this week that will complicate efforts to tame the flames.

Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, said Monday and Tuesday were “absolutely crucial days” before temperatures rise again from Wednesday.

EU officials have said wildfires could still be burning until early November in what threatens to be a record-breaking year for the area of land burned.

A fire in the hilly terrain of Ávila, west of Madrid, has become Spain’s largest on record, burning 50,000 hectares (123,000 acres). Authorities are battling two separate fires north-west of Madrid, taking the total area of scorched land near the capital to 70,000 hectares.

France was also in “a race against time” to control wildfires before another heatwave this week, said Eric Brocardi, a fire service spokesperson. Weather forecasters have said temperatures could reach 40C (104F) is some parts of the country from Tuesday.

This would complicate efforts to control the wildfire in Gironde in south-west France, which the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, described as “extremely intense and unpredictable ... generating its own winds and advancing erratically toward the Bordeaux metropolitan area”.

The French president, Emmanuel Macron, on a visit to Bordeaux, said: “The coming weeks will be tough and we have to hold out.”

But he said a smaller fire in the adjoining Landes – which forced the evacuation of more than 30,000 people – was “contained” but remained “virulent”. “We must be extremely cautious over the next few hours and the coming days,” he said.

The Gironde fire has so far burned 42,000 hectares, making it one of the biggest devastations of land in France since the second world war.

In the Cestas commune, about 10 miles (17km) from the city of Bordeaux, firefighters used mechanical diggers to uproot trees in an attempt to create a firebreak.

The vast fire, which has triggered the evacuation of 220,000 people, had not progressed during the early hours of Monday but was “not contained” and remained “very complicated to control”, Nuñez said.

Speaking after an emergency meeting of the French government on Monday, he described this year’s wildfires as “completely exceptional”. More than 116,000 hectares of forest and vegetation have been burned since January, far exceeding the 70,000 hectares reported for the whole of 2025.

Spain’s government said the 172,000 hectares of forested land burned this year was six times greater than the equivalent figure for 2025.

The prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, told a climate conference the wildfires were not isolated incidents. “It is the most painful manifestation of a climate emergency that is making … wildfires more voracious and heatwaves more frequent, and as a result our land more vulnerable,” he said. “It is no longer an exception. It is the rule.”

The European Commission’s lead official on the green transition, Teresa Ribera, said Europe was not prepared for the consequences of the climate crisis. In an interview with El País she said the commission would propose an adaptation strategy in October that would be much more comprehensive than policies implemented so far.

A series of heatwaves, including record-breaking temperatures in June, that scientists say would have been impossible without the climate crisis, has left parched soils and tinder-dry vegetation that have fuelled this summer’s fires.

A European Commission official said the wildfire season had begun in April and could last until early November. Officials also stressed the rising risks for fighting wildfires from the middle of the week in France, Spain and Greece.

The EU executive has coordinated the despatch of seven planes and four helicopters to France, as well as six planes and three forest firefighting teams to Spain, after the countries triggered the bloc’s emergency assistance mechanism. EU officials have also been sent to the Bordeaux region to assist local authorities.

Officials stressed the unprecedented nature of recent fires, which have spread rapidly over large areas. A commission official said that a recent fire in southern Spain that killed 13 people had reached speeds of 6km/h (more than 3mph), while firefighters are able to react only to fires moving 300 metres an hour or less.

The scale of Europe’s wildfires has raised questions about the continent’s ability to respond. Italy is among about 10 European countries that have sent firefighting equipment or teams to France and Spain while grappling with its own blazes.

Firefighters fought to extinguish a major wildfire in the southern region of Puglia on Monday. More than 400 people, many of them tourists staying in campsites set among pine forests, were evacuated by sea from the Gargano peninsula on Sunday as the blaze, fanned by strong winds, encroached on beaches.

A further 58 people were evacuated from their homes in Maratea as a wildfire swept through neighbouring Basilicata.

Italy is bracing for its fourth heatwave this year as temperatures edge up towards highs of 38 to 40C from Wednesday.

Smoke from the fires in France is continuing to cause a “marked deterioration” in air quality across a swathe of the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region and beyond, with health authorities warning about the danger.

Elderly people, pregnant women and those with respiratory issues and chronic conditions were advised to take precautions. Local health authorities said people should close windows, wear an FFP2 mask outside and avoid strenuous activity.

The prime minister’s office said more than 1.5 million FFP2 masks had been sent to the region.

I work in a hospital – and didn’t know I was having a heart attack. Here’s what more women should know

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 16:35:40 GMT

Women and men exhibit different heart attack symptoms. Knowing these lesser-known factors can help save your life

A few months ago at work, when I rose from my seat and walked a few steps, something felt off. There was a strange pressure in my chest and rib cage, but I ignored it, took my water bottle from the kitchen and returned to my desk.

The next day it happened again. There was no pain and my breathing was fine. But whenever I stood up and took a few steps, the odd squeezing would return. I work at a hospital as a neurosurgery coordinator, and the wall was lined with posters about stroke and heart distress signs. I barely glanced at the pictures, having memorized them years ago.

I stood in the hallway waiting for the sensation to pass. One of my co-workers, a nurse, saw me and asked if something was wrong. I told her I felt achy in my upper body, and that my neck and chest felt odd. She suggested I go to the ER.

“You never know,” she said. I thought it was probably just a pulled muscle, but I followed her advice. I owe her my life.

Deaths from heart disease are the number one killer of women, according to the American Heart Association. It causes a third of deaths a year – more than all forms of cancers combined.

At the ER, I mentioned the pressure in my chest area so the triage staff ran tests to check for heart trouble. However, they saw nothing abnormal on my electrocardiogram (which measures electric heart rhythm) or troponin levels (a protein blood test used to diagnose heart attacks).

The emergency staff sent me home with cholesterol and blood pressure medication. The following morning, I called a cardiologist because I was still having the odd sensation. After checking my arteries with a catheter, the doctor admitted me to the hospital. They had found blockages in two of my arteries; one was in the largest coronary artery, the kind of blockage that leads to so-called “widowmaker” heart attacks.

According to the physicians, it was severe enough to discuss heart bypass surgery. Fortunately, a stent was sufficient. The ER staff thought I might have had a heart attack and would have been on my way to another without medical intervention. When I heard the news, I was stunned. I worked in healthcare and was familiar with the signs of cardiac issues. How could I not know my heart was in serious trouble?

It turns out that this issue is fairly common. Symptoms show up differently in women – something I am now grateful to know.

A heart attack is a specific event, in which the blood flow to the heart muscle is suddenly blocked. (Conversely, heart disease refers to any condition that affects the heart – a common example is coronary artery disease, a buildup of plaque in the arteries. Symptoms for heart attack and heart disease are not the same, but there is some overlap.)

Symptoms of heart attacks are different for men and women, according to the American Heart Association.

The most common signs for men are pain in the chest, left arm, jaw, neck or back; nausea, vomiting, indigestion; and shortness of breath.

For women, the list of possible symptoms is longer: chest pain or pressure in lower chest, upper abdomen, jaw, neck and upper back; nausea or vomiting; fainting and shortness of breath; indigestion or extreme fatigue. Chest pain or pressure is not always present.

In addition, issues such as high blood pressure during pregnancy, menopause, hormone replacement therapy and use of birth control should be considered in evaluating overall risk.

However, this list is not exhaustive. Women should be prepared to look into other areas that may not stand out as symptomatic. For instance, the heart and stomach share nerves, and many women do not know that indigestion, nausea and GI distress can also be heart disease symptoms, said Dr Sirisha Vadali, a cardiologist at HonorHealth in Scottsdale, Arizona, specializing in women’s heart disease: “Lesser-known external factors are vital to getting an accurate diagnosis.”

Vadali also said it was important to notice even small physical changes that may not seem related to the heart. I told Vadali about my unexpected diagnosis. “I hate to say it, but I’m not surprised,” she said. “I’ve spoken to many women who feel something is wrong, and don’t present the way men do. It’s difficult to explain to medical personnel that nothing really hurts, but your body is telling you there is real trouble – somewhere.”

According to the British Heart Foundation, symptoms may come on acutely, like they did for me. Vadali cautions women to take note of any sense that their body is responding differently and consult a medical provider if concerned.

“I had one young woman who couldn’t walk up a flight of stairs today, but she did two last week just fine,” she said of a patient who ended up needing prompt cardiac assistance.

Vadali mentioned many women dismiss their own symptoms as anxiety, or just assume they are unfit.

“There’s an under-appreciation of cardiovascular risks in women,” said Dr Americo Simonini, a cardiovascular specialist with Cedars-Sinai medical center in Los Angeles. Other than the usual sugar, cholesterol and blood pressure checks, what else should we be checking for?

“We aggressively measure other things in men that we should be measuring in women,” said Simonini. He mentioned certain types of tests for proteins in the blood and inflammation can present a clearer picture in preventing a future incident, including:

Elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, or hs-CRP, score: the level of these proteins increases with inflammation, and a high level can indicate blood vessels in the heart are narrowing (cardiovascular disease).

Lipoprotein(a) elevation: a genetic test for inherited LDL (“bad”) cholesterol; high levels significantly increase risk of heart attack via plaque buildup in arteries.

Apolipoprotein B elevation: measures the amount of Apo B, which carries substances in your blood that make the plaque.

Coronary artery calcium score (high CAC): a high score probably means a large amount of plaque is present in arteries and the risk of a future heart attack is high.

“There is a misconception that women are protected until menopause. That’s simply not true,” Simonini said. Women can develop heart disease at any age, but your risk increases after your periods stop. Before menopause, your body makes more estrogen, which helps protect against heart disease. That’s also why women generally develop coronary artery disease later than men.

after newsletter promotion

Women of all ages are surprised to learn they have heart disease, said Dr Sonal Chandra of Focus Cardiology, a private practice in Chicago, Illinois.

“Women are far less likely to receive imaging or other interventions. This happens even when they are showing comparable indicators and classic symptoms of heart distress,” she said. “No one should feel they have to walk away without some answers.”

If patients feel their complaints are not being addressed, they can and should ask for additional diagnostic testing. The more information you have on how symptoms are evolving, the better.

Physicians need to pay attention to women who notice any abnormal physical changes, rather than assume it’s temporary or simply fatigue and stress, Simonini said. Doctors should ask questions and find out why a patient is having those symptoms at that time.

He acknowledged that doctors need more education about women and their disease risks. All of the experts I spoke to encourage women to advocate for themselves by doing the following:

Ask your primary care doctor what kinds of cardiac testing are available to you. If bloodwork is suggested first, do it. If you have a family history of heart attacks and want to check your arteries now, discuss proteins and inflammation markers. You may need to consult a specialist for these steps.

Provide as much information as possible, even if you don’t think it’s related to your current problem. It could make a difference in someone deciding on a scan or sending you to the ER. The more details you provide, the better someone can assist. For instance, if you have a stomach ache that hasn’t gone away in three days, disclose it.

Keep asking about next steps. You are entitled to an answer and it’s the doctor’s job to help you find it. If your inquiries are not being taken seriously, book an appointment elsewhere. Do not give up or wait it out. Persistence can help you identify serious risks.

Not every pain or ache means you have a serious health issue, nor that it is cardiac related. It’s important to remember that, outside of a sharp shooting pain above your heart, it truly could be something minor. There is also no single test that can predict your future health. Numerous variables and overlapping conditions are part of a much larger map. Experts simply encourage you to take notice of your own risk factors and monitor how you feel.

Historically, large-scale research specific to female biology and genetics has not been available. In the 2010s, one heart health researcher noted that the participants in typical cardiovascular disease clinical trials were 85% male and that female participants were predominantly postmenopausal.

For example, an influential large-scale clinical study that began in 2011, known as the Million Veteran Program (MVP), involved mostly white, male participants from a similar age group. Participants were monitored for kidney function, blood pressure and diabetes over a span of 20 years. “They had all this data but only from a specific group,” Simonini noted. This massive pool of data informed how treatments and drugs for cardiac disease were developed – and that knowledge became the standard. The MVP has since added new data sets to include a more diverse population.

If research trials were more accommodating, greater female participation would probably follow, said Chandra.

“Women are often primary care givers and work full-time, and it can be a hardship for them to participate during business hours,” she said.

However, the experts I spoke to agree that over the past 10 years, education about gender differences in cardiac health has been slowly improving.

In 2016, the University of Pennsylvania established a dedicated women’s cardiovascular health curriculum for its cardiology fellowship program. Columbia University offers program electives for medical students, residents and graduate students on cardiovascular risks unique to women. This year at Harvard Medical School, continuing medical education credits (CME) are being offered for “diagnosing, managing, and treating medical conditions unique to and prevalent in women”.

Experts stressed the importance of regular testing and checkups from your primary care provider. This can provide both of you with baseline information to compare future measurements against. Check in with them more than once a year if changes such as medications or procedures are necessary, experts say. Provide as much detail about family, environment and diet as possible. This can help your doctor design a prevention plan for the next five years or beyond. This may involve nutrition, genetic testing, imaging, medication or other lifestyle changes.

“Keep asking more and more questions; we are in a profession where we can’t afford to be wrong,” Simonini said.

Julie Charnet is a healthcare worker and writer in Philadelphia

Jockey Club staff cull leaves Derby feeling flat with Ascot and Goodwood riding high

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 16:35:12 GMT

Jim Allen’s drive, enthusiasm and focus will be a big loss to the five-year Epsom project to revive the Classic

The King George card at Ascot on Saturday was an day that showcased Flat racing at its best and the sense of optimism at the end of the afternoon was only enhanced by the prospect of five days at Glorious Goodwood this week.

Scandinavia and Trawlerman will reprise their Ascot Gold Cup rivalry in Tuesday’s Goodwood Cup. The big three of Bow Echo, Gstaad and Opera Ballo have been declared for Wednesday’s £1.5m Sussex Stakes. Diamond Necklace, the French Oaks winner, is lined up for the Nassau Stakes on Thursday while on the final day the fierce punting challenge of the Stewards’ Cup, one of the biggest betting races of the summer, lurks on the Saturday card.

Racing rarely proceeds seamlessly from one highlight to another, however, and news emerged last week that Jockey Club Racecourses, the biggest commercial operator in British racing, is to lose up to 30 staff after a restructuring overseen by Jim Mullen, the former boss of Reach, who joined the Jockey Club as chief executive in June 2025.

For the moment at least, the redundancy process remains voluntary, but 30 jobs is nearly 5% of a 650-strong workforce, not all of whom are being offered the chance to leave, so some compulsory redundancies may yet be required. The most surprising departure so far is Jim Allen, the general manager at Epsom since October 2024, who is an originator as well as the public face of the track’s five-year plan to revive the status and popularity of the Derby.

Allen, who opted for voluntary redundancy in preference to applying for a newly created role overseeing a “London Hub” of tracks that includes Epsom, told the Racing Post on Sunday he is “sure [the five-year plan] will stay”, though “it will be tweaked and improved as there’s still a way to go and it was never going to happen in one year”.

For Allen, the Derby project was not just a professional commitment. He had a deep personal investment in the scheme having grown up near the course and started his career in racing as a work-rider on the downs. His rich and varied path through the sport has included senior roles in racecourse management and a spell as a trainer in the United States. He may now return to a more hands-on role as a trainer or syndicate manager.

“It’s all very amicable,” he told the Post, “and I’m hoping I’ll be back at next year’s Derby festival with some sort of runner.”

Amicable though it may be, Allen’s drive, enthusiasm and focus will be a big loss to the Derby project, which has the ultimate aim of returning to a 100,000 attendance for the two days of Epsom’s Classic meeting.

It is not a loss that can be easily quantified on a balance sheet, and Mullen – who oversaw a 25% cut in headcount during his six-year tenure at Reach – has targeted cost savings to arrest a decline in JCR’s profitability.

Mullen signed an exclusive £100m, 20-year deal in March with the hospitality company Levy with the aim of improving the raceday experience for spectators, but JCR’s recently filed accounts for 2025 reflect the extent to which the business’s costs – including the wage bill and increased national insurance obligations – have been rising faster than revenue.

“With that in mind,” a Jockey Club spokesperson said on Monday, “we have been working over the past six months on a plan to ensure we have an organisation able to maximise the potential of investing the £100m … realised earlier this year.

“Our aim is to give our racecourse teams more autonomy when it comes to commercial decision-making and ownership of the customer experience at their venues. It is also about us creating a more successful and sustainable business that can play a larger role in supporting, investing in and growing the sport while promoting racing and the thoroughbred.”

JCR remains the biggest commercial entity in the sport and is unlikely to surrender that status any time soon. A round of job cuts, though, is a sharp contrast to the mood at tracks such as Ascot, Goodwood and York, where the Ebor meeting will take centre stage next month.

What is also unclear – because the accounts do not single out individuals tracks’ profit-and-loss figures – is the extent to which JCR’s profits depend on the major National Hunt festivals at Cheltenham and Aintree in March. That only Cheltenham has been left as a stand-alone entity in the restructuring probably tells its own story.

It is an odd turn of racing history that has led the Jockey Club, which is so firmly rooted in Newmarket and Flat racing, become increasingly reliant on the runaway success of Cheltenham and its festival meeting over the past two or three decades.

The five-year scheme to revive the Derby was, and remains, a way to bring Flat racing – which, unlike jumping, has a global audience – at least a little more back into the JCR mix. There are still plenty of very capable people at the operation’s HQ, but losing Jim Allen’s passion for the project feels like a setback it could well do without.

David Jonsson: the London rising star handpicked to be the new Black Panther

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 16:31:48 GMT

Jonsson has come a long way from east London’s Docklands, winning accolades on stage and screen

Few characters carry the cultural weight of Black Panther. Since 2018, the Wakandan king has become a global symbol of Black excellence, credited with reshaping expectations of representation on screen.

The first film grossed more than $1.3bn (£1bn) worldwide, won three Oscars and became the first superhero movie nominated for best picture.

Now, six years after the death of the film’s star, Chadwick Boseman, Marvel has found its next T’Challa: British star David Jonsson, who will play Boseman’s son in Black Panther 3.

The character’s grip on fans is so huge that when Jonsson was introduced on stage by director Ryan Coogler at Comic-Con in San Diego at the weekend, the crowd erupted into chants of “Wakanda forever”.

According to Marvel, Coogler first suggested Jonsson for one of Hollywood’s most coveted blockbuster roles six months ago.

“He called me and said: ‘I found him’,” Marvel Studios president, Kevin Feige recalled. “‘He’s this guy, David Jonsson.’”

It is a remarkable ascent for an actor who grew up in the east London Docklands, was expelled from school, and, only a few years ago, was best known for his part in the HBO/BBC banking drama Industry.

Coogler later told Feige he knew Jonsson was right for the role after meeting him privately following the completion of Sinners. “He’s the guy,” he said. “I felt it in my soul. He’s a good man, and he is the next Black Panther.”

Jonsson, 32, grew up in Custom House in Newham, the youngest of four children. His father worked as an IT engineer at Heathrow, his mother worked for the Metropolitan police. He describes his heritage as Creole, with roots in Nigeria, Sierra Leone, the Caribbean and Sweden.

He has spoken of the upheaval that followed his parents’ separation when he was 11. He pushed boundaries at school and was eventually expelled for fighting as a teenager.

“I wasn’t a bad kid at all,” the self-described introvert told the Guardian. “I was just a bit … distracted at the time.”

It was around then that Jonsson told his mother – one of the first Black police community support officers in London – that he wanted to be an actor.

At a new school in Hammersmith, a 90-minute commute across the city, he began performing in school plays, and at 16 won a scholarship to the American Academy of Dramatic Arts in New York. Returning to Britain two years later, he joined the National Youth Theatre before winning a place the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art.

Jonsson left drama school early to join a revival of Mary Stuart opposite Juliet Stevenson, which transferred to the West End; his 2021 performance in And Breathe … at the Almeida won him a Black British Theatre Award.

Television came alongside his stage work. After early roles in the ITV detective drama Endeavour and the Fox UK espionage thriller Deep State, his breakthrough came as Gus Sackey in Industry, the cult drama about young graduates clawing their way up a London investment bank.

To prepare, Jonsson immersed himself in a world of elite schools and Oxbridge privilege far removed from his own upbringing. He left the show in 2022. “Life is short, art is long,” he later told GQ.

His ascent since then has been rapid. His first film lead came in Raine Allen-Miller’s acclaimed 2023 romcom Rye Lane, which premiered at Sundance to critical acclaim and earned him a British Independent Film Award (Bifa) nomination.

He became the first Black lead in a television adaptation of Agatha Christie with the BBC’s Murder Is Easy.

Then came the sci-fi horror Alien: Romulus in 2024 – which earned him the Bafta Rising Star award, the Stephen King adaptation The Long Walk, and the British prison film Wasteman, which earned him his second Bifa nomination.

Jonsson has long been conscious of what his roles represent. “Every character I do, no matter what, I’m going to be a Black man first,” he has said.

Accepting his Bafta award last year, he added: “Growing up, I had the Denzel Washingtons and Idris Elbas, but they’re not me.

“There’s not enough space for diverse talent in this industry. I realise I have an important role in defining what Black is.”

Paul Roseby, CEO and artistic director of the National Youth Theatre, said: “I remember watching David play the lead in our adaptation of Pigeon English with Bristol Old Vic in 2013. He was electrifying.

“His kindness and generosity as a creative and a person continues to shine through. We’re very grateful to him for taking the time in recent years to share his experience with our current generation of talent, and very proud of everything he is going on to achieve.”

Interviewers have described him as warm, with “an innate sense of decency” – which would make him the perfect successor to Boseman, who was deeply respected for his humility and grace.

The mantle of Black Panther passed once before, to Letitia Wright’s Shuri in Black Panther: Wakanda Forever (2022).

Jonsson plays the next generation of Wakanda’s royal family, inheriting both the character’s name and its huge legacy.

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 16:23:37 GMT

Welsh sprinter Azu: ‘I would never disrespect the flag’

It took Elliot Jones, an unheralded English 100m sprinter making his major international debut at the grand age of 28, to cut through the noise. Asked about all the no-shows at these Commonwealth Games, he began to shake his head, almost in disbelief.

“The national pride I have is so, so high,” Jones said. “I personally don’t understand why athletes wouldn’t want to come and represent their country, regardless of timetables. I’m going to take every international call I can get.”

For those not counting, nine Team England athletes have withdrawn during the past week, including the former world champions Katarina Johnson-Thompson and Dina Asher‑Smith. Most have not given a reason why. The poster girl of these Games, Scotland’s Eilish McColgan, also withdrew on Saturday after failing to recover from injury in time.

Yet those absentees have created a potential real-life golden ticket for others. And no one grabbed it harder on Monday than Jones, a part‑time athlete whose day job is working for Uefa on matchday operations in the Champions League and the Europa League.

On Thursday night, he received a phone call from the England team’s sprints manager to ask whether he fancied running in the 100m after Louie Hinchliffe pulled out. “Let me think about that,” Jones replied, before shouting: “Yes!”

“I had to get the Glasgow bus at nine the next morning, quickly pack and restructure my training plan but it’s fine, we’re always ready,” Jones said. “It was supposed to take us six hours but it took us seven with the traffic.”

And having got here, Jones was in no mood to mess about in his first major championship as he ran 10.07sec to qualify third overall for the semi-finals on Tuesday.

It was heartening to hear – especially given that several Olympic and world champions are missing, including Keely Hodgkinson, Letsile Tebogo and Julien Alfred, the women’s 100m champion in Paris whose poster is outside the Scotstounhill train station.

A similar message was delivered by the Wales athlete Jeremiah Azu, the world indoor 60m champion last year, after he had scooted through his 100m heat in 10.10. Asked why he had decided to go to Glasgow, he pointed to the word Cymru on his vest. “Because of this,” Azu said. “To put this vest on is such a privilege and an honour, and I would never put that opportunity to the side. I would never disrespect the flag like that.”

Despite the absence of the 100m world champion Oblique Seville, a strong men’s field still includes athletes such as Nigeria’s Kanyinsola Ajayi, who ran 9.84 to win the London Diamond League meeting ahead of Seville just over a week ago.

On the women’s side, though, the story is very different. Six of the top 10 100m times in 2026 have also been run by Commonwealth athletes – none of whom are actually running the event in Glasgow. However, England’s Imani-Lara Lansiquot, who has two 4x100m Olympic medals to her name, said she was delighted to be at the “Friendly Games”.

Lansiquot said: “I think this competition is a great springboard for athletes. And it’s a great springboard for us as a country, in a time where it feels very divided. You walk around our hotel, the energy is buzzing. Everyone has that sense of togetherness, and that’s what I love about this competition.”

That mood was reflected in a surprisingly strong crowd of 7,500 on the opening morning, despite temperatures in the low teens. As Billy Connolly once joked: “There are two seasons in Scotland, June and Winter.” Yet on the track and off, it soon warmed up.

And they cheered everyone on, including stragglers such as Tye Leo‑Stroud of Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha, who ran a season’s best 11.85 in the men’s 100m – nearly two seconds behind. “It was cold – I didn’t expect it,” Leo‑Stroud said. “Where I am from is very hot, both during day and at night. There will be lots of good races in the days ahead, especially in the men’s mile when the new world record-holder, Josh Kerr, faces off against his compatriot Jake Wightman and the brilliant new Australian star, Cam Myers. The women’s 800m, meanwhile, is also a tantalising rematch between Kenya’s Lilian Odira and England’s Georgia Hunter Bell, who finished first and second at the world championships.

At the end of the first session on Monday the England Athletics team leader, Scott Grace, defended those who had pulled out, saying that some had preferred to focus on the European championships in Birmingham in two weeks’ time. “Because when you’re a world-class athlete, putting your body through three rounds here, three rounds there, is hard,” Grace said.

Families in London temporary housing told they cannot use in-built air conditioning

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 16:21:53 GMT

Exclusive: Two children taken to hospital during heatwaves after residents told units in glass-fronted block ‘not offered as amenity’

Homeless families placed in temporary accommodation in London were told they could not use the in-built air conditioning as it had “not been offered as an amenity” for them, leading to two children being hospitalised during recent heatwaves.

Other families placed in Britannia Point in Colliers Wood, south-west London, also experienced such stifling conditions that young children became ill. The company managing some of the tenancies involved told the Guardian households in temporary accommodation had now been told they could use the air conditioning.

However, some residents said they were informed that if they used the system they would be billed via a standing charge rather than for how long the air conditioning ran, which could result in bills of up to £500 for the summer.

The 19-storey glass-fronted block is owned by Criterion Capital, set up by the billionaire property magnate Asif Aziz. The company was accused this year of trying to mass-evict tenants shortly before no-fault evictions were banned, something it has denied.

The temporary accommodation tenancies, in which councils place otherwise homeless households in properties for periods that can last from weeks to years, are managed separately by lettings agencies, one of them London-based Aura Assets Management.

After a tenant complained to the building management about their air conditioning not working, they were sent an email, seen by the Guardian, which said that under the tenancy as managed by Aura, air conditioning “has been switched off” for households in emergency accommodation.

It went on: “Air conditioning has not been offered as an amenity under these arrangements, and the units cannot be switched back on as a result. You are welcome to use a portable fan or portable air conditioning unit at your own arrangement in the meantime.”

Residents say the all-glass construction of the block and the fact that windows open only slightly mean that, without air conditioning, their flats have become unbearably hot.

“It is very difficult to cool the flats down,” one person said. “I find that as soon as I enter the building, I become much hotter, start feeling sick and sweat profusely.”

Alice Rogers, who lives in Britannia Point with her four-year-old son, Hassan, said they regularly had to leave the block due to the heat. “There is a window that you can open, but there’s not much of a difference that makes,” she said. “Whether you open it or close it, it’s just literally the same.”

She added: “My son had a nosebleed the other day and was faint. I’m very much worried about his life.”

Stuart Neaverson, a Labour councillor in Merton who has been trying to help people in Britannia Point along with the local MP, Labour’s Siobhain McDonagh, said he had been told about two children being taken to hospital because of the heat, calling the situation “disgraceful”.

‘It felt like being in a disaster movie’: uncertainty after evacuation from France’s Gironde wildfire

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 16:13:56 GMT

Residents describe their fear as they were forced to leave their homes because of the ‘extremely intense’ blaze

Sitting in their suburban apartment in Mérignac on the outskirts of Bordeaux, Krishma, an interpreter, and her husband, Nassir, first felt a sense of dread when a strange black cloud turned the sky dark in the middle of the day. Then a bitter burning smell filled the air outside.

“The sky changed colour. It seemed like a cloud but it was smoke covering the sun – it wasn’t a natural phenomenon. It didn’t seem real,” said Nassir, an English literature graduate from Kabul who has been living in France for seven years. “We couldn’t breathe easily, you could feel it in your lungs.”

The acrid smell, which at first seemed like burning rubber then unmistakably like wood smoke, was blowing on the wind from the massive wildfire in Gironde in south-western France. The blaze has torn through 42,000 hectares, an area four times the size of Paris, causing one of the biggest devastations of land in France since the second world war. The government said on Monday that although the fire had stopped growing, it was still blazing and a new heatwave this week could make it harder to fight.

As authorities carried out one of the biggest evacuations in modern French history, Krishma and Nassir were among 220,000 people ordered to flee their homes in Gironde. Many people were evacuated from wooded areas directly hit by fire, where at least 240 homes were destroyed. But in an unprecedented move, tens of thousands more were ordered by police to evacuate from more built-up, urban streets as the fire reached 9 miles (15km) from the outer edge of Bordeaux’s vast suburban area.

Krishma and Nassir had to evacuate their suburban street at midnight on Friday. With their two children aged 10 and eight, they quickly packed toothbrushes, toys, one change of clothes and personal documents into their car. On Monday afternoon, they were sitting on camp beds among hundreds of people sheltering in a hangar at Bordeaux’s exhibition centre. They had slept there for three nights and did not know when they would be allowed home. The fire had not reached their residential area, but with the French government warning that the blaze was “extremely intense and unpredictable”, authorities would not yet allow a return, they said.

The couple’s main feeling was great sadness to see the Gironde forest destroyed. Krishma said: “When we were in Afghanistan there were lots of explosions, suicide attacks, but that was related to around 30 years of war. When we came here, we never thought there would be a situation like this. It brought us back to the bad memories from our past.”

Across the vast hangar, Yves, who used to work on road maintenance in Bordeaux, was sitting with his 13-year-old mastiff dog, Ichka. Yves had fled his suburban house and garden in Le Haillan outside Bordeaux with his dog’s bed under one arm and had carefully laid it out next to his camp bed. He had been ordered to evacuate in the early hours of Saturday morning.

“We had to leave because of the smoke,” he said. His wife, an administrator who did not want to be named, said she still felt shaken. “It was terrifying – you would look up at the sky and it was completely orange, even after nightfall. It was bizarre. The fire was causing that, and it really made you anxious. I feel quite a lot of anger that all this forest has burned and been lost. Seeing all that is beautiful in nature just go up in smoke is extremely painful and sad.”

Others who had fled slept in their cars. Loïc, 66, a widower who worked in the metals and glass industries before becoming a decorator, had to leave his house in Saint-Jean-d’Illac outside Bordeaux. “I had been watching this strange fog in the sky. It was a darkness almost like an eclipse,” he said. “There was a kind of ochre mist as light from the sun was diffused through falling ash. So much ash was falling that my car was turned completely grey.”

At 1am on Saturday, Loïc was woken by banging on the door from his neighbour, a fire officer, saying he had to leave immediately. He grabbed only his wallet and car keys and ran to the car, leaving his mobile phone behind. There were so many people on the road and heading to the evacuation centre that he decided to stop elsewhere and get a bit of sleep in his car.

When he woke on Saturday, listening to the news on the car radio, he knew he could not go home and headed instead for central Bordeaux, thinking the cinema would be a safe and comfortable place. “I watched the two-part Charles de Gaulle epic – the wrong way round, with the second film first, but I knew the story already – then I watched The Odyssey. Then I went back to sleep in my car.”

The next day, he visited the graveyard where his wife was buried. On Monday morning, he arrived at the Bordeaux evacuation centre to get information on what to do next. He felt deeply saddened by the loss of the forest. “My generation grew up really attached to nature,” he said.

Florence, a former teaching assistant in a primary school, sat on a camp bed with her two cats in their travelling cases after having to evacuate Le Haillan outside Bordeaux. “I was distraught,” she said. “I’m asthmatic, I put tape around the windows of my apartment but I could still smell the smoke which was seeping in under my front door, so I put down wet rags. The sky was orange and grey, and there was soot everywhere.”

She said having to suddenly evacuate knowing a fire was raging in Gironde felt like something out of a war. “It felt like being in a disaster movie,” she said. “I’ve always really loved disaster movies – but now I feel like I’ve actually been in one, so I don’t ever want to watch a disaster movie again.”

Swathes of Cairngorms unrecognisable after 12 days of ‘cataclysmic’ wildfires

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 16:00:14 GMT

With large areas still burning, damage from national park’s worst blaze could take decades, if not longer, to put right

It is the jewel in the crown of the Highlands, one of Scotland’s most impressive natural landscapes, but 12 days on from the start of an enormous wildfire that is tearing through moorland and forest, the Cairngorms national park is unrecognisable.

Hectares of blackened land were visible as low cloud cleared on Sunday, with smoke billowing into the air from large areas still ablaze. In the evening, the sky glowed an eerie orange.

Authorities have warned the danger is far from over in what has been described as the worst fire the Cairngorms has ever seen. It will be weeks, if not months, before the blaze is fully extinguished but emergency services are hoping they can stop it spreading much further. The damage so far has been significant and it will take decades to put right.

Flames have claimed areas of the Caledonian pinewood forest, which contains Scots pine trees 300 years old, but most of the older forest has been saved by fire breaks urgently bulldozed into the land in the early days of the fire.

“For rare habitat loss, it really is a challenge,” says Ian Allsopp, the Forestry and Land Scotland planning manager for the north region, saying larger animals, such as deer, would have escaped but smaller mammals, lizards, insects and ground-nesting birds would have perished.

Grant Moir, the chief executive of the Cairngorms national park, told the Guardian it was the worst fire the park had seen. “The fact that this is right in the centre of the Cairngorms, in the actual Cairngorm mountains and Abernethy – it is such a precious place,” he says.

A national park bylaw was introduced in April, banning campfires and barbecues over the summer to help reduce ignition points. It is still unknown what caused this fire but the vast majority of UK wildfires have a human origin and can be something as small as a discarded cigarette or abandoned glass bottle.

Police Scotland said on Saturday night it was no longer treating the fire as a major incident. However, anxiety is still high, particularly among local people who were told it was “contained” last week, only for strong winds to fan the flames, leading to the evacuation of Nethy Bridge village on Friday night.

Residents have been told they can return home. Inside Nethy Bridge community centre, which is being used as a makeshift base for the emergency services, a long table against a wall is groaning under the weight of donated food, while the fire service, police and volunteers bustle around, many looking exhausted.

“It’s absolutely heartbreaking,” says Sandy McCook, a retired press photographer from the village. “The flames on Friday were cataclysmic.”

He is angry too. Many locals feel the fire could have been prevented. McCook shows the Guardian a photo he took of the wildfire when it was only the size of a tennis court.

“Had we had a helicopter there on government contract to deal with such incidents, that fire could have been dealt with within two hours of it being reported,” he says. He wants to see a model similar to the Scottish air ambulance, with a specialist firefighting helicopter and crew able to scramble to tackle hard-to-reach fires, and he is not the only one.

Three private helicopters have been contracted to provide assistance in the Cairngorms, depositing approximately 750,000 litres of water a day on wildfire hotspots, something that is essential to getting the blaze under control. Allsopp says it was “so lucky” the helicopter companies were able to assist in water-bombing what he says was an “inferno”.

The Cairngorms area is an “extremely challenging landscape”, including steep mountains and forest, “access is so difficult, you just can’t get people up here”.

On Monday, the Scottish Green party called for publicly available firefighting aircraft during the wildfire season, saying Scotland “cannot continue to rely on a patchwork of private operators and borrowed resources”.

It came after the UK government offered military support on Sunday but said it had no access to specialist firefighting helicopters requested by the Scottish government.

Firefighters said an “intensive operation” was still under way but better weather conditions, including heavy rain and low winds, had slowed the fire and limited its spread. More than 75 firefighters remained at the scene, the Scottish fire and rescue service said on Sunday.

Light rain has brought some relief but everyone on the ground is anxious in the face of more dry weather to come. “Wet weather is not enough to put out the fire on its own,” says Allsopp. It requires helicopter water-bombing “for days and days and days” to contain it.

The operation is a massive coordinated effort between Forestry and Land Scotland, the national park authority, the police, fire service, RSPB, Highland Council and other partners, with assistance being offered from the Scottish and UK governments.

Allsopp says each organisation has worked well together, pooled skills and knowledge, and helped each other out. “Even our accountants are here, running errands and getting water and sun cream for people,” he said. “At times, it has been completely overwhelming and we’ve been struggling to keep up. It feels like a war strategy.”

Jodrell Bank Observatory facing closure after major funder cuts support

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 15:39:38 GMT

Scientists say decision is blow to UK astronomy as deep space observatory is home to world-leading facilities

Jodrell Bank Observatory, the hub of a world-leading network of radio telescopes, is facing closure after government funding for the facility was slashed.

The deep space observatory includes the Grade I-listed Lovell telescope and is prized by astronomers who study galaxies, black holes, star formation, planets beyond the solar system and the afterglow of the big bang.

The observatory’s funder, UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), said on Monday it would withdraw funding for the e-Merlin network, the UK’s national radio astronomy facility at Jodrell Bank, when the current agreement ends in March 2028.

Scientists said the decision was a blow to UK astronomy, with observations at Jodrell Bank due to end completely unless other funding is found. “Jodrell has been delivering spectacular discovery science for decades,” said Prof Catherine Heymans, Scotland’s astronomer royal. “To see this world-leading facility cut is just devastating.”

Further deep cuts were announced for dozens of facilities, instruments and projects, which are expected to result in about 800 job losses. Brian Cox, the TV scientist and professor at the University of Manchester, said he was stunned that the funder had pressed ahead with cuts and not worked with the new government to avoid them.

“These devastating and irreversible cuts are a legacy from a series of hasty and ill-considered decisions taken by UKRI, overseen by a government department that no longer exists,” Cox said. “I am astonished that UKRI are still ploughing ahead, and not working with the [Andy] Burnham government to find a solution.”

The UKRI has an annual budget of nearly £10bn, but the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), which it funds, needs to make substantial savings after cost overruns as a result of soaring electricity and staff costs at UK facilities and high foreign exchange rates for international collaborations, such as the Cern nuclear research laboratory near Geneva.

Prof Simon Garrington, an associate director of the Jodrell Bank Observatory, said staff were shocked by the decision. “Withdrawing the funding from e-Merlin effectively pulls the rug out from under Jodrell Bank,” he said. The move threatens 28 jobs at the observatory and will affect nearly 3,000 researchers who work with the facility.

Garrington intends to challenge the decision but hopes that new uses for the telescope in tracking satellites and space debris might draw in some alternative funding.

Jodrell Bank was among dozens of facilities, instruments and projects hit by the cuts on Monday. There will be a 20% cut to UK participation in the Rubin Observatory in Chile, which only began work last month to capture the largest astronomical movie of all time. Another telescope, the Next-Generation Transit Survey, which is searching for solar systems similar to the Earth’s, received a 45% cut.

The Royal Astronomical Society president, Prof Jim Wild, said: “At a time when technological innovation is crucial to our country’s prospects, discarding unique, globally significant observatories threatens both our scientific future and the inspiration of future generations of astronomers.”

When it comes to predicting the future, why are TV writers better than politicians?

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 15:32:37 GMT

From BBC drama The Rapture on the climate crisis to Apple’s Criminal Record on the rise of the far right, culture often sees what politics fails to

In the BBC’s new apocalypse drama, The Rapture, the UK is engulfed in a terrifying heatwave. I watched a preview of the programme in May, while preparing to interview the lead actor Ruth Madeley. I thought at the time: “This will be much more frightening when it chimes with the real life weather, bad luck for them that it’s not coming out for a couple of months.” But, by the time of meeting Madeley the following month, we were already in the middle of a heatwave that would lead to the highest ever recorded June temperature in the UK. The whole encounter made the show feel even more prophetic. She was in a central London hotel, air-conditioned inside, but all the door handles and surrounding street furniture – benches segmented by metal arm rests, to make life just that little bit harder for homeless people – had got way too hot. It was like playing The Floor is Lava, except instead of “floor”, “everything”. It surely can’t hit the screens at a more apposite time than this, I thought, failing to predict that by late July we’d be in heatwave number three, and France would be on fire.

The Daily Mail’s reviewer was upset that Christianity was portrayed “as a bastion of anti-science nutjobs and fundamentalists” in the show, wondering rhetorically whether the BBC would ever create such a drama about a “Muslim imam”. Peculiar thing to get upset about, I thought, since the religion is really more of a symptom of, or even a garnish to, the central atmosphere of engulfing heat. It’s like complaining that cats get a bad rap in the 1974 film The Towering Inferno (yes, there is a cat in it).

TV puts a particular pressure on itself to describe the world it lands in, even when a show is developed at least a couple of years before. Often, the safe way to play it with surrounding factors – weather, politics, fashion – is to keep things so general that they could be any time this century. Every so often something will land that relates so tightly to current events, you forget to admire its foresight and just assume it was written yesterday. Season two of Criminal Record (Apple TV), the police drama, which Peter Capaldi lifts so far above procedural you forget the police even have procedures, opens with a little demo outside the Ministry of Defence. It turns deadly after the far right smashes through a lackadaisical police cordon that thought it was just there to deal with a bunch of peaceniks. It felt extremely 2026, yet it was conceived before violent far-right protests were a regular news event – before the riots after the the Southport attack, before asylum seeker hotels being set alight, before Elon Musk started talking about the inevitability of civil war in the UK. It tightly described a riven politics that had not yet arrived, the series creator and writer Paul Rutman committing himself to quite a new, distinctive and sad chapter in our civic life – unnecessarily, really, because watching Capaldi look sketchy and chase people is an evergreen delight in any context, but it paid off.

The Rapture was adapted from Liz Jensen’s novel, which came out in 2009, so she must have been looking ahead to the climate crisis 20 years ago. Novels can often hit the future on the nose because they’re not trying to predict it by committee; books describing the now obvious billionaire death wish – a new kind of morbid fantasy, in which it’s not their own death they’re planning for but everyone else’s – are notable for their synchronicity. Eleanor Catton’s Birnam Wood and Naomi Alderman’s The Future came out in the same year, 2023. The ideas must have germinated at around the same time, 2020, which is surely before even the tech tycoons themselves had landed on this post-humanist outlook, and were still figuring out how to capture all the money in the world as quietly as possible.

Without diminishing any of this creative perspicacity, these are things we all know; extreme weather is coming, a lot of billionaires are preparing for mass death events; politics is getting more divided because people with money are paying to cleave it. The only people not acknowledging this are politicians. They are still, in the middle of a wildfire, complaining that net zero costs too much, and squabbling about the teaspoon of crude oil left in the North Sea. The really remarkable thing is the determination of that averted gaze, denying a future that’s already arrived.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

Roster dating – is having five partners really the key to finding love?

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 15:19:06 GMT

It used be called playing the field, but now young people are claiming dating multiple people at once is intentional and growth-enhancing

Name: Roster dating.

Age: The term seems to be about a decade old; the practice is much older.

Appearance: Hectic.

What is it? It’s dating more than one person at a time.

You mean what we used to call cheating? No, more like what we used to call playing the field.

If it’s not new, why are we talking about it? Because gen Z have cottoned on to it.

Them again. I’m afraid so.

Let me guess: have they taken a messy arrangement born of indecision, insecurity and poor scheduling, and recast it as something intentional? Intentional and growth-enhancing.

How so? Because roster dating is, at its core, a journey of personal discovery. “One of the biggest pros of roster dating is that you can learn so much about yourself,” one dating expert told Vice.

If you ask me, these gen Zers know too much about themselves already. The important thing is to be open and honest about your intentions with everyone on your dating roster.

You mean you tell them? Not necessarily – you may simply assume that everyone on your roster also has a roster. But you shouldn’t lie.

How many potential suitors make up a decent roster, then? The dating coach Sara Tick recommends keeping it to five or fewer.

Five? How am I supposed to keep track of five separate people? The idea is that they each fulfil a specific need: an exciting one, a devoted one, an artistic one, a rich one …

Then how am I supposed to find five completely different people who like me? They might not all like you – they might just have an open spot on their roster they need to fill.

Let’s just call this what it really is: an inability to commit on any level. Commitment isn’t necessarily the destination with roster dating – it’s about letting go of expectations, and not wasting all your energy on a single connection.

Fine, but all this presumes that dating is fun, when really it’s anxiety-ridden, soul-destroying and expensive. The last is certainly true – research indicates that the average cost of a gen Z date has risen to $205 (£155).

In that case, I can’t even afford a roster of three. Reading between the lines, you get the impression that the singles who swear by roster dating are never the ones paying.

Do say: “I really think we’ve got something very special, but I have limited availability this month.”

Don’t say: “Of course I’ll marry you, Frank! Sorry, I mean Fred.”

The real love story behind Colin from Accounts: ‘I wouldn’t want to write with anyone else’

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 15:00:13 GMT

As the show takes its final bow, Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer reflect on ‘having a ball’ playing exes while being married with kids, ignoring notes from US TV executives and having ‘big old cries’ at the end

It began, as all great romances do, with a nipple flash. When Colin from Accounts, the little comedy that could, started airing back in 2022, the world fell in love – hard and fast. It was a surprisingly prickly Australian show about Ashley, a student doctor (Harriet Dyer), and Gordon, an older, brewery owner (Patrick Brammall), who fall in love after she pops a boob at him, he hits a dog with his car, and they jointly land an astronomical vet bill and a new pet.

The show shared its name with its furriest star – full name: “Colin from accounts payable, who is working on the big merger” – and it was as charming as the title suggested, winning fans across Hollywood and the world. That Brammall and Dyer were actually a couple, now married with two kids and a dog (no wheels), just made everyone love the show even more.

But Colin from Accounts is now ending with its third season – which some may feel is premature, but undeniably confident. “We don’t want to flog a dead horse,” Brammall says. “It definitely feels right.”

As Dyer adds: “It is not that the horse is dead yet – we don’t even want to find it is having trouble breathing.”

Wrapping their show, which they both also write, has yet to fully sink in for Brammall. “I don’t think it’s hit me, honestly,” he says. “There was lots of mini moments – ‘Oh shit it’s the last time I’m gonna do this, it’s the last time I’m gonna do that’.” Dyer, meanwhile, has had three “big old cries”: “The last one was when I was in the editing suite and I just looked around at the little grey room and it came out like vomit.”

Season one of Colin was a will-they-won’t-they story. Season two said well-they-have-but-should-they? Season three asks could they again? The new episodes open three years after Gordon made an excruciating marriage proposal to Ashley at a friend’s wedding: Ashley and Gordon have since split up and are dating other people, but are reunited when Gordon unwittingly makes a doctor’s appointment at Ashley’s work.

A married couple with a hell of a lot of chemistry playing exes is fun to watch. “And it is fun to play,” says Brammall. “Obviously, we love playing the stuff where we’re falling in love, but we love having big arguments just as much. We’re actors by trade, so we love pretendies. I had a ball. I think Harri did too.”

Season three has “a slight forlorn quality and an awkwardness – it’s almost like taking them back to the start”, adds Dyer. “All tension is good, I think. Yearning. It’s very easy to play that, especially with someone that you know so well.”

Splitting Ashley and Gordon up just seemed like a fun, creative road to go down; the three-year time leap, meanwhile, was practical. “I’m almost 38 and Ash was 30 in the second season – we had to catch up a little bit!” Dyer laughs.

The couple have previously said that they have one big fight each season. What was it over this time?

“Golly gosh, I think we didn’t have one,” Dyer says. “We’ve been having to get very economical with our energy.”

Brammall laughs. “The last two seasons we’ve had one kid. This time we had two and it’s like, who’s got time? Who’s got the luxury of having a big fight?”

“Those days are over,” Dyer adds. “Now it’s like, how do I say this in the least offensive way so we can make this butter cheese pasta and put the girls to bed?”

It is rare that an Australian show set in Sydney would be completely devoid of the Harbour Bridge and Opera House shots the world expects. This wasn’t a conscious decision; Gordon owns a microbrewery, so Brammall and Dyer made him work in a part of Sydney populated by them: the inner west. But the result has meant international viewers have got a glimpse of a city that doesn’t feel too far from their own, bar the magpie song and gum trees.

“In episode five of this season we go to a beach, but that’s probably the first grain of sand in all the episodes of Colin. Which, yeah, as a Sydney show feels almost blasphemous,” Dyer says. “People haven’t seen that side of Sydney, which makes it interesting. Something about terraces and warehouses – it didn’t feel quintessentially Sydney, which gives it a universality.”

“We don’t need to sell Sydney to the world, we don’t need to sell Australia to the world,” Brammall adds. He remembers an early attempt to market Colin as “a new Australian comedy”, to which Dyer responded: “Don’t say Australian comedy. It’s a new comedy.”

Sign up to Five Great Reads

after newsletter promotion

“Why are we so quick to brand it as Australian?” Brammall says. “How about we’re world class and we don’t have to do that? Let’s tell the story we want to tell and the Sydney of it, the Australia of it, can follow.”

There are enough local references in there for the home crowd – the band T-shirts, the soundtrack, the occasional “cunt” dropped by a nana. But they once did get a note from an American executive about using the word “arvo”: “They said, you should make that ‘afternoon’ so people in America know what we’re talking about. And we were like … no. It stayed in.”

Part of Colin’s appeal comes from the palpable sense that every argument, every calamity, every embarrassment, has actually happened to someone in the show. A version of the poo incident in the very first episode happened to Dyer; the jibes about Gordon and Ashley’s age gap ring true too (Brammall is 50, Dyer is 37; a fan once mistook him for her father).

Even Gordon hitting Colin with his car after being distracted by Ashley’s boob flash: Dyer once walked a pram into a pole after seeing a hot guy. “It wasn’t my baby,” Dyer says, as Brammall laughs. “I wasn’t a very good babysitter. The baby was fine.”

There are also the more serious moments, like Gordon’s fertility problems after surviving testicular cancer, which Brammall thinks was an unconscious link to his own infertility, caused by childhood illness. (Brammall and Dyer have two adopted daughters, Joni and Mabel.) “It’s not until you read it later that you go ‘Oh I see that connects to something in my life’,” he says. “These little truthful thoughts or feelings or ideas or experiences can float through and generally, if it’s funny or if it feels real, then it’s in the show.”

“We touch on taboo subjects that you sometimes wouldn’t dare touch. But we touch them kind of gently,” Dyer says.

“And always with warmth,” Brammall adds. “We do the light and the dark thing – get people laughing and then punch them with something really heavy.”

“It’s not all gold, but Pat and I are always trying to make it the best it can be,” Dyer says. (Brammall: “Oh fuck yeah.”) “We don’t think that we are authorities on anything.” (Brammall: “Oh fuck no.”) “We’re nervous today because we still care so much about whether people like it.”

People already love Colin From Accounts, including famous fans Nick Offerman, Lena Dunham, Phoebe Waller-Bridge, Richard Curtis and Anne Hathaway; Brammall recently played the latter’s boyfriend in The Devil Wears Prada 2. From such great heights, what does success look like for Brammall and Dyer now? Dyer answers instantly: “balance”.

“Because the hours of this life are so demanding – it’s not really designed for a married couple to leave and come home at the same time when you’ve got little people looking for you,” she says. “To me, success looks like balance and finish reading my book. But we’re definitely going to work together again because I wouldn’t want to write with anybody else.”

“That’s going to be an amazing life,” Brammall says.

The first two episodes of Colin from Accounts season 3 are available to stream on Binge in Australia now, with new episodes streaming weekly. UK and US airdates are yet to be announced.

Wilson, whose work on Homer’s epic was praised by Nolan, said his film was grandiose and superficial with ‘nothing convincing to say’

Peter Bradshaw reviews The Odyssey ‘At times I felt I’d bitten off more than I could chew’: Christopher Nolan interviewed What Nolan’s Odyssey changed, invented – and left out

Emily Wilson, the classicist whose 2017 translation of Homer’s Odyssey was cited by Christopher Nolan in early publicity for his hugely successful adaptation of the poem, has roundly criticised the film, saying “it has nothing convincing to say” and that it “lacks psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth”.

In a scathing essay for the London Review of Books, Wilson writes: “I had hoped that Nolan’s affinity with these Homeric themes might push him to new creative heights, and enable him to conjure more believable characters. But The Odyssey features his usual combination of grandiosity and superficiality … the film’s vision is too confused, its characters too underdeveloped, to deliver what it half-promises in terms of big ideas – although it is very good at conveying big bangs and big giants.”

Wilson adds: “Nolan’s Odyssey lacks many of the elements that make the poem great. It has nothing convincing to say about time, memory, history, war, or about the relationship between one warrior’s glorious return and the lives of his family, adversaries, comrades, friends and neighbours. It lacks psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth. Its narrative structure is gimmicky. The writing is abysmal. None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible.”

Wilson also noted Nolan’s admiration for the opening line of her Odyssey translation: “Tell me about a complicated man” – but added: “I would be ashamed to have written any part of this script.”

Wilson, who is department chair and professor of classical studies at the University of Pennsylvania, also went on the attack in an interview with the Sunday Times, saying: “It didn’t land emotionally for me at all. Which I think is partly about the fact that, unlike Homer, it’s not very well written.”

“The characters don’t have the kind of depth the Homeric characters have. I felt, ‘Do I really care if this guy gets back to his wife?’ You haven’t given me any reason to.”

Nevertheless, Wilson acknowledged the impact the film is already having on cultural awareness of ancient Greek literature as well as cinema itself. Saying “the release of The Odyssey is still an event to celebrate,” she suggests: “This epic is bringing audiences back to cinemas … translations of Odyssey, including mine, are flying off the shelves … [and] perhaps the film will persuade a few college administrators not to cut their literature, language and history departments.”

“Nolan,” Wilson says, “is doing his best to get the general public reading again, and I am grateful.”

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 14:34:54 GMT

Gibraltar-based Ros Astengo inspired four men to report sexual assaults carried out by Allan Grimson in 1990s

Ros Astengo, a journalist based in Gibraltar who usually focuses on politics and social issues, had qualms when she began investigating the case of the suspected serial killer Allan Grimson as he neared release from prison after serving more than 20 years.

She worried that she might reopen the scars of survivors of Grimson – but also that she could be putting herself in the “crosshairs” of a dangerous man who had sexually assaulted and battered two young men to death in the late 1990s when he was a Royal Navy petty officer.

“But the public interest overrode it,” Astengo said. “It would have been so easy for me to have just done nothing. But I thought to myself, how would I feel if as soon as they let him out he reoffended and harmed another young man. My motive was to keep the public safe.”

Because of Astengo’s work, four men came forward to report sexual assaults by Grimson carried out on them in the same era as the two murders.

On Monday, a jury at Winchester crown court found Grimson guilty of 13 sexual offences relating to the men, which may mean he remains in prison for years to come.

Judge Dugdale told Grimson he was an extremely dangerous man in the 1990s and asked for reports to be prepared to help him understand if he still posed a serious risk.

The judge also asked for victim personal statements to be taken from the men. He thanked the jury for hearing a “very unusual case” and invited them to return to court when he sentenced Grimson in November.

“The men were incredibly brave to come to court, bring all this back into their lives,” Astengo said.

Grimson was jailed for life in 2001 and told he would serve at least 22 years in prison for sexually abusing and murdering Nicholas Wright, 18, and Sion Jenkins, 20, in Portsmouth, both of whom had served in the navy. The sentencing judge described him as a “serial killer in nature if not by number”.

At the time, Grimson also admitted in police interviews sexual offences or contact with another four men – three young sailors and a teenage boy. He said he had thought of killing two of them but the Crown Prosecution Service did not pursue the allegations because he was going to serve a long jail term for the murders anyway.

While in prison Grimson was on best behaviour in the hope that he would be released after serving his 22 years and in November 2020 the Parole Board recommended he be moved to an open prison to prepare him for freedom.

At this time, Astengo was covering the search for the body of another sailor, Simon Parkes, who vanished in Gibraltar in 1986. Grimson was in the British overseas territory at the time. He has long been a suspect but denies involvement.

No remains were found and Astengo said she was deeply moved when Parkes’s elderly parents, Margaret and David, from south-west England, described it as their last chance to get justice. “It was a very lonely journey for them.” She promised them she would write a book about their son’s case to keep his memory alive.

She began her research and was disturbed to find he had made admissions over the four boys and young men but no action had been taken.

“I was astonished that he was never charged over them,” Astengo said. She was alarmed that Grimson seemed close to being released. “I knew what he had done to those boys. That really worried me. How could he be fully rehabilitated? I was worried he would go back into the community thinking he’s gotten away with it. I realised I was putting myself in the crosshairs of a killer but I thought something needed to be done.”

Astengo tracked down one of the four and travelled to the UK to speak to him. “I found a very angry man who was still hurt, angry and upset that he had never seen justice. He started talking about the fact that he was older now and a parent. He understands today what he didn’t back then – that was that he was groomed.”

Astengo told the man he could file a fresh complaint about Grimson. “I said to him, think very carefully about what you’re doing because you are going to open a can of worms for yourself.”

The man went ahead and spoke to police. Initially no action was taken so Astengo contacted the child sexual abuse review panel, which examines allegations of non-recent child sexual offences.

It agreed that the case was worth re-examining. Detectives interviewed the man and tracked down the three others. In February 2025, Grimson was charged over the attacks on the four.

The month-long trial highlighted how far the justice system had come in dealing with sexual crimes.

In the late 1990s and early 2000s it was not uncommon for serious sexual allegations not to be pursued if a defendant faced a long jail sentence for even more serious crimes. Now it is considered the state’s duty to do so.

It is also a reminder that until the turn of the century, gay people were not allowed to serve openly in the armed forces, meaning some of those assaulted by Grimson were keen not to talk about what had happened back then because they feared dismissal.

In court, Grimson’s legal team tried to argue that it was unfair for him to be charged with offences that the authorities had not pursued a quarter of a century ago. They made it clear he felt he was being prosecuted now as a tactic for keeping him in prison, to “stymie” his parole.

His legal team also criticised Astengo, suggesting she had been motivated by making money from her book, which is due to come out next year.

John Price KC, prosecuting, urged the jury to ignore “conspiracy theories” about Astengo’s involvement and said good was achieved by energetic journalists.

Astengo said it was not about money. Every time she travelled to the UK she has had to pay her own way, take leave – and could make very little, if anything, from her book. She said: “The defence tried to paint me as somebody who has exerted undue influence all because I’m writing a book. For me, it was about justice and to prevent a serial offender from being released.”
