‘You say genocide, I say war’: Boy George releases pro-Israel song, We Will Dance Again

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 14:31:12 GMT

Culture Club singer sings ‘I stand with the Jews / I don’t feel brave, I just need to behave like a human’, in song defending Israel’s response to Hamas attack

Boy George has released a new song entitled We Will Dance Again, which voices support for Israel’s military action in Palestine.

Posted on X and Instagram with the Hebrew title עוד נרקוד alongside its English translation, the song features a pop-reggae backing. The opening lyrics are: “You say genocide, I say war / When you’re attacked, that’s what the army’s for / Does it get ugly? You bet it does / When I know you wanna kill every last one of us.”

Boy George cites the attack by Hamas at the Nova music festival in October 2023, saying the civilians killed there were “murder[ed] … for the crime of dancing”. A total of 344 civilians and 34 security personnel were killed and 44 people were taken hostage.

The overall Palestinian death toll since the war started is more than 73,000.

The title phrase We Will Dance Again, repeated for the song’s chorus, has been used by Israelis to express hope and solidarity in the wake of the 7 October attack, and was used as the title of an acclaimed documentary about it.

Elsewhere in the chorus, Boy George asserts: “There will be no war / But if you’re ever confused / I stand with the Jews / I don’t feel brave, I just need to behave like a human.”

He also criticises the pro-Palestinian movement, including musicians who have condemned Israel: “You condemn the Jews, with selective memory / Musicians holding flags, mouthing like sheep / Propaganda fuelled by the internet feels so weak.” Musicians who have supported Palestine include Stormzy, Damon Albarn, Clairo and Brian Eno, the latter of whom conceived an all-star charity single, Lullaby, which vied for Christmas No 1 in 2025.

Boy George, who is not Jewish, has recently voiced support for Jewish communities. In an interview with the Telegraph, when discussing his admiration for Jewish peers in the 1980s during his time fronting Culture Club, he said: “Over the years it’s been a really personal thing. It doesn’t mean that I don’t have compassion for Palestinians, it doesn’t mean that I agree with what’s going on in Israel, but I am always going to defend the people that I love. I have a lot of Jewish friends and there would never be a situation where I’d turn my back on them.”

He also voiced his support after the knife attack in Golders Green in April which left two Jewish men injured, saying: “We need to make our Jewish community know we support them.”

His new song marks an intensification of his support for Israel, having said earlier in the year that he didn’t have an opinion on the country.

Speaking ahead of an appearance with San Marino for their Eurovision song contest entry (which didn’t reach the contest’s final), he was questioned about the boycott of Eurovision from countries opposing Israel’s inclusion in the contest. “I have many Jewish friends, whom I’ve known since I was 15 or 16 years old,” he replied. “Are people asking me, as someone with principles, to turn my back on my Jewish friends? That is not going to happen – it will never happen. From the beginning of my career, I wore the Star of David … I feel very connected to the Jewish people. I’m not necessarily connected to Israel. I don’t really have an opinion on that. But the mission of music is to unite people.”

His characterisation of Israel’s action against Palestine as a legitimate military response rather than genocide runs counter to a United Nations inquiry, which stated in 2025 that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. Israel’s foreign ministry called the report “distorted and false”. Last month, another independent UN inquiry found that Israel was continuing to commit genocide by targeting children. That report was dubbed a “libellous sham” by Israel.

Boy George was one of the most flamboyant and recognisable pop stars of the 1980s, with Culture Club scoring four UK Top 10 albums including 1983’s chart-topping Colour By Numbers. Hit singles include Do You Really Want to Hurt Me? and Karma Chameleon, which were both hugely successful in the US as well as UK, and have endured as staples on oldies radio.

The band also had a hit with an anti-war track, The War Song, which reached UK No 2 in 1984 and featured the chorus: “War is stupid and people are stupid / And love means nothing in some strange quarters.”

Last month, Boy George launched a new company called Artist Included, which will use AI to allow artists to create new versions of earlier songs which resemble the originals, as a way of wresting back control of master recordings. It launched with a new version of Karma Chameleon, which Boy George recorded then de-aged. “When I heard it, I was absolutely gobsmacked,” he told the Hollywood Reporter. “It sounds like another take from that original session.”

Mayo beat 75-year-old ‘curse’ to become Gaelic football champions

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 14:15:29 GMT

Team to return for euphoric homecoming after winning all-Ireland men’s final against Kerry, ending decades of defeats

The hex is broken, dispelled, banished, and a story that bewitched Ireland for decades has ended in fairytale: Mayo are all-Ireland champions.

Seventy-five years after a supposed curse condemned its Gaelic men’s football team to endless defeat, the county prevailed and uncorked a wave of emotion that engulfed even its rivals.

The team will return to the west of Ireland for a euphoric homecoming on Monday evening after winning the senior football championship, a victory that thrilled Ireland and Mayo’s diaspora, including Joe Biden, Mark Carney and Noel and Liam Gallagher.

“Mayo 1-20, Kerry 1-17. Chisel it on the gravestones, scribble it in the sky,” the Irish Times exulted. “Croke Park untethered, the whole place afloat for an hour on a lake of the sweetest tears that were ever cried.”

Most pundits had favoured Kerry to win the 138th all-Ireland final and write another chapter of Mayo woe at Sunday’s contest at the Dublin stadium. Instead the underdogs triumphed and even some Kerry fans wept at the catharsis.

Few seriously believed in the curse – it was said no member of the last winning team from 1951 would live to see another – but there was no doubting the drought that followed, with 11 defeats in 11 finals since 1989. A book about Mayo’s quest ​was titled House of Pain.

Whenever the county made it to a final, a frisson gripped television viewers and the 82,000-strong stadium crowd: was this the day they would witness the end of the hex? On Sunday it was.

“To every young boy and girl across Mayo and our diaspora across the world, never stop dreaming, stick your chest out and be proud to be from Mayo,” the team captain, Jack Coyne, declared as he held aloft the trophy named after Sam Maguire, a legendary player. “The wait is over. Sam is home.”

Authorities had provisionally estimated a crowd of 40,000 would greet the team at McHale Park in the county town of Castlebar on Monday but that looks conservative, Gerry Bourke, the homecoming committee chair, told RTÉ. “After what I saw in Croke Park yesterday, I think we’ll have to revisit the plan.”

Mayo, a landscape of bogs, rocks and Atlantic cliffs, is the third biggest of the island of Ireland’s 32 counties. It is sparsely populated, with just 130,000 people, but players and supporters have a reputation for fervency in the Gaelic Athletic Association, the sport’s governing body.

According to lore, the young victors of 1951 were on their way home to celebrate when they passed through the village of Foxford and failed to pay their respects to a funeral, prompting the enraged priest to utter the fateful words: “For as long as you all live, Mayo won’t win another all-Ireland.”

Seven decades later, the last surviving member of that team, Paddy Prendergast, told friends he would willingly “roll over and die” if there was any truth to the curse, but that it was a myth.

“There was supposed to have been a funeral in the local church; I don’t know whether there was or not. I saw people standing around the church but we didn’t get off the truck because we couldn’t get off the bloody truck,” he told an interviewer in 2017.

Researchers who probed church records, press cuttings and other sources failed to find any verification of the supposed curse, which gained currency in the 1990s. The legend, however, is intact: Prendergast died in 2021, aged 95, two weeks after Mayo lost the final.

Biden – who concluded a 2023 presidential visit to Mayo with the rallying cry “Mayo for Sam!” – congratulated his ancestral home county. “Today, the dream becomes reality,” he posted. “You earned this victory. Enjoy every minute.”

Carney, the Canadian prime minister who made his own ancestral pilgrimage to Mayo last month, echoed the joy. “The curse is broken,” he posted. The Gallagher brothers of Oasis, who also have family ties to Mayo, expressed pride. “Finally!! Up Mayo!!” Noel posted.

Bill Oddie: the comedy legend tragically undervalued by the BBC

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 14:13:00 GMT

The beloved star of The Goodies went on to become TV’s most famous birdwatcher. But behind these triumphs were pain, frustration and mental health issues that led him to leave the show he loved

Bill Oddie, naturalist and broadcaster, dies aged 85 Bill Oddie – a life in pictures

Bill Oddie, who has died aged 85, had two separate, substantial TV presences – as a comedy actor and an ornithologist. Both roles brought him fame but also pain. The peak of the former career was 76 episodes from 1970-82 of The Goodies, which he co-wrote and co-starred in with Graeme Garden and Tim Brooke-Taylor. They played an eccentric trio of investigators and fixers who rode into action on a three-seater bicycle called a “trandem”.

As a birdwatcher, his onscreen zenith was Springwatch, which he initially co-hosted with Kate Humble, from 2005. It began a BBC Two natural history franchise marking the change of seasons, its success leading to wintry, autumnal and summery spin-offs. Binoculars lowered to show eyes awed or enthused, and Oddie became TV’s signature birdwatcher.

Born in Rochdale, he came early to both comedy and ornithology. He was a teenager when his sightings first appeared in the annual report of the West Midland Bird Club. In his early 20s, he appeared in the West End and on Broadway in transfers of the Cambridge University revue in which he first worked professionally with Brooke-Taylor and Garden, who is now the only survivor of the three. Oddie wrote the music for the revue and then The Goodies, who released five spin-off singles in 1974-75, spending a combined 38 weeks in the pop charts, with Funky Gibbon, an anthropomorphic jungle dance number, reaching four in the Top 10.

Each of Oddie’s TV hits, though, was overshadowed by sadness. In the case of Springwatch, it was personal. Particularly bad incidents of the bipolar condition he experienced throughout his life led him to miss a number of episodes. He returned to the programme, but his departure in 2008 – which he made clear was not voluntary – was triggered, by his account, by another serious depressive downturn.

In the case of The Goodies, there was an underlying resentment shared by Brooke-Taylor and Garden relating to the show’s treatment by the BBC. The series attracted 12 million viewers at its mid-70s peak – very high for a BBC Two show – and won the Silver Rose of Montreux, the second prize at Europe’s leading TV festival. The gong was for Kitten Kong, an inspired movie spoof in which a massive moggy terrorises London using some special effects impressive for the period.

However, The Goodies was never valued by many corporation executives who – due to the relatively high quotient of slapstick, puns and visual gags involving animals – designated it a “children’s show”, which was intended as an insult and taken as such by two of the creators. For what proved to be the final series, the trio moved to London Weekend Television.

Unlike most hit shows of its period, The Goodies has not been regularly repeated on terrestrial TV, any re-airings by the BBC largely in archive slots. This upset and frustrated Oddie, Brooke-Taylor and Garden. During the home video and DVD boom, when it sometimes seemed that the BBC was systematically releasing all material ever shown, the threesome negotiated a box set release with a commercial outfit, which did something to redress the neglect.

A few other shows from the era have also been denied repeats and releases because they contain language or attitudes now considered unacceptable. BBC off-the-record briefers have sometimes suggested that this was why The Goodies has been so difficult to watch or buy. There is an occasion on which the three men start to apply blackface, but it occurred in an extraordinary 1975 episode called South Africa. This begins with the Goodies undertaking an advertising campaign to attract Britons to South Africa and ends in a Britain with a Black Enoch Powell presiding over a regime of reverse apartheid.

Although there is some silly wordplay – at one point, a regime of “apart-height” requires the diminutive Oddie to become a slave to his taller colleagues – the broadly progressive politics and complexity of the storyline make the “children’s television” tag seem particularly absurd. Indeed, absurdity is a more fitting label for South Africa and many other editions.

In The Goodies, the writer-actors played exaggerations of aspects of their character: Garden (a qualified doctor) professorial and absent-minded, Brooke-Taylor posh and patriotic, and Oddie sulky and scrappy. Those characteristics meant that some colleagues found him hard to work with – which may have contributed to his departure from Springwatch – but some such behaviour was explained, if not entirely excused, by his mental health issues.

Oddie was quite right, though, to be annoyed by the diminishment in BBC and TV history of The Goodies, memories of which will make its viewers smile amid the sadness at his death. His admirers will also hope that any afterlife contains a chorus of birdsong.

How to create the perfect women’s holiday capsule wardrobe: 12 pieces worth packing

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 14:00:11 GMT

Too many outfits and not enough suitcase space? Whether it’s sightseeing or sundowners, our fashion writer shares her secrets for packing smarter

The travel essentials that made your holiday better Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

When you hear the words capsule wardrobe, you probably picture beige knits and minimalist tailoring. A capsule isn’t just about dressing neutrally, though: it’s about choosing a handful of pieces that work together in countless combinations.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

There is no time that skill is more important than when you’re packing for a holiday. I have streamlined my approach by sticking to a simple rule of thumb: instead of packing for every possible scenario, I focus on versatile staples that can be dressed up or down and worn more than once.

Every holiday capsule should include three essentials: a dependable basic, one statement piece, and shoes that can take you from sightseeing to dinner. Build everything else around those foundations and you’ll find yourself wearing every item you pack.

Airism T-shirt

The cornerstone of any wardrobe. I love this T-shirt because of its boxy silhouette and subtle side slits that create a slightly flared shape. Plus, the Airism cotton fabric is sweat-wicking and feels cool against the skin. I wear mine with pretty much everything from denim shorts during the day to a statement skirt for dinner.

Minerva bow-drop beaded earrings

You only really need a few pieces of jewellery: something understated and everyday, and something to transform an outfit in seconds. These sculptural earrings will lift even the most minimal outfit.

Teva mid-form sandals

I often travel with one pair of shoes, so need a pair that does it all. These strappy sandals are comfortable enough for long days exploring, but smart enough to wear for dinner thanks to their minimal design.

Multi-way skirt

Multifunctional clothing is the holy grail of holiday packing. A smocked waist maxi skirt can also be worn as a bandeau midi dress thanks to its stretchy waistband. It’s two outfits in one, saving valuable suitcase space. This pillar-box red one is made from 100% cotton and has an adorable frill detail highlighting the flattering drop waist.

Ilia multi-stick

The same logic applies to your beauty bag. Ilia’s multi-stick adds buildable colour to cheeks and lips without feeling heavy in warm weather. Its compact packaging is ideal for travelling and its stick shape makes it easy to apply on the go.

Palma Solesi waterproof necklace

Holiday jewellery should be effortless, joyful – and waterproof, especially if you’re dipping in and out of a pool or the sea. This gold and pastel green beaded necklace is water- and sweat-proof, and will lift an evening outfit, too.

Sightseer linen striped pant set

A good co-ord is three outfits in one: worn together, or each piece styled separately. This ocean-blue striped linen set feels relaxed, but pair it with a sleek sandal and it could easily feel at home at dinner. With an elasticated waist and adjustable straps, it’s comfortable too.

Lyrebird lace trim silky shorts

My summer evening staple has been this pair of lace trim shorts from Reformation. Paired with a white T-shirt they look subtle but dressy, thanks to the sheen of the fabric. I also love this more affordable powder-blue pair from Anthropologie. With a flattering high waist and elasticated fit, they’re comfortable without compromising on style.

Large mesh beach bag

Accessories are the easiest place to introduce personality, and a colourful bag will instantly brighten a simple outfit. I love this cobalt blue Dragon Diffusion bag, but I wouldn’t necessarily want to take something so precious to the beach. Alternatively, this affordable bright blue mesh bag from Marks & Spencer is large enough for your daily essentials while adding a welcome pop of colour.

Oversized sunglasses

Channel Jane Birkin and go for maximum coverage with a pair of oversized sunglasses. This softly squared style from & Other Stories feels timeless enough to wear year after year, so look after them on holiday.

Cotton reversible bucket hat

A sun hat is one of the most important holiday accessories, which is why it has to be the most versatile. This reversible style from M&S gives you two looks in one, and its neutral colour palette will complement almost anything in your suitcase. In an easy canvas fabric, it will pack down to almost nothing too.

Abstract spot-print square silk scarf

Tied around your hair, looped through a bag, worn as a belt or even styled as a top, a silk scarf is one of the most versatile accessories there is. Best of all, it takes up little to no room in your luggage. I love this blue polka-dot print one: it’s larger than the average bandana style, making it much easier to style multiple ways. Charity shops are also brilliant hunting grounds.

Tariffs are Trump’s favorite plaything – and his justifications are absurd

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 14:00:11 GMT

The president is using forced labor as a pretext to slap tariffs on countries around the world

With the midterm elections less than four months away, it’s a precarious time for Donald Trump and Republicans: Trump’s war against Iran is going badly, his approval ratings are in the toilet, gas prices are soaring and pushing up inflation, and nation after nation is furious about Trump’s insults, bullying and ugly American unilateralism.

So amid all this mess, what does Trump do? He turns to his favorite economic plaything: tariffs. On Monday, Trump signed orders to slap a 50% tariff on many Canadian goods, and four days later, he imposed across-the-board 10% or 12.5% tariffs on goods from more than 80 countries. Trump was no doubt thumping his chest, while millions of people overseas were dumping on him for yet another unnecessary, hostile act.

Too bad for Republicans, and most Americans, though, because Trump’s fixation on tariffs will only worsen their troubles. Trump’s new tariffs will push up prices – let’s not forget that tariffs are taxes on imports, and US consumers will pay those taxes. A corollary of that: Trump’s tariffs will worsen Americans No 1 economic concern: affordability. In bad news for typical Americans, the Yale Budget Lab estimates that Trump’s tariffs will increase costs for the average US household by $1,100 each year. The tariffs are also likely to push Trump’s approval ratings deeper into the sewer. If Trump thinks these tariffs are going to distract Americans from thinking about the Epstein files or the disastrous mess he’s made with his Iran “excursion”, he’s deluding himself. The American people aren’t going to forget those things.

It’s hard to tell whether Trump’s repeated use of tariffs is a fixation or an addiction. Emperor Donald I evidently loves tariffs because he can use them to clobber other countries whenever he wants. They’re a powerful cudgel he won’t let go of. Trump imposed his new tariffs on more than 80 countries on the very day that another set of tariffs he slapped on dozens of countries was due to expire. To paraphrase the actor Charlton Heston, I can imagine Trump saying: “I’ll give up tariffs when you take them from my cold, dead hands.”

With these new tariffs, Trump is again engaged in his delusional, destructive tariff tomfoolery. They’ll push up prices, squeeze Americans’ wallets and anger other countries. Trump said his tariffs would boost US manufacturing, but the US has lost 75,000 factory jobs since he returned to office, with many executives complaining about all the herky-jerky uncertainty Trump has wrought. Assessing Trump’s effects on the economy, Atsi Sheth, the chief credit officer for Moody’s Ratings, told the New York Times :“Volatility and unpredictability is the new normal.”

Like so much that Trump does, his new tariffs are clearly based on pique and false premises with lots of shamelessness and absurdity thrown in. After the US supreme court overturned Trump’s me-against-the-whole-world tariffs in February, Trump, refusing to let go of his tariff toy, turned to other strategies. To justify his new 50% tariffs against Canada – which are piled atop numerous other tariffs he’s imposed on a country that was long the US’s closest ally – Trump relied on a never before used provision of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, a widely derided 1930 law that greatly worsened the Great Depression of a century ago. With this new tariff, placed on hockey sticks, paper, plywood, dairy products and many other Canadian goods, Trump invoked a Smoot-Hawley provision that allows retaliation against countries that engage in trade discrimination against the US.

In making that case, Trump’s exhibit No 1 is something rather preposterous, or should I say rather shameless? After Trump imposed high, punitive tariffs on Canada last year, 11 of Canada’s 13 provinces and territories halted liquor imports from the US because they were so irate about those tariffs along with Trump’s outlandish and belittling statements that he wanted to make Canada the 51st state. The White House called this ban on US liquor illegal discrimination, while Canadians view it as a type of traditional trade retaliation that countries engage in when another country – here the US – slaps tariffs on them, a situation made worse by the fact that Trump’s tariffs against Canada are an egregious violation of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement.

Trump also insists that Canada has improperly discriminated against the US because Canada imposed a 25% tariff on select US-made cars after Trump slapped a 25% tariff on Canadian-made cars.

He is essentially telling Canada: I have a right to punch you in the nose whenever I want. But if you punch me back, that’s illegal discrimination against the US. That’s the logic of America’s leading stable genius, who also offered another far-fetched justification for his decision: “We’re going to put a big tariff on Canada because of the smoke,” he told reporters on Friday, referring to wildfire smoke that has crossed the US border.

Ontario’s premier, Doug Ford, isn’t happy about Trump’s painful, new 50% tariff. “We won’t back down,” he said on social media. “The fastest and only way to get US alcohol back on Ontario shelves is for the U. S. to drop its illegal tariffs on Canada.”

As for the new tariffs hitting more than 80 countries, Trump, who over the years has shown next to no concern about worker exploitation, turned rather surprisingly to the issue of forced labor to slap on those tariffs.

After the supreme court overturned his Liberation Day tariffs, Trump hit dozens of nations with a replacement tariff that would expire after 150 days. Eager to follow the boss’s wishes and impose a new tariff as soon as that one expired, Trump’s toadies uncovered a trade law provision that lets Washington punish countries that fail to take enough action against forced labor. No surprise here: Trump’s US trade representative issued a report that made the boss happy. That report found that dozens of countries, including Canada, the UK, Australia, Norway, Japan and China, plus the European Union, were not doing enough to enforce a prohibition against forced labor. That report pointed to forced labor in producing rice in Myanmar, tobacco in Malawi, and cotton and polysilicon in China.

It’s deeply perplexing that Trump is punishing some of these trading partners. Norway has pioneered laws to crack down on forced labor in overseas supply chains, while the European Union’s new ban on goods produced with forced labor will take effect in December 2027. Canada already bans imports made with forced labor, and is moving to strengthen that prohibition.

It’s not as if Trump has shown much concern before about worker exploitation or forced labor. In 1998, Trump agreed to pay $1.375m to settle a lawsuit brought by undocumented Polish workers who said they were underpaid for their work demolishing a department store to make way for Trump Tower in New York. Some trade experts criticize Trump for slamming all these longtime allies about forced labor even as he is pushing vigorously to improve ties with China, which the Biden administration found to have serious forced labor problems in its Xinjiang region.

Trump’s newfound concern about forced labor rings especially hollow considering that his administration chopped more than $500m from the labor department’s efforts to investigate and fight against forced labor, child labor and human trafficking. “This was a completely indiscriminate meat ax that was taken to these projects, and workers will suffer,” said Thea Lee, who served as the labor department’s deputy undersecretary for international labor affairs under Biden. Bemoaning that $500m-plus in cuts, Kelly Fay Rodriguez, who was Biden’s special representative for international labor affairs, told Equal Times. “Unfortunately, it is extremely likely that child labor and forced labor practices will increase. We know these problems are endemic but … we’ve wiped out the resources and the prioritization for fighting them.”

Imagine a world where Donald Trump truly cared about worker exploitation and forced labor. He would be pushing to raise the absurdly low $7.25-an-hour federal minimum wage – something he has never lifted a finger to do. He would be increasing, rather than cutting, the number of safety inspectors for mines and factories. He would be pushing to strengthen – instead of repeatedly moving to weaken – the nation’s labor unions, long the most effective voice in fighting against worker exploitation. He would be pressuring China’s President Xi Jinping to stop all the forced labor in his country. But that would be a make-believe Donald Trump – he cares far more about what’s good for billionaires than what’s good for workers.

Bottom line: there remains far too much forced labor in the world – more than 27 million children, women and men are in forced labor, according to the International Labor Organization. It would be great if Donald Trump sincerely seized on that issue rather than used it as an insincere pretext to clobber other nations with tariffs.

Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issues

Manchester City hope Rodri will sign new deal as Real Madrid weigh up offer

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 13:44:47 GMT

Rodri’s reliability during the summer has also allayed concern regarding his physical robustness after two injury-plagued seasons, although he is to undergo surgery on a back injury having returned to England from North America.

Maybe not direct transfers, but eventually. You can’t turn down one of the world’s best clubs.”

Real’s interest in signing Rodri may well initiate interest from other elite clubs. Barcelona could move for him after Frenkie de Jong’s medial collateral ligament injury ruled him out for months, while Paris Saint‑Germain are known to admire him.

Real may need to generate finance in order to sign Rodri – especially if, as expected, they sign Yan Diomande from RB Leipzig for a fee “well in excess” of €100m (£85m) – which may mean the sale of Aurélien Tchouaméni. The 26-year-old Frenchman is thought to have agreed a new contract with the club though this has not been announced. His current deal ends in summer 2028.

Pogacar is level with Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Induráin and he is expected to continue racing in pursuit of a record-breaking sixth win.

“When it’s not fun any more, that’s when he will stop,” his mother, Marjeta, said. Asked how long her son might continue at his current level, she replied: “Maybe 10 years – I don’t know, we’ll see.”

The French media were, broadly, supportive of Pogacar’s success, with L’Équipe lauding his membership of the “club of five”, while Le Figaro described him as “untouchable, implacable and unbending”.

Pogacar’s CV is indeed untouchable. His record of victories is arguably more complete than Merckx’s, with only Paris-Roubaix and the Vuelta a España, which starts in Monaco on 22 August, still to be won.

The stats reveal just how dominant a Tour champion he has been. Over the 16,911km he has ridden during his five wins, he spent almost 9,500km in the yellow jersey. Given he took the lead in his first Tour win, in 2020, on the penultimate day, that is extraordinary.

Pogacar was the youngest of the five‑time winners to take the title and achieved his successes in just under 404 hours of racing; it took Anquetil almost 613. Pogacar’s average speed, 41.99kmh, was faster than any other five-time winner and he has won more mountain stages. These figures reflect changes in technology, equipment and athlete ability, allied to shorter stages, increased rest days and the diminishing number of time trials in the Tour.

While Pogacar and his team thrived, with Isaac del Toro joining his team leader on the Paris podium by finishing third, others plumbed the depths. Their dominant UAE Emirates XRG team won €832,750 (about £712,000) in prize money, while the Picnic PostNL team won €12,770.

French cyclists had a mixed experience. For only the third time there were no home stage wins, but three French riders – Paul Seixas, Lenny Martinez and Jordan Jegat – finished in the top 10.

Seixas represents the future for the home nation but the 19‑year‑old rider, who began the Tour recovering from a crash in June and nursing a cold, was disappointed to finish fourth in the general classification. “I’d hoped to make the podium in Paris as there wasn’t much between me and Del Toro,” he said. “But between myself and Pogacar, it’s a world apart.

“But it’s motivating and inspiring. It will make me work harder. I’ve a concrete vision of what I need to do, to get closer to my dream of winning the Tour.”

PM urged to uphold climate pledges made as mayor and ban new North Sea oil drilling

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 11:01:22 GMT

Experts who helped Burnham draw up Manchester carbon neutral pledge say backtracking would send wrong message amid wildfires and heatwaves

Leading climate scientists who created Greater Manchester’s carbon neutral by 2038 commitment are urging Andy Burnham to unequivocally reject new drilling in the North Sea.

In a letter to the prime minister they said he, as mayor of Greater Manchester, had unveiled one of the UK’s most ambitious local climate programmes that tackled housing, green growth and public transport.

Reports over the weekend continued to suggest Burnham was set to give the green light to controversial new drilling in the North Sea by approving the Jackdaw and Rosebank oilfields, which were given approval under the Conservatives but put on hold by legal action. The ruling in court said a more detailed assessment of the environmental impact was required to take into account the effect on the climate of burning any fossil fuels extracted.

Prof Kevin Anderson and scientists from the Tyndall Centre at the School of Engineering at the University of Manchester, who wrote the open letter to the prime minister, said it was “with considerable concern” that they had read reports suggesting his government intended to approve the further development of the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gasfields.

To do so would send a signal around the world that the UK was backtracking on its international climate commitments, they said.

If the reports were accurate that he intended to give the go ahead to drilling at Jackdaw and Rosebank, the scientists wrote, “they represent a profound departure from the principles you promoted as Mayor of Greater Manchester”.

Labour made a manifesto promise that no new oil and gas licences would be issued, but Jackdaw and Rosebank were already in the system at the time of the last general election. A consultation on Jackdaw will finish on 8 August.

With extreme heat and wildfires across the UK and Europe this summer, the academics said the evidence showed global emissions must be cut by 8% every year if the world was to meet the upper limit of a maximum of 2C of heating in the Paris climate agreement.

Anderson and his colleagues urged Burnham to adhere to commitments he made when announcing the Greater Manchester carbon neutral by 2038 policy.

They undertook the carbon budget analysis that underpinned the target championed by Burnham in 2024, when he said Greater Manchester could be front and centre of the green industrial revolution.

At the time Burnham said he needed greater powers than those of a mayor to deliver the pace of change required to tackle the climate crisis.

Now he has those powers, the scientists who helped him create the carbon neutral plan in Manchester said he must not abandon unequivocal scientific evidence in the face of short-term political pressure.

“The scientific evidence has only strengthened since those earlier commitments were made,” the letter said.

“Global temperatures have already risen to the lower limit of the Paris Agreement’s temperature range (1.5°C). Extreme weather events are becoming increasingly evident across the UK, most vividly the widespread moorland fires driving air quality to unsafe levels in Greater Manchester.”

Remaining global carbon budgets, which give policymakers headroom for action, continue to shrink rapidly. If governments are to respect even the weaker 2C interpretation of the Paris Agreement, global carbon dioxide emissions must now fall by almost 8% every year, starting immediately, they said.

“Against that backdrop, approving the further development of oil and gasfields cannot be reconciled with the UK’s repeated commitment to honour its international climate obligations,” the letter said.

Anderson and his colleagues said any approval of new drilling would send the wrong signal to the rest of the world.

“It would suggest that, on climate change, the UK is prepared to step back from obligations it has repeatedly urged other nations to uphold.”

The letter urged Burnham to show the same commitment to evidence and political courage that characterised his leadership in Greater Manchester in response to pressure to open up new drilling in the North Sea.

“Future generations will not judge governments by the ingenuity with which they justified expanding fossil fuel production,” the scientists wrote. “They will judge whether, when faced with unequivocal scientific evidence and clear international commitments, they had the courage and compassion to act in a manner consistent with the obligations they had freely entered into.”

Why are Democrats so quiet about the Tate brothers?

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 11:00:08 GMT

The party’s silence shows how broadly male supremacist thinking has seeped into the conventional wisdom of political strategists

It’s not exactly strange that elements of the Magaverse have embraced Andrew Tate. What’s strange is that the Democrats do not seem interested in holding the Trump movement to account for it.

Andrew Tate, the misogynist influencer who is accused by numerous women around the world and now by British prosecutors of rape and strangulation, as well as assault, sex trafficking, possession of child abuse images and extreme pornography, and various other forms of gender violence and exploitation, was arrested in Miami last week, along with Tristan, his brother and sidekick. Or I should say, they were rearrested: the men were previously charged in Romania, where they were under house arrest until, following some conveniently timed diplomatic moves from the Trump administration, they were allowed to leave the country and resettled in the US. When asked if the Trump administration had secured their release from Romania back then, the Tates’ lawyer said: “Do the math. These guys are on the plane.” Now, finally, they are awaiting extradition to the UK, where they are dual citizens.

The Tate brothers have long made their living by making provocative, contemptuous statements about women online. But in June, the New Yorker’s Heidi Blake published a long investigation that centered not on what the Tates have said, but on what they’re said to have done – detailing a long and documented history of alleged sex trafficking, violence and sexual assault along with a disturbing pattern of police mismanagement, incompetence and indifference that allowed the men to go free. The Tates denied wrongdoing in that piece; their lawyer called the new British charges against them “garbage”. But if anyone thought the Tates’ misogynistic influencer career was mere bluster, the Blake investigation offered a formidable bit of counterevidence: she painted a picture of the men acting exactly the way that they talked.

In a world where people take misogyny as seriously as they claim to, the Tates would long ago have been ostracized, and condemned, for their hatefully sexist rhetoric and alleged violence against women. In this world, they got rich, and ingratiated themselves to powerful figures in the Republican party.

Tate is a natural fit on a Maga right that has served to unite its many different factions – from Christian conservatives to Silicon Valley eugenicists, to beer-chugging barstool denizens, conspiracy mongers, and the male hosts of multi-hour podcasts – around a foundation of male supremacy. Contempt for women is the uniting force on the American right, more uniform across the competing styles within the movement even than the hatred of immigration or devotion to the prerogatives of capital. Donald Trump cemented the presidency, after all, when he was revealed to have bragged about “grab[bing]” women “by the pussy” and still maintained his base of support. In the decade that followed, his domineering, narcissistic, vulgar style of masculinity, and the alternately belittling and hateful treatment of women that accompanies it, have come to be seen on the right as a feature, not a bug. Other men within the Maga movement now imitate Trump’s style of misogyny with a gleeful competitiveness; the coalition welcomes men who collect harems of women to breed their children, those who have been multiply accused of sexual abuse and those who decry our right to vote. Andrew Tate, in this milieu, is not an exception. He is the rule.

But just because Tate’s style of masculinity is popular on the right – in which sex is seen to elevate men’s status at women’s expense, in which women’s aspirations to education, skilled work, dignity, public participation, or even mere decency are mocked; and in which men’s mistreatment of women is the key way for them to gain the esteem of other men – does not mean that it is popular with the public. Tate’s version of vulgar, avowed, preening misogyny has a constituency of Republican politicians and unlikable teenage boys; it does not have a constituency among the majority of the American public.

Why are Democrats not making the Tates into symbols of Maga’s hateful and bizarre cultural project, of Trump’s personal alleged affinity for sexual misconduct, or of the antisocial, anti-democratic and anti-equality stances of the Maga movement?

Rape, after all, might be the most quintessentially anti-democracy act: a violent refusal of equality in the most intimate terms. One could imagine an opposition to Trumpism that built from anti-rape principles into pro-democracy ones; less ambitiously, one could imagine an opposition to Trumpism that merely drew a link between Trump’s pathetic narcissism and that of the sleazeball Tates and their manosphere ilk. It seems like an easy win.

That the Democratic party is not taking it shows how broadly male supremacist thinking has seeped into the conventional wisdom of political strategists, and how anathema even the most basic and remedial feminist claims are now understood to be by those same forces. Because one explanation for why the Democrats are not taking advantage of the Tates’ links to Trump is as simple as it is dark: they do not want to alienate the Tates’ base of manosphere content consumers.

It is by now a cliche to say that Democrats are losing men, a demographic reality that is treated as a much greater emergency than the GOP’s parallel loss of women. Sects within the Democratic consultant class have made the recruitment of manly men candidates into their singular mission. Following the 2024 election, major party players fundraised a massive $20m for a “Speaking with American Men” project, meant to lure men back to the party; the California governor, Gavin Newsom, a likely 2028 presidential candidate, has forged his own podcast project, in which he has taken to embracing some rightwing cultural positions on things like trans rights. The party is running white male candidates who say cartoonish things like it’s OK “to be a manly man” – as if anyone was confused.

It is this desperate and frantic effort to re-masculinize the party at any cost that led to the recruitment of Graham Platner, the ex-marine who dropped out of the Maine Senate race earlier this month after being accused of rape (he has denied the allegations). Major players in the Democratic party did the right thing in that case, calling on Platner to drop out en masse. But many of them still believe in the strategy that elevated him in the first place: that of prizing men over women, of coveting men’s votes and men’s support as somehow more legitimate, more valuable, than women’s.

In this sense, there is another reason that some in the Democratic party won’t seize upon the Tate issue: even if they don’t condone his alleged violence, on his most fundamental principle – that men are better and more important than women are – they may not entirely disagree.

Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

‘The greatest album never made’: the untold story of George Michael’s secret, star-packed duets project

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 10:00:38 GMT

Suing his record label and sick of being a sex symbol, the singer spent 1992 working on the Trojan Souls for stars including Aretha Franklin and Bryan Ferry. Now, newly released studio footage shows him in his creative prime

Wham! special: read Andrew Ridgeley on their bizarre 1985 trip to China

The George Michael album that never was began in defiance and ended in grief. It was 1992. Mired in a toxic dispute with Sony Records, Michael chose to keep busy and declare his independence by making an album of songs to be sung by several of his musical heroes, including Aretha Franklin, Janet Jackson and Sade Adu, under the alias the Trojan Souls. Michael worked on the album for months until his Brazilian boyfriend Anselmo Feleppa died of Aids in March 1993 and he lost interest in music. It was never revived.

Tracks from the sessions have since leaked, along with some of the fly-on-the-wall footage filmed by Michael’s close friend and informal adviser Andros Georgiou, who has spent years trying to get unauthorised clips removed from YouTube and TikTok. Now, months before the 10th anniversary of Michael’s death, he is releasing 90 minutes of unedited video as Trojan Souls – not exactly a film but an unfiltered view of Michael in his creative prime. “I thought these fans were making money from my rights so I decided to stop fighting and get it out there,” Georgiou says. He hopes it will open a door on what he calls, with characteristic hyperbole, “the greatest album never made”.

Georgiou called his self-published 2012 memoir Rock: The Luckiest Man in Pop, the luck being that his father and Michael’s father were cousins who emigrated to England from Cyprus together in 1953, so he grew up alongside one of the greatest artists of his generation. They remained close until a bitter falling out in 1998, of which more later.

Ever loyal to his childhood friends (another, David Austin, now runs his estate), Michael gave Georgiou creative opportunities. They first collaborated as Boogie Box High, whose cover of the Bee Gees’ Jive Talkin’ was a Top 10 hit in 1987, and co-founded Aegean Records in 1996. Georgiou was also a regular on-the-road companion. When they were in Tokyo during the Faith tour, Sony gave Georgiou a state-of-the-art Hi8 video camera which enabled him to make high-quality home movies.

Georgiou makes the origins of the Trojan Souls sound as a dramatic as a heist. When Michael released Listen Without Prejudice Vol 1 in 1990, he was so sick of his sex-symbol image that he disappeared from view: no appearances in videos or on record sleeves, no interviews, no concerts. “He wanted to make music but he didn’t want to play the lying game any more,” says Georgiou. Michael believed that Sony then punished him by underpromoting the album. The singer felt trapped.

In January 1992, he and Georgiou flew to LA for some winter sun but Michael soon got bored and suggested going to Dave Stewart’s Chapel Studios in Encino to bang out a quick cover in the spirit of Boogie Box High. The 1979 disco hit Ain’t No Stoppin’ Us Now was a symbolic choice because Gene McFadden and John Whitehead originally wrote it to rebuke their own label, Philadelphia International. Michael decided they should return in July to start an album, recruiting vocalists he had loved growing up. According to Georgiou, only David Bowie politely declined. He says the name came to him in a dream: The Voice of Reason by the Trojan Souls. “From the Trojan horse,” he says. “The soldiers came in and then came down fighting.”

Back in London, Georgiou was contractually obliged to offer it to Sony first, despite the bad blood. “Of course they said no. I called George and he said, ‘Fuck Sony!’ I went, ‘I’ll be home in two hours with a deal, trust me.’” Georgiou called an A&R at Warner and dashed over. “Rob Dickins, the chair, was there. He said, ‘What do you want?’ I said a million pounds. He goes, done.” In October, Michael filed a lawsuit against Sony, alleging that his contract was unreasonable restraint of trade. “He wanted to get back at Sony any which way he could,” says Georgiou.

Despite the project’s bitter origins, the three songs in the film have a sunny, funky dynamism. “He was so happy,” Georgiou says. “For the first couple of months we probably had the best time of our lives making this record.” The lush ballad One Day I’ll Know was destined for Stevie Wonder and the shimmering Maybe It’s Not Your Time for Bryan Ferry. The instrumental track Wendy Melvoin’s Song featured virtuosic rhythm guitar by one half of Wendy and Lisa, in the hope that she would lure her former employer Prince on board.

Obsessed with protecting his mystique, Michael was never officially filmed handling an instrument or building a track. “If you’re a fan,” says Georgiou, “this is your first chance to see how he directs everyone in the studio.” It’s fascinating to watch how precisely Michael drills his world-class musicians – Melvoin, keyboardist Chris Cameron, bassist Deon Estus and Lynn Mabry’s backing singers – through take after take, even grabbing Estus’s bass guitar at one point to show him what he means. To the viewer the takes may sound identical but Michael was always chasing the perfect sound he heard in his head.

“He had a 48-track studio in his mind,” says Georgiou. He recalls how, even when they were kids, Michael used to deconstruct songs by their favourite artists and explain how he would have changed this or that. Or how, when they were working at Sarm West in Notting Hill, Michael would get in the car with a cassette of a skeletal backing track and have a melody written by the time he got home to Hampstead.

“He was quite a frustrating person to work with because he had quite a strange creative process,” says Sathnam Sanghera, author of Tonight the Music Seems So Loud: The Meaning of George Michael. “He would often sing at musicians and say, ‘This is what I want it to sound like.’ I’ve talked to a lot of musicians who worked with him and almost all of them said the same thing: ‘At the time it drove us fucking mad.’ But looking back they can see that of all the people they’d worked with he was the most talented. He just had these amazing ears.”

The fragments heard in Trojan Souls are tantalising but only the Elton John collaboration This Kind of Love was ever completed. By the start of 1993, Feleppa was fading fast. “It was terribly difficult for him to finish anything so we went from track to track,” Georgiou says. “And then it got too much for him.” Leaving work unfinished was not unusual for Michael, though. “George had a history of losing interest,” says Sanghera. “A lot of projects never came to fruition: Listen Without Prejudice Vol 2, the Daft Punk collaboration, the duets album …”

A few years later, Georgiou’s friendship with Michael ended, too. On 7 April 1998, Michael was arrested for “engaging in lewd conduct” in a public toilet in LA’s Will Rogers Memorial Park and the closeted star was outed to the world. “Basically it all went wrong when he was arrested,” Georgiou says. “He laughed it off but it seriously affected him mentally and that was the beginning of the end.”

When I interviewed Michael in 2004, he connected the incident to losing his mother to cancer a year earlier. Having finally worked through the creative drought occasioned by Feleppa’s death to make 1996’s Older, he was poleaxed by grief once again. “Really since 1991, when I found out [Feleppa] was HIV positive, all I’d done was either wait for someone to die or grieve,” he told me. “It was just so easy to feel picked on and angry and nihilistic.”

Michael’s compulsive cruising on Hampstead Heath created a rift. Georgiou thought it was self-destructive; Michael resented his friend’s judgment. “I couldn’t understand the risks he was taking,” Georgiou says. “He was loud and proud, which I absolutely respected, but you can’t carry on doing what you’re doing.” He claims that the final straw was Michael suddenly ordering him to drop Aegean’s entire roster. “The next day I was just like, you know what? Fuck you. And I walked out.”

An alternative account is that Georgiou crossed a line by telling his story, and giving family photographs, to Hello! magazine. Either way, Michael told me, “losing that relationship absolutely devastated me. Everything I took for granted in my 20s I lost.” Georgiou says that they tentatively reconnected in 2016 and planned to meet up in the new year. “It took a lot. We’re both Greeks at heart and have our arrogance and pride. And then he died. Even talking about it now, I can’t believe it.”

The Trojan Souls material wasn’t mothballed entirely. Ain’t No Stoppin’ Us Now was released on Aegean Records in 1998, as one of the first ever commercially available MP3s, and Michael rerecorded This Kind of Love, sans Elton, not long before his death – Sanghera calls it “his one great unreleased song”. As for the rest, we can only imagine. Could The Voice of Reason ultimately have been a triumph?

“I think it could have worked as a duets album, because 90% of George was his voice,” Sanghera says. “He was at his creative peak. This could have been Listen Without Prejudice Vol 2 if his lover wasn’t dying, if he hadn’t sued Sony. But I think he would have needed another two years for a fully realised album. This is just the beginning of something that could have been amazing.”

Georgiou has often been regarded with suspicion by Michael’s fans for monetising his proximity to pop genius. Now he is preparing a rewritten memoir, an accompanying film, the release of more footage on his website, and even a duet version of This Kind of Love if he can get Elton John’s blessing. Then again, these are his videos and Trojan Souls was his project, too. Given his long estrangement from Michael, the home movies document not just an unfinished album but a much-missed friendship. “It’s my legacy in a way,” he says. “I was there for nearly 40 years. What a time!”

Trojan Souls is available for streaming at trojansouls. com

There was one thing I swore I’d never do on WhatsApp. And now I’ve gone and done it

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 10:00:37 GMT

Leaving your blue ticks on used to be a sign that you were trustworthy. These days it conveys a certain ‘pick me’ energy

Genuine question: am I the last person in the world who still has my blue ticks on? In the early days of WhatsApp, if someone had gone into their privacy settings and turned them off, so you could never be sure when or even if this person had read your message, that told you all you needed to know. No blue ticks = red flag. Here was a slippery, sneaky individual, not to be trusted under any circumstances. As opposed to those of us who left them on – honest, noble, open books with nothing to hide. No blue ticks was an indicator that you were probably messaging a serial killer.

But recently the tide has turned. Now everyone seems to have gone all mysterious and switched them off, to leave you guessing. I’m starting to feel like a desperate blue-tick loser, over-keen and needy, falling over myself to volunteer the unnecessary information that I’ve read your message, when you are far too cool to care. Blue ticks on has real “pick me” energy. It’s attention-seeking, the coloured symbol equivalent of sending a selfie of you reading the message in question, while grinning and doing a thumbs up.

The only possible mitigating factor in turning your ticks off is that it instantly extinguishes the very worst aspect of WhatsApp: being stuck in blue-tick purgatory, AKA left on read. This is when the recipient has seen your message but is yet to reply. Even though, logically, you know they were just called into a meeting or run over by a bus, your mind starts to play tricks and you become convinced that they hate you.

Then, as more messages arrive in their inbox, you slip down the list, out of sight and mind, into the blue-tick abyss where you will languish, your paranoia increasing exponentially by the hour. Plot twist: the ticks-off brigade were the good guys all along?

Polly Hudson is a freelance writer.

Here’s why India’s cockroach protests were such a success – and why the Mamdani effect means more to come

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 09:16:55 GMT

The young leaders are eloquent and organised – and now they know what victory looks like. That could be a huge headache for Narendra Modi

The rebellion in India of the young, led by the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), unfolded against a backdrop of large, abstract, geometrical structures – arcs, planes, hemispheres – that together make up an observatory called Jantar Mantar, built in the early 18th century to refine almanacs and tell time. Jantar Mantar has been a byword for political protest for decades: it marks the space that the Delhi police assigns to the politically disgruntled so they can vent in a contained way. But it had never before hosted a political insurgency that started from scratch and forced the Indian state to back down in less than eight weeks.

When its founder, Abhijeet Dipke, brought the CJP to Jantar Mantar, it was a social media hashtag with 20 million followers. While he was studying in Boston, Dipke took the remarks of chief justice Surya Kant, who is accused of referring to the swathes of unemployed young people and activists as “parasites” and “cockroaches”, and turned them into a here-we-come meme. When he brought the CJP home to Delhi on 6 June to make it real, people were intrigued. Given the mostly dismal fate of civil society movements during prime minister Narendra Modi’s time in office, no one anticipated the David and Goliath contest that came to a head last Saturday.

Like other political tourists, I visited Jantar Mantar on 6 June out of curiosity. On that inaugural day it was modestly crowded and not that different from the dozens of demos I had attended over 50 years. The one difference was how young these so-called cockroaches were. I had seen young people mobilise against Modi’s government at close quarters before when the students of Jamia Millia Islamia, the university I taught in, came out against a pernicious citizenship bill. Their courage and idealism was defeated by a combination of police repression and organised rioting. This government’s willingness to use police brutality, vigilante violence and a pliant judiciary to snuff out protest hung over the fledgling CJP campaign like a shadow.

But when I returned a month and a half later on 20 July, the scheduled day for the march to parliament, Jantar Mantar was unrecognisable. A hunger strike had raised the political temperature of the protest. The government had forcibly removed the main hunger striker, Sonam Wangchuk, from the site and detained him in a hospital. The calculation was that his absence would defuse the tension and demoralise the protesters. That didn’t happen.

There were tens of thousands of people crammed into the barricaded space and thousands of police officers in attendance. The government had underestimated the size of the crowd that poured in by bus, train and car from Delhi and beyond. In the afternoon the Delhi police force and its masters compounded its miscalculation by attacking this giant gathering of young people with lathis (bamboo sticks) and teargas.

This tableau of brutality was shocking enough in real life, but in the hands of young digital natives, whose phone cameras were extensions of themselves, it became a gush of online content that brought the violent drama of this confrontation into every home. The callous violence of the police and the raging, mocking, laughing defiance of the young protesters played out on every mobile phone.

The cockroaches won where other protesters, not unlike them, such as Jamia’s students, had lost. They won, in part, because they weren’t visibly Muslim. There were Muslims among them, but this was a protest about the corruption of competitive examinations, an issue that concerns every middle-class family in India. It couldn’t easily be tarred as an anti-national conspiracy in the way that the struggle for secular citizenship led by Jamia’s mainly Muslim students was. This didn’t stop India’s mostly tame mainstream media from trying, but the scandal of the medical school examination was so egregious that no one gave them a hearing.

Also, this was in the heart of New Delhi, a stone’s throw from parliament. Once the government had made, from its point of view, the cardinal error of letting gen Z occupy the commanding heights of the capital, every day of the protest produced hundreds of new episodes of a national drama – a digital Mahabharat – in which the vulnerable and charismatic children of light faced off against the armed and uniformed enforcers of darkness. Bharatiya Janata party governments have sanctioned massive police violence against minorities in India’s borderlands, in Manipur, Assam and Kashmir. But this was Jantar Mantar, the sacred centre of the republic.

The leaders of the movement, Abhijeet Dipke and Saurav Das, had set themselves up for success by demanding a difficult but doable concession: the sacking of the education minister. It was difficult because Modi had never dismissed a cabinet minister in response to political pressure; this stubbornness was central to his strongman persona. It was doable because there were precedents in the history of the republic for a minister taking responsibility for a disaster and resigning.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Modi did everything he could to wriggle out of this standoff. He even produced a comically inept Instagram video promising fast-track courts to address the corruption in the examination system. When that didn’t work, his government capitulated and Dharmendra Pradhan, the education minister, departed. There was an assembly election scheduled in Uttar Pradesh next year and Modi knew that the BJP would haemorrhage political support if the Jantar Mantar impasse wasn’t resolved.

The quarrel that some commentators on the left have with the CJP is that Pradhan’s dismissal was a symbolic victory but not a substantial one. Pralhad Joshi, the man who has replaced Pradhan as education minister, is not an improvement. Like Pradhan he is a member of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the BJP’s far-right parent body. He publicly defended the premature release in 2022 of 11 men convicted for rape in the notorious Bilkis Bano gang-rape case.

The CJP’s argument is that Pradhan was always a proxy for Modi. The point of the protest was to diminish Modi by forcing him to back down publicly. Also, it isn’t clear what a systemic victory would look like or how it would be achieved.

The striking thing about the CJP’s leadership is its youth and poise. Zohran Mamdani, the youthful mayor of New York, now seems a template. He is 35. Dipke, the CJP’s Dalit leader, is 30 years old. Ashutosh Ranka, who negotiated the end of the protest with the BJP’s leadership, is about the same age. Das, the other negotiator and spokesperson, is all of 26. Neha Bora, the president of a leftwing student organisation, the All-India Students’ Association, is 25. It’s hard to know how their politics will evolve. What they have in common is eloquence, message discipline, all-round unflappability and the potential to leave a legacy. They may be an enduring problem for this government. Jantar Mantar may have just produced an echelon of homegrown Mamdanis.

Mukul Kesavan is an essayist and author based in Delhi

Amid the social and political panic about falling birthrates, why not ask new mothers what they think?

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 08:00:35 GMT

New research reveals deep anxieties. Medals and cash bonuses have been mooted as incentives, but the priority is for policy that addresses women’s real concerns

It seems as though every week brings another news story on declining global birthrates. A number of political leaders have been panicking for a while, of course, instructing citizens to reproduce in tones so beguiling, who could possibly resist? JD Vance: “I want more babies”; Jacob Rees-Mogg: “We need more babies”. While in France this year, a government direct-mailing campaign urged 29-year-olds to have a baby before it’s too late.

People are busily scratching their heads and trying to work out why this is happening. The trend is described as a catastrophe for civilisation, with leaders drumming up incentives and policies in response, from medals (Russia) and a €1,000 birth bonus (Italy) to expanding access to IVF (the US, with Donald Trump crowing – and if you’re eating you may want to skip the rest of this sentence – he’ll be known as the “fertilisation president”).

We hear ever-multiplying theories, from housing costs, contraception, education for women and smartphone addiction to lower rates of hooking up, problems with car seats, global heating and urbanisation. But something is missing in these discussions. Here’s a clue. It begins with M and it has seven letters.

In all the panic about falling birthrates, the experiences of the people actually doing the births and those parenting infants – most often mothers – are strangely absent. We hear about the ruinous effect of low birthrates, but comparatively little of the difficulties mothers face, such as maternity discrimination and mental health issues. It’s as though there is something about the way we organise society that means new mothers, caregivers, are unseen.

Thank goodness, then, for a major new report from the thinktank Theos – for which I wrote the foreword – which aims to make the experience of becoming a mother more visible. It is rich, fascinating and in depth, covering subjects such as mortality and tax, sleep and debt, the body and politics. While the experience of becoming a mother is obviously individual, there are recurring themes that should make us, as a society, take notice.

One of the most striking findings is that many mothers feel “undervalued”. What does it mean to organise society in a way that people who are growing and raising new humans feel like this? It can’t be good. But perhaps it is convenient. While most people in the study thought that childcare was as vital to the economy as paid work, the maximum state maternity pay in the UK – from six weeks to 39 weeks after giving birth – is £6,412.56, far below the minimum wage. It is no surprise, then, that in a society where value is priced against profit mothers feel undervalued.

What is it like to be a mother today? While many found childcare rewarding and enjoyable, the study also points to data showing that 48% found it stressful and 40% found it overwhelming. Perhaps this has something to do with the finding that mothers with young children carry an expectation to “do it all”: to work, manage the household and raise children. Many mothers also felt “invisible” once they had their babies. “You sort of cease to exist as a person, and you just become a mum,” said one.

Another talked about people giving up their seat on the tube when she wore a badge in her pregnancy. But “it’s very rare for people to offer you a seat once you have a baby and a pram, which is funny, because I actually feel like, particularly after my C-section, I probably needed it a bit more”. This oversight should be easy to address, with a fuller rollout of priority seats on public transport for parents travelling with babies and young children, or even – as many European countries have – specific areas on trains for prams and families.

What was birth and its aftermath like for the women in the study? Many described it as a time of “overwhelming exhaustion, sleep deprivation and anxiety”, with some finding postnatal visits rushed and “tick-box”, overlooking the mother, with the same at the routine six-week check. Experiences of maternal healthcare during birth and post-partum support were mixed: one woman spoke of “being handled like a piece of meat”.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The study found that the interviewees were nervous or scared of sharing feelings of overwhelm after giving birth, because of the stigma attached to struggling in new motherhood. The focus on perinatal mental illness is obviously important, but it’s not the whole story. A better understanding about the dimensions of ordinary matrescence would help. The report’s recommendations also include enhancing the six-week check and improving care for new mothers in the immediate hospital stay.

When we had our first child, I had never really thought about “motherhood”. I imagined my body – because I carried our kids, though of course not all mothers do – would be like a box or a flowerpot, and that when she was born I’d return to who I was, more or less. Instead, I soon realised the biological, socio-political and psychological experience of becoming a mother was a lot more complicated and intense than I’d been led to believe, from the messaging of antenatal care to the philosophy, politics and culture I had absorbed through my life.

There are two intersecting problems. First, there is a lack of recognition of the heft of the experiences of pregnancy, birth and new motherhood. Second, there is a lack of social support in the perinatal period. Both are needed to improve the experience of people becoming parents.

More widely, we need to understand how and why new mothers are feeling like this, what it reveals about our current value system, and how we might evolve a culture and society that is able to value birth and care, for all people. No need for any medals.

Lucy Jones is a journalist and the author of Matresence and Losing Eden

A TV and cinema calamity could be disastrous for what you watch and what you know. Act now to stop that

The Guardian Mon, 27 Jul 2026 05:00:32 GMT

The Paramount-Warner Bros merger is being fought in the US and UK. Britain’s culture secretary knows the risks and can intervene. She should

Though it has yet to become front-page news in the UK, you should know about the proposed Paramount-Warner Bros merger. It threatens to inflict immense harm on the British public. As actors and public figures who have spent our careers in the arts in Britain – working with British crews, on British stages and sets – we have a responsibility to the public who support, enjoy and consume the art we make.

The UK is being threatened by a media merger that would harm our workers, our culture and the public – but we can stop it. We are encouraged by Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport, who recently sent letters to Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros Discovery, as well as a statement to parliament, indicating that she is “minded to intervene” in Paramount’s $110bn takeover of Warner Bros.

She is correct to investigate this major threat to the UK’s public interest. And she will not be acting alone. This month, 12 US states, led by California, sued in federal court to block the merger, warning that it would raise prices, shrink the number of films made and degrade the quality of what audiences see. And they just won a major victory: on Friday, Paramount agreed to delay the merger until trial, which could be months. These states acted even after Washington’s own justice department – despite the reported reservations of career staff – waved the deal through.

Their lawsuit confirms the danger; it cannot, however, do the UK’s work for it. US courts fight on the antitrust front for US markets. The EU, which last week conditionally backed the merger, also makes its own decisions. The UK’s public interest, our public service broadcasting, our news plurality, the plurality of voices British audiences hear, can only be defended here, by our own secretary of state and the Competition and Markets Authority.

The fight against this merger now runs on two fronts, and Nandy commands one of them. Should her department decide to intervene, it may prove one of the most important decisions any culture secretary has taken for UK film, television and media in a generation.

This is why. We have spent our lives working in this industry. We know what it looks like from the inside: the sound stages at Leavesden, the crews who move from production to production, the editors and camera operators and costume designers whose names scroll past in the credits at the end of a film. These are our cherished friends and colleagues, who create the shows we all love, who produce the news that educates the public and film the sport events we enjoy together. UK film and television are not just images on your screens; they are the lives and livelihoods of thousands of workers and families, whose work supports local economies. The industry supports more than 180,000 jobs, generated £6.8bn in production spend last year alone and adds roughly £12bn a year in value to our economy. It is one of the things the UK still does better than almost anyone, and a cultural heritage we must protect.

We have watched, with growing alarm, what consolidation does to the breadth and depth of the work we produce: independent film acquisitions at the leading independent film festival Sundance fell by half between 2019 and 2025. Award-winning documentaries – films that won Oscars and topped festival juries – have struggled to find commercial distribution because they touched subjects the remaining handful of buyers found inconvenient. Every merger of this kind narrows the funnel through which stories can reach audiences.

That is precisely what makes the Paramount-WBD merger so dangerous. It’s why the intervention of Nandy and her department matters so much.

Paramount proposes to swallow Warner Bros Discovery in one of the largest leveraged buyouts ever attempted, loading the combined company with an estimated $84bn in debt. To service it, executives have promised investors around $6bn in “synergies”. In plain English, that means redundancies, cancelled productions, fewer films commissioned and fewer risks taken.

We have seen this before. When Discovery merged with WarnerMedia in 2022, it shelved finished films and cut thousands of jobs; when Skydance merged with Paramount last year, it laid off about 2,000 people. Now the same executives are making the same promise, and UK crews, producers, talent and audiences will pay when the bill comes due.

But jobs are mostly a matter for the Competition and Markets Authority, whose review should end in a full phase 2 investigation. The job of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport goes further: to determine whether the merger is in the public interest. It most certainly is not. In her statement to British MPs, Nandy cited the need for a sufficient plurality of views in news media and a sufficient plurality of individuals controlling media enterprises. She has also highlighted the potential impact on streaming services, content homogenisation and children’s television. The Enterprise Act protects something we should all care about: who decides what we get to watch, and what we get to know.

Consider the breadth of what this single company would hold. Channel 5, one of our five public service broadcasters, which serves the evening news to people without the cost of a subscription. CNN International, which Ofcom research in 2018 found UK viewers rated above every other TV news source for quality, accuracy, trustworthiness and impartiality. The CNN and CBS news archives – among the world’s most important broadcast news collections, with more than 4.25m videos, images and media spanning nearly half a century of history. If one commercially interested owner controls access to both, they control the raw material of our historical memory.

One owner controlling this much of the news, and the truth, endangers the public in a way no ordinary consolidation does. When separate owners run separate newsrooms, a story judged inconvenient by one can still reach audiences through another. Fold those newsrooms into a single company, and one boardroom’s commercial anxieties – or political debts – determine what millions of people see and what they never learn existed.

And we know something about this particular proprietor’s intentions. Paramount’s chief executive reportedly told Donald Trump that he would make “sweeping changes” to CNN if the deal went through. When the buyer of the world’s most trusted international news channel makes editorial promises to a politician, a British secretary of state is entitled – and, really, obliged – to ask questions before the ink dries.

Nandy has been scrupulous in noting that no final decision has been taken. Good. It is important to take the time to get this right. But the case for a full public interest intervention, with Ofcom assessing plurality and reporting back, is overwhelming.

Actors are often told to stay out of legal arguments. We understand the instinct. But we have spent our lives on enough UK sets, worked alongside enough UK crews and watched enough brilliant work from the UK struggle to find a buyer to know that this is not someone else’s argument. It is ours. Nandy has opened the door to intervention. She must walk through it, for the sake of everyone who makes UK television and film – and everyone who watches it. If she does not, we will be left without the ability to protect our industry and our culture from this consolidation. We must not push the public’s interest aside; we must stand up for it and block this merger.

Alan Cumming, Benedict Cumberbatch and Benedict Wong are actors working in the UK and Hollywood
