Trump Asks Supreme Court to Allow Order Restricting Mail Voting

The New York Times July 27, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

The Trump administration asks justices to intervene after an appeals court blocked key parts of a mail-in voting executive order.

By Abbie VanSickle

Reporting from Washington

The Trump administration on Monday asked the Supreme Court to clear the way for an executive order by President Trump that restricts voting by mail, setting up a legal showdown as the president pushes for more control over voting ahead of the midterm elections in November.

The administration filed the emergency application to the justices after a federal appeals court on Saturday blocked key parts of his executive order.

In the application, Solicitor General D. John Sauer called the lower court ruling “indefensible,” asserting that it imposed “serious irreparable harm on the federal government” and would bar federal agencies from implementing an executive order “promoting election integrity in the upcoming federal elections in November.”

The legal battle stems from an executive order signed up Mr. Trump in late March that had attempted to place limits on mail-in voting, including using federal oversight of the U. S. Postal Service to gain greater control over mail-in voting practices.

The executive order directed the Department of Homeland Security to create state-by-state citizen lists that would help determine voter eligibility. It then called on the Postal Service to use lists provided by states to determine if voters should be allowed to vote by mail.

More than 20 Democratic attorneys general challenged the order in court, arguing that it violated several provisions of the Constitution, including the separation of powers, by having the executive branch take control of functions usually regulated by Congress and the states.

The Supreme Court on Monday asked the challengers to respond to the government’s emergency application by Monday, Aug. 3.

Got a news tip about the courts? If you have information to share about the Supreme Court or other federal courts, please contact us.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly criticized mail-in voting and sought restrictions on it. For years, he has made unfounded claims sowing doubt about voting by mail and claiming that it allows widespread fraud.

So far, federal courts have stymied many of Mr. Trump’s efforts to restrict mail voting.

In late June, a federal judge issued a ruling that blocked key parts of the executive order. Judge Indira Talwani, a federal district judge in Massachusetts, concluded that “the Constitution does not grant the President any specific powers over elections.”

She underlined the words “does not.”

This weekend, a three-judge panel from the U. S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit upheld her decision.

The judges wrote that if the president’s order were allowed to go into effect for the midterm elections in November, “it would sow confusion and threaten disenfranchisement of many eligible voters.”

The Constitution gives the states and Congress powers over elections, but it does not give those powers to the president, the judges wrote.

The Supreme Court has shown skepticism of Mr. Trump’s efforts to restrict mail-in voting. In late June, the justices upheld a Mississippi law that allows mail-in ballots postmarked by Election Day to be counted if they are received up to five business days later, a rejection of the Trump administration’s efforts to overturn the statute.

In that ruling, Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. and Justice Amy Coney Barrett joined the court’s three liberals, announcing that nothing in federal law requires ballots to be received by Election Day provided they are cast by that day. Although the ruling focused on Mississippi’s law, it also appeared to leave in place similar laws in at least 18 other states and territories, including Nevada and California, that harbor battleground congressional districts in the midterm elections.

After the decision was announced, Mr. Trump posted on social media, calling the ruling a “tremendous loss” and urging Congress to pass legislation that places restrictions on mail-in ballots and adds new voter identification requirements.

Abbie VanSickle covers the United States Supreme Court for The Times. She is a lawyer and has an extensive background in investigative reporting.

At least one tornado was confirmed near Northern Lake Winnebago in Wisconsin.

Tom Nelson, the county executive for Outagamie County, which includes Appleton, Wis., told The Associated Press that there was “extensive and severe damage” in Menasha and Fox Crossing, and reports of collapsed buildings. “All indications are that this was a devastating system that has caused extensive damage,” he said.

Photos and videos on social media appeared to show buildings damaged in areas around Appleton. The Appleton Police Department said there were several large tree limbs down throughout the city and that it was working with other nearby agencies to “respond to many storm related calls” on Monday afternoon.

By early afternoon, the National Weather Service had already issued multiple tornado warnings as the storms began sweeping through, including at least one described as a “particularly dangerous situation,” the most severe warning.

The utility We Energies said it had about 35,000 customers without power in and around Appleton on Monday afternoon. “We have reports of broken power poles, downed lines and damaged equipment in the Appleton area,” said Brendan Conway, a company spokesman. “We have all available crews working to restore power as quickly and safely as possible as we also prepare for more storms throughout the day.”

The storms in Wisconsin were also producing large hail, with one preliminary report near Gresham noting that ice the size of a grapefruit had fallen from the sky.

By 5 p. m. local time, nearly 450,000 homes and businesses were without power in Wisconsin, Illinois, Indiana and Michigan, according to Poweroutage. com, which tracks utilities.

Gordon Hintz, the top elected official in Winnebago County, Wis., told The A. P. he was not aware of any deaths or injuries, but the authorities were watching for that possibility. “Obviously, the footage looks devastating,” Mr. Hintz said. “Clearly some significant damage done with power lines down and things like that.” He also told The A. P. he had heard reports of destroyed buildings.

Thunderstorm watches were issued for most of eastern Wisconsin, down into Illinois and Indiana, across the Great Lakes and across the western shores of Michigan. In addition to tornadoes, the Weather Service warned that the storms could bring damaging winds, sometimes gusting as strong as a hurricane’s.

By midafternoon, another intense storm was moving out of Northern Illinois into Indiana and was expected to produce strong winds, damaging hail and potentially a tornado or two. This system was likely to continue sweeping across Indiana through the afternoon and the evening. Flooding was becoming a threat as more storms formed over the same areas, and several flash-flood warnings were in place across the region. The worst of the storms were more likely in the Midwest on Monday afternoon, but there was a chance a few thunderstorms would reach into in the Northeast, including New York City.

Working with dolls, family photographs, fabric scraps and other found objects, she became a leading figure in assemblage art.

Bettye Saar in 2019. Credit... Erik Carter for The New York Times

Supported by

By Jori Finkel

Betye Saar, the groundbreaking California assemblage artist who confronted stereotypes about Black women through her dreamy memento boxes as well as her arresting images of Aunt Jemima armed with rifles and other weapons, died on Sunday at her home in Los Angeles. She was 99.

Hannah Gottlieb-Graham, a publicist for Roberts Projects in Los Angeles, the gallery that represented Ms. Saar, confirmed the death.

Assemblage refers to sculpture made from found objects, and Ms. Saar was a leading practitioner in California starting in the 1960s and ’70s, along with George Herms, Edward and Nancy Kienholz, John Outterbridge and Noah Purifoy.

More than her male counterparts, Ms. Saar was known for incorporating into her work delicate fabrics associated with domestic life, strong images of the Black female body and a heavy dose of spirituality. Her most celebrated pieces from the 1970s served to confront and complicate stereotypes of Black people that were embodied in minstrel characters or figures of Black “mammies,” the women hired to care for white children.

One way that Ms. Saar transformed these derogatory figures, which were easy to find at the time in the form of collectibles, was by arming them. In her acclaimed 1972 assemblage “The Liberation of Aunt Jemima,” inspired in part by her rage after the assassination of the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., she supplied a plastic figurine of the character made famous on pancake boxes with a broom, rifle and grenade. The work incorporates emblems of the Black Power movement, from a swath of kente cloth to the image of a raised fist.

In her book “South of Pico” (2017), about Black artists in Los Angeles in the ’60s and ’70s, the art historian Kellie Jones described Ms. Saar’s Aunt Jemima as “incredibly strident, promoting the threat of violence.” Angela Davis described it as the spark that lit the Black women’s revolution.

“I had this Aunt Jemima, and I wanted to put a rifle and a grenade under her skirts,” Ms. Saar told The Los Angeles Times in 2016. “I wanted to empower her. I wanted to make her a warrior.”

Betye Irene Brown was born on July 30, 1926, in Watts, Calif., shortly after the town was annexed by Los Angeles. She was the oldest of three children of Jefferson Maze Brown and Beatrice Lillian Parson, both of mixed heritage: African, Native American and Irish on her mother’s side, and African and Choctaw on her father’s. Mr. Brown died when she was 5, and Betye grew up in Pasadena with her mother.

In a 2011 oral history for the Getty Research Institute, Ms. Saar described her upbringing as middle class and not entirely segregated. The public pool and parks were, she recalled, but theaters and streetcars were not.

Her mother was a seamstress, and Ms. Saar grew up making things — at art classes at school and on her own, often creating gifts for friends and family. She spent her last two years of high school studying ceramics, illustration, watercolors and art history at Pasadena Junior (now City) College.

In 1949, she graduated from the University of California, Los Angeles, where she majored in design, and found work designing jewelry, home goods and greeting cards before starting her career as a printmaker.

Ms. Saar credited her interest in assemblage to two influences. One was the slowly growing “Watts Towers,” which she liked to visit as a girl with her grandmother. The Italian immigrant Simon Rodia spent decades building these soaring structures by hand, embedding in concrete an array of broken glass, tile, ceramics and more.

“I was fascinated by how he used bottle caps and corn cobs and broken plates — trash, essentially — to make art, to make something beautiful,” she told The New York Times in 2024. In the Getty oral history, she compared the towers to “strange castles” from the fairy tales that she loved as a girl.

The other eye-opener, she said, was a major exhibition at the Pasadena Art Museum in 1967 of the work of Joseph Cornell, with its array of surrealist-tinged, memento-laden boxes, featuring poetic assortments of marbles, letters, feathers and more. She remembered each box being as dramatically spot-lit as a precious gem.

The Cornell show inspired her to set out to create what she often called her own “magical little worlds.”

Living in the hippie enclave of Laurel Canyon, she began collecting objects from local yard sales, thrift stores, flea markets and more; later she would add items purchased during travels to Nigeria, Senegal, Mexico, Haiti, Brazil and elsewhere.

Ladies’ gloves and brooches, faded family photographs and embroidered handkerchiefs were recurring objects in her work. Images of hands and celestial bodies were also favorites, reflecting her interests in palmistry, astrology and tarot-card reading. When a beloved great-aunt, Hattie Parsons Haynes Keyes, died in the early 1970s, Ms. Saar inherited a trunk filled with personal effects — letters, photographs, handkerchiefs, trinkets — that she began to use, too.

“I’ve always felt that old objects hold a power,” she said in 2024. “They’ve survived, and they have a sense of the previous owner. They have a spirit.”

By the 1970s, Ms. Saar had also begun using actual window frames to contain and organize her artworks, first layering her own prints and drawings in the frames before adding other objects.

One of her most important windowpane assemblages, “Black Girl’s Window” (1969), features in its upper section stars, moons and a lion representing the artist’s astrological sign, Leo, floating above a daguerreotype of the artist’s grandmother. The lower pane shows a dark silhouette of a girl’s face and hands pressed against the window, as if she is some sort of mystic seer gazing across a spiritual divide.

The work has often been read as an expression of a young Black woman’s ancestral yearning and spiritual longing — what the art historian Richard J. Powell has called Ms. Saar’s “version of a crystal ball.”

By the late 1990s, Ms. Saar began revisiting some of her pathbreaking themes and images in new work. For starters, she brought back Aunt Jemima with “newer weapons and a tougher attitude,” as she wrote in a 1998 catalog introduction. One innovation at this time was her use of vintage washboards as her canvas — a symbolic material for exploring the plight, past and present, of Black women.

Ms. Saar exhibited throughout her lifetime. But it was only when she reached her 80s and 90s that she received the international museum attention and scholarship needed to secure her place in the canon. She was awarded several lifetime achievement awards, including one from the International Sculpture Center in New York in 2018.

Carol S. Eliel, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art curator who organized the 2019 exhibition “Betye Saar: Call and Response,” said in an interview in 2018 that Ms. Saar was “not nearly as well known as she deserves, likely because she is Black, a woman and working in Los Angeles — three strikes against her in the art world until all too recently.”

From 1952 to 1970, Ms. Saar was married to the ceramist Richard Saar, who died in 2004. They had three daughters. Their youngest, Tracye, became a writer, while Alison and Lezley became prominent visual artists in Los Angeles in their own rights, showing work with their mother on occasion.

They survive her, along with six grandchildren.

Since 2016, her gallerist, Ms. Roberts, has worked closely with Ms. Saar on a definitive volume of her work, known in the field as a catalogue raisonné.

“I still want to make art,” Ms. Saar told The Times in 2024. “Sometimes in the morning when I wake up, it’s hard to get out of bed, hard to get back into my body and get it to move. But I do it. Not everyone has a reason to get out of bed, something they love to do and that gives their life meaning. I am so lucky that I have that as part of my life.”

Ash Wu contributed reporting.

Seattle Police Search for 2nd Shooter in Sunday’s Deadly Attack

The New York Times July 27, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

One 15-year-old suspect is in custody, but authorities said they were looking for a second shooter in the attack at a food festival that left three dead.

By Anna Griffin

Seattle police have arrested a 15-year-old and are seeking another suspect in a shooting on Sunday night that killed three people and injured as many as eight, including a toddler, at a food festival near the iconic Space Needle.

The 15-year-old will face initial charges of first-degree assault at a court appearance on Monday as investigators work to find the other suspect and determine which of them is responsible for the deaths.

Mayor Katie Wilson said the shootings at the Bite of Seattle festival were the third major occurrence of gun violence in the city in just a few days.

“This has been an especially tough week in Seattle,” she said.

Though crime is down in Seattle, city officials, including its new mayor, have struggled to respond to the city’s ongoing public safety problems in a few specific neighborhoods. Those problems include gang violence, drive-by shootings and human trafficking.

Ms. Wilson said Monday that investigators believed two people exchanged shots outside the armory building at Seattle Center, a tourist hub. They believe eight people were caught in the crossfire, including a 2-year-old boy whose injuries were not life-threatening.

Two adult men died at the scene, and an adult woman died later at a Seattle hospital.

Little is known about the second shooter, including whether that person is among the dead, authorities said.

“There is a second shooter,” Chief Shon Barnes said. “We are trying to identify who that person is. Our officers need your help.”

The city’s closed-circuit video surveillance system, the subject of intense debate when it was installed, does not extend to Seattle Center. Police investigators are using private camera footage and asking witnesses to turn over any cellphone video of the shooting or the moments afterward.

In April, gunfire disrupted the mayor’s announcement of new investments in meals and child care outside a community center southeast of the downtown area. Multiple bullets struck the building about 50 yards from where the mayor, community advocates and journalists had gathered for the event. No one was injured and the police said it was not a targeted attack. The mayor’s young daughter was at the event and was hustled to safety along with Ms. Wilson.

Much of the recent attention on violence and the debate over how to stop it has centered on a stretch of Aurora Avenue, a busy north-south corridor where drive-by shootings, open-air drug markets and commercial sex have challenged city leaders for years. Police have attributed the problems along Aurora Avenue to gangs and organized crime networks.

Last week, three people were injured in an early morning drive-by shooting just off Aurora Avenue north of downtown. Over the weekend, residents in nearby neighborhoods reported multiple bursts of gunfire, including one incident in which stray bullets narrowly missed a home with an infant inside.

Over the weekend, two bystanders were injured during a late-night shootout in the Capitol Hill neighborhood, a nightlife hub. Police have said they are investigating the Friday night violence as a gang-related incident.

Chief Barnes said Seattle was suffering from a spate of gun violence tied to “small groups that appear to be at odds with each other.”

Ms. Wilson said Monday that she planned to launch a renewed gun violence reduction strategy, with a special emphasis on youth violence prevention.

Though the mayor has approved expanded use of security cameras in the neighborhoods most affected, frustrated residents have resorted to building homemade barricades to deter through-traffic and the crime they believe accompanies it.

Anna Griffin is the Pacific Northwest bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of Washington, Idaho, Alaska, Montana and Oregon.

Maine Democrats Have a New Working-Class Hero. Can He Deliver?

The New York Times July 27, 2026

Advertisement

Newsletter

Troy Jackson, a former logger, faces the tall task of taking down Susan Collins.

By Jess Bidgood

Reporting from Bangor, Maine

He rubbed his hands together. He cocked his eyebrows. He gave a little shrug. And as Troy Jackson looked out at hundreds of Democrats cheering his name, he seemed as surprised any anyone to find himself here, in an antiseptic convention center on a hot day, moments away from accepting his party’s nomination for U. S. Senate after the implosion of Graham Platner’s candidacy.

“I went into the woods right after high school — all of us, I was no different,” Jackson said on Saturday, speaking with a gravelly northern accent that swallows some of his words whole. “I’m nothing special.”

Certain aspects of Jackson’s electoral history would support that assessment, politically speaking. A former state legislator, he lost the primary for governor this year, coming in third. He lost the primary when he ran for Congress in 2014. He is not well known outside the State House and the sparsely populated stretches of Northern Maine he represented as a state senator.

But Democrats whom I have spoken to, both in the buzzy hall on Saturday and well beyond, believe that Jackson’s life story makes him very special indeed. They have chosen an honest-to-God lumberjack to finally topple Senator Susan Collins, and they are hoping his working-class bona fides will hold down her margins in the reddest parts of the state — which could push Democrats to elevate similar candidates elsewhere.

“He is a true working-class champion — he’s not an academic that’s stepped in, or a political operative,” said Joseph Geevarghese, the executive director of Our Revolution, a progressive group that emerged from Senator Bernie Sanders’s first presidential campaign (which Jackson worked on in 2016).

Jackson’s candidacy, Geevarghese said, will be an “example and case study in how our movement succeeds or fails going forward.”

Jackson’s general-election campaign, which is only officially two days old, is leaning heavily on his biography. A fifth-generation logger from the tiny town of Allagash, Maine, he joined a 1998 blockade of the northern border to stop cheap Canadian labor from going in and American wood from going out.

“The people that I worked beside were getting screwed, and no one in power seemed to care about that,” Jackson said on Saturday, explaining the origins of the populism that would take him first to the State House — where he was elected in 2002 as an independent — and then to the State Senate, where he served as president.

“We’re not from the left, we’re not from the right,” Jackson said before some of the delegates piped up to join him. “We’re from the bottom, and we are rising.”

Jackson is, of course, the second man with a working-class persona Democrats have turned to this year to take down Collins. The party’s primary voters decisively rejected Gov. Janet Mills, a former prosecutor and the choice of the party establishment (and, as she frequently pointed out, the only Democrat who has actually won a statewide election since 2006).

Democrats are quick to say that Jackson’s politics and life story make him an obvious inheritor of Platner’s insurgent movement. What they don’t say out loud is that someone who actually worked as a logger might be a better avatar than Platner, a prep-school alum and gentleman oyster farmer whose working-class credentials were open to debate but who seized on a wave of populist anger anyway.

“We need people like loggers, millwrights, papermakers, ditch diggers — anybody in there that can represent us because they are us,” Joel Hooper, 63, a Democrat and former millwright who lost his job when the mill where he worked closed down, told me on Saturday, shortly after voting to make Jackson the new nominee.

“We’re trying,” he added, “to make this party represent the working class again.”

Jackson is one of several Democratic candidates around the country who are leaning on hardscrabble personal stories to make inroads with working-class voters who have peeled off from the party in the Trump era.

Some Democrats have done that successfully. Take Representative Jared Golden, who represents northern Maine, including the turf Jackson represented as a state lawmaker, or Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington State, who owns an auto shop.

But it doesn’t always work. Remember when Democrats hoped that Gov. Tim Walz of Minnesota, with his camo hats and working knowledge of a car engine, would help former Vice President Kamala Harris win over white men?

“This is the category error that the left is making,” Matt Bennett, a co-founder of the centrist think tank Third Way, told me, “which is, if you find someone that looks the part, that they will be satisfied with that.”

Republicans are moving to tie Jackson to Platner and present him as too far left for Maine, hoping to neutralize any cultural affinity he might have with voters in the rural and conservative areas of the state.

Democrats are talking little about the 20 years he spent in state government. And they are hoping that his life story is enough to paper over the obvious weaknesses of his candidacy, including his stark fund-raising disadvantage; his halting speaking style; and the reports, including some from my colleagues, that he was quick to anger during his time in state government.

“If there aren’t more stories that we don’t know, I think that’s just who Troy has always been,” said Representative Chellie Pingree, a Democrat. “I guess without thoroughly excusing anybody’s anger, people are so frustrated. They are looking for candidates who show their passion and do a little fist pounding.”

Jess Bidgood is a managing correspondent for The Times and writes the On Politics newsletter, a guide to this pivotal moment in American politics.

Chinese A. I. Start-Up Shows the World What It Has Built

The New York Times July 27, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Moonshot said some users will have to get licenses to access its Kimi K3 model as the company threads a needle between sharing and profiting from its technology’s popularity.

By Meaghan Tobin

Meaghan Tobin is the Asia technology correspondent. She reported from New York.

The Chinese start-up Moonshot publicly released the details of its latest artificial intelligence model on Monday, showing the world how it was built. But in a departure for most Chinese A. I. firms, Moonshot indicated that people or companies who want to use it on a large scale will have to secure licenses to use it.

The model, called Kimi K3, sent shock waves through Silicon Valley and U. S. technology stocks this month when Moonshot said that it performed some tasks as well as the best models from American rivals, including OpenAI and Anthropic.

Kimi K3 followed the release of other high-performing Chinese A. I. models. Most of these were open source or open weight, which means the company publicly shares the details of how it built the technology, making it easier for anyone to use it. China’s tech industry has embraced open source, which has helped Chinese firms improve their models quickly and won them customers around the world with lower prices.

The model’s release has also inflamed a fierce debate in Beijing, Silicon Valley and Washington about whether governments should take steps to limit access to Chinese open source models.

In the United States, executives, investors and officials are divided over whether the increasingly widespread use of Chinese models goes beyond being a threat to the profits of American A. I. firms to constituting a threat to U. S. national security.

In China, the debate centers on how to capitalize on making a technology that is accessible and popular, while finding ways to make money from it. Chinese companies must navigate those forces alongside evolving policies set by a government that has placed A. I. development near the top of its economic priorities.

With its release of programming code and other information on Monday, Moonshot is showing its work in public, which is consistent with China’s open source ethos. But the company is also moving to capitalize on its model’s popularity by saying that large users will need to enter into commercial licensing agreements.

The model is so large that it could not be downloaded and used on a basic computer. While Kimi K3 is technically open, most people who use it will either get a subscription from Moonshot or get access to the model from another company that has reached a licensing agreement with Moonshot.

Chinese companies have tried different approaches to bring in enough money to sustain the enormous expense of building A. I. systems. Moonshot is notable for being the first to make this commercial requirement so explicit, said Kevin Xu, the founder of Interconnected Capital, a hedge fund that invests in A. I. technologies.

In the past, Chinese start-ups have shared technical details at the same time they unveiled a new model. But Moonshot waited nearly two weeks.

The delay signals just how sensitive this technology has become as a geopolitical flashpoint between China and the United States.

Since Meta announced late last year that it would acquire Manus, an A. I. start-up founded in China, the Chinese government has placed enormous scrutiny on how A. I. systems made in the country are used by people outside it. In April, the Chinese government ordered the transaction be unwound, indicating that it was considering whether A. I. systems made by Chinese companies could be regulated as exports.

Now, Chinese officials are grappling with how to regulate the technology to allow Chinese companies to compete with rivals in Silicon Valley, while keeping the strategic and economic benefits firmly inside China.

On the same day that Moonshot announced Kimi K3, Xi Jinping, China’s leader, made a speech at the World A. I. Conference in Shanghai that cast China as the global champion of an open approach to the technology.

“The crux of the debate in China is how do you square these different signals about the strategic benefit of Chinese tech being used around the world,” said Samm Sacks, a senior fellow at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies who attended the conference in Shanghai. “Beijing wants champions, but how not to kill the golden goose?”

China’s A. I. industry has faced years of U. S. trade restrictions that limit its ability to buy the computer chips that power A. I. systems. It also has far less money to buy such computer power compared to deep-pocketed American rivals.

Two days after Moonshot announced Kimi K3, the company was forced to announce that it needed to stop accepting new users because it couldn’t get enough computer chips to serve them. The company is not accepting new subscribers. Moonshot declined to comment on its subscribers on Monday.

Jeffrey Ding, a professor at George Washington University who studies A. I. competition between the U. S. and China, said that Chinese companies had embraced open source in part as a tool to help them catch up quickly to the best A. I. systems in the world.

“Chinese companies are not doing open source for the sake of open source itself; they are employing it at as a strategy, as a tool of the challenger,” he said. “Eventually the goal is to make money.”

Xinyun Wu contributed reporting from Taipei, Taiwan.

Meaghan Tobin covers business and technology in Asia for The Times, with a focus on China. She is based in Taipei.

How the Houthis Cornered Saudi Arabia Into a New Conflict

The New York Times July 27, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen has seized on a vulnerable moment for neighboring Saudi Arabia, which does not want another war. The group hopes to force political concessions in Yemen that could give it more authority and more access to resources.

By Vivian Nereim and Shuaib Almosawa

Vivian Nereim reported from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and Shuaib Almosawa from Sana, Yemen.

After four years of political deadlock in Yemen, the Houthis were growing increasingly frustrated. A truce between the Iran-backed militia and neighboring Saudi Arabia had turned into a brittle stalemate, and the Houthis, feeling they had little to lose, wanted greater authority over Yemen and its oil resources.

Saudi officials, for their part, had no interest in another clash with the Houthis. Their previous bombing campaign in Yemen had turned into a decade-long quagmire thatcontributed to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Yemenis from violence, hunger and disease. They wanted to avoid another expensive conflict that could endanger their plans to transform the kingdom into a business and tourism hub.

Into this tinderbox, the U. S. war with Iran flung a spark. Over the past few weeks, the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have spiraled into new clashes that risk expanding into another full-blown war.

“The Houthis have one solution for every problem in the world, which is go to war,” said Farea al-Muslimi, a Yemen-focused fellow at the London-based research group Chatham House. “The Saudis solve every problem by trying to shower it with money,” he added, “and the Houthis by shooting at it.”

The last Saudi-Houthi war pushed Yemen to the brink of famine. It paused with a fragile truce in 2022, but talks toward a durable peace deal eventually stalled.

The limbo was never going to last, but Saudi Arabia, distracted by other crises, appeared to hope it would hold a bit longer.

The Saudi ambassador to Yemen, Mohammed al-Jaber, said in a social media post on Saturday that the kingdom was keen to de-escalate. He blamed the Houthis for “insisting on a path of escalation and violence” and accused them of serving foreign agendas in an apparent reference to Iran.

But the battle-hardened Houthis may think they have much to gain from a new confrontation with Saudi Arabia, including access to Yemeni oil revenue and greater authority over the country, according to officials and diplomats who have dealt with the militia.

“Our souls are content with any level of sacrifice,” Abdulmalik al-Houthi, the group’s leader, said in a televised speech on July 16, after tensions with Saudi Arabia spiked.

The Houthis are acting in support of their main ally, Iran, but also to force Saudi Arabia and the international community to make political concessions in Yemen, according to researchers who study the group.

In the past week, the Houthis have fired missiles and drones into Saudi Arabia and at ships in the Red Sea, disrupting already volatile global energy markets, while a Saudi-led military coalition has carried out airstrikes in Houthi-held territory for the first time in years.

“There is a real concern that the internal Yemeni war could reignite,” said April Alley, an analyst who worked on Yemen’s peace process at the United Nations and is now a senior fellow at the Washington Institute, a research organization.

This account of the situation in Yemen is based on interviews with Yemeni officials, current and former Western diplomats involved in Yemen’s peace process and regional analysts. Many spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the details of sensitive political negotiations.

The Houthis have chosen a vulnerable moment for Saudi Arabia, analysts say. Saudi Arabia typically exports most of its oil through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway that Iran has effectively blocked since the Iran war began. The kingdom now depends on the Red Sea to export oil — the lifeblood of its economy.

“The Houthis are good at smelling blood in the water,” said Ms. Alley.

The Saudi response so far has been calibrated to try to avoid getting sucked into a broader war, said Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen at International Crisis Group. But if they hold back entirely, they risk emboldening the Houthis, he added.

“The Saudis were cornered, and they feel like there will be a higher cost if they stay silent,” he said.

Trapped in the middle of this power struggle are tens of millions of Yemeni citizens suffering from widespread deprivation. Some of them say that even a return to fighting would be better than their current despair.

“We’ve had enough of this hardship and we needed a way out, whether through dialogue or war,” said Ayman Abdulhaq, a 43-year-old father of four and taxi driver in the Houthi-controlled capital of Yemen, Sanaa. “People are always looking for a breakthrough, no matter the consequences,” he added.

The Houthis began as a ragtag group of Shiite Muslim rebels in Yemen’s mountainous north, with a slogan calling for death to America and Israel. With Iranian support, they started a civil war by overrunning the capital in 2014, routing the internationally recognized government in Sanaa.

Saudi Arabia, Yemen’s neighbor to the north, was alarmed at the idea of an Iran-backed militia on their border. A Saudi-led military coalition began a bombing campaign, backing anti-Houthi forces inside Yemen that were trying to restore the government.

But the war dragged on for years, and Saudi Arabia pulled back amid international pressure over its role in exacerbating Yemen’s already severe humanitarian crisis.

By the time the truce was declared, the Houthis had created a de facto state in northern Yemen. The south is nominally controlled by the internationally recognized government, which is financially and militarily dependent on Saudi Arabia.

Saudi officials still have final say over a variety of Yemeni affairs.

At first, it seemed like military fatigue and political will on both sides could lead to a lasting peace. In late 2023, with the help of the United Nations, Saudi Arabia and the Houthis came close to signing a preliminary peace deal — referred to by officials as a “road map” — that would have provided an outline for a long-term political resolution, according to Yemeni and Western officials involved in those efforts.

A key component of that deal was an agreement to enable salary payments to Yemeni government employees in Houthi territory, whose paychecks had been suspended during the war. The amount at stake was significant — between $1 billion and $2 billion annually, according to two Western diplomats and a Yemeni official briefed on the plan.

The money was mainly to come from Yemeni oil revenue, those people said, with additional Saudi government funding to fill any gaps, according to the Yemeni official. Yemen’s oil resources are outside Houthi territory, and the Houthis have been eager to gain access to them.

Before the deal could be finalized, however, the Hamas-led attack on Israel in October 2023, followed by Israel’s devastating war in Gaza, derailed Yemen’s peace process. The Houthis announced a military campaign in solidarity with Palestinians, shooting missiles and drones at Israel and at ships in the Red Sea.

Throughout the war in Gaza, the Houthis avoided attacking Saudi Arabia. But their attacks in the Red Sea drew the ire of countries that depended on the waterway for shipping. When President Trump began a second term in 2025, he declared the Houthis a foreign terrorist organization and launched a bombing campaign against them.

That designation worsened an already painful economic situation in areas under Houthi control, and growing resentment put pressure on the group, said Mr. al-Muslimi, the Chatham House researcher.

Abu Bakr al-No’man, a 48-year-old father of two in Sanaa, used to earn about $130 monthly as a civil servant but said he now struggles to find enough food and water for his family to get through the day. Like many, he has become desperate for a way out.

“Escalation is the solution,” he said.

Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a senior Houthi political official, blamed Saudi Arabia for “failing to implement any of the provisions of the road map, foremost among them the payment of salaries for all state employees.”

He said in an interview that Saudi Arabia was at fault for the current escalation, and he accused the kingdom of imposing unjust restrictions on aviation and shipping to Yemen, which the Houthis and many Yemenis in their territory describe as a blockade.

In February, when the United States and Israel went to war with Iran, the Houthis seemed willing to stay on the sidelines. Months later, after a cease-fire between the United States and Iran fell apart, the calculus for the Houthis altered.

That change may have been triggered by Iranian pressure to get involved, although intervention also serves Houthi goals, several analysts said.

This month, the Houthis began insisting that an Iranian plane fly into Sanaa, where flights had been suspended for a year. Houthi officials called the plane’s arrival a bid to break the blockade.

Describing themselves as the sovereign government of Yemen, the group demanded the lifting of all restrictions — including a U. N. inspection regime — on planes and ships entering their territory.

One Western diplomat said there were talks about reopening flights but the Houthis had refused several proposals.

When a second Iranian flight tried to land in Sanaa, the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing the airport. The Saudi-backed Yemeni government claimed it had launched airstrikes to force the plane to divert and accused the Houthis of using the flights to import Iranian weaponry, which the Houthis denied.

The Houthis subsequently declared a blockade on Saudi ships in the Red Sea. Each side has claimed attacks on the other since then.

Whether things escalate further could depend on the Trump administration’s stance.

A senior Trump administration official told the Times that the United States will empower its allies to take the lead in regional security and supports a diplomatic resolution in Yemen.

On July 23, Mr. Trump threatened on social media to inflict “major military punishment” on the militia if they continue to attack Saudi oil tankers. He expressed disappointment with the Houthis, saying that they had, “until now, acted very professionally and smart.”

Vivian Nereim is the lead reporter for The Times covering the countries of the Arabian Peninsula. She is based in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

Apple Reclaims Title as the World’s Most Valuable Public Company

The New York Times July 27, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

The company slipped by the chipmaker Nvidia, amid growing concern about costs associated with the artificial intelligence boom.

By Kalley Huang

Reporting from San Francisco

Apple overtook the chipmaker Nvidia on Monday to become the world’s most valuable publicly traded company, about two years after it lost the crown.

The company’s ascent was as much a result of a sell-off of Nvidia’s stock as it was an endorsement by investors. Apple’s stock price finished the day up more than 1 percent, leading to a market valuation of $4.9 trillion. But Nvidia’s stock, driven by spending concerns, was down almost 5 percent, leading to a market cap of $4.8 trillion, according to Bloomberg.

Apple has sat on the sidelines of the artificial intelligence race for much of the past four years, leading to more frequent questions from investors about its plans. In 2024, after more than a decade at the top of the stock market, it lost the most-valuable-company crown to Microsoft.

While Apple’s reign over the stock market could be short-lived, it returned to the top as investors re-evaluate A. I. Earlier this month, stocks slid amid increasing concerns about spending on the technology and growing competition from China. As questions abound over whether the next big bet by the technology industry will pay off, investors appear to be returning to a safe gamble.

“Apple is a little bit of a flight to safety,” said Daniel Newman, the chief executive of Futurum Group, a technology analysis company. “People see the A. I. trade is volatile, and they see Apple as almost like owning an index,” he added.

In the four or so years since OpenAI released its ChatGPT chatbot and kicked off the A. I. boom, Nvidia’s market valuation has ballooned more than tenfold. Demand has surged for its chips, known as graphics processing units. They are key components for developing and running A. I., but there are growing concerns about costs associated with A. I. development.

Unlike the rest of the technology industry, Apple is not overhauling itself around A. I. Its fellow technology giants are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on making their own version of the technology and building data centers that house chips from Nvidia. But Apple is using A. I. models and cloud computing services from Google for its own products.

Apple has suggested it will continue to avoid the spendthrift ways of its peers, even as the company transitions from Tim Cook, its longtime chief executive, to John Ternus, most recently its head of hardware engineering. In April, during a call with analysts and investors, Mr. Ternus said he planned to maintain the financial discipline that defined Mr. Cook’s tenure at Apple.

The company’s prolonged absence from A. I. was not wholly by design. It first tried to weave the technology through its devices and upgrade its digital assistant, Siri, in 2024. But those efforts were plagued by delays and quality problems, culminating in the company’s postponing the release of the new technology until it could be improved.

In June, Apple reintroduced an improved version of Siri, which it said would arrive this year. At the time, the company argued that its approach to A. I. was different from that of its peers in Silicon Valley.

“Some appear to be racing forward, seemingly pursuing A. I. for the sake of A. I., without clear regard for the people — all of us — that it’s ultimately meant to serve,” Craig Federighi, Apple’s head of software engineering, said in June.

Kalley Huang is a Times reporter in San Francisco, covering Apple and the technology industry.

Case to Be Dropped Against Labor Leader Nabbed in L. A. Immigration Raid

The New York Times July 27, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

The arrest of David Huerta last summer helped spark a wave of protests against the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

By Jill Cowan

Reporting from Los Angeles

Federal prosecutors moved on Monday to dismiss their case against David Huerta, a Los Angeles labor leader whose arrest during an immigration raid last year helped spark a wave of demonstrations against the Trump administration’s crackdown in the nation’s second-largest city.

The U. S. attorney’s office in Los Angeles said in a statement that the case would be officially dismissed by the end of next month, as long as Mr. Huerta continued to follow the terms of his pretrial release agreement and not violate any laws. He had been scheduled to go to trial in August.

Mr. Huerta, the California president of the Service Employees International Union, was arrested in June 2025 after federal agents said he had impeded their work by trying to block a car and had encouraged others to join him as officers conducted an immigration raid on a clothing wholesaler.

Other protesters captured video of the arrest, which was violent enough to send Mr. Huerta to the hospital with a head injury. The next day, President Trump deployed thousands of National Guard troops to Los Angeles, saying they were needed to help address protests and protect federal agents enforcing the law.

Mr. Huerta was initially charged with conspiring to impede an officer, a felony offense that carries a sentence of up to six years in federal prison. He was released on a $50,000 bond, after about three days in federal custody. In October, prosecutors downgraded the charge to a misdemeanor.

Mr. Huerta, who has not admitted any wrongdoing, said on Monday that he was vindicated by the move to dismiss the charge.

“This means the government is finally admitting what we knew from Day 1 and what was obvious to anyone who saw the videos: The charge against me was baseless, meant to intimidate anyone who dares to speak out, organize, or demand justice,” he said in a statement. “There was never a real case, only an attempt to punish and silence me for exercising my constitutional rights.”

The U. S. attorney’s office said in a statement that the dismissal of the case did not mean that Mr. Huerta was wrongly arrested in the first place.

“The Department of Justice does not arrest people for peacefully protesting,” the statement said. “For the last 13 months, he has been compliant with the terms of his bond and has not engaged in the same obstructive behavior that led to his arrest and criminal charges being filed against him.”

When Mr. Huerta was arrested, immigrant rights advocates and local leaders — including Mayor Karen Bass, who visited Mr. Huerta in the hospital — said that they were troubled by the aggressive response to what they said was peaceful and routine protest.

Even before the Trump administration’s crackdown, they said, Mr. Huerta and other advocates would often rush to the scene of immigrant detentions to help connect those who were being detained with legal resources or other help.

A little more than a year later, The New York Times reported that the federal government had either abandoned or lost hundreds of criminal cases against people who protested the administration’s immigration enforcement.

Legal experts said that the pattern of filing charges that later unraveled — either because juries acquitted defendants, judges threw out charges or prosecutors abandoned them — suggested that the administration’s use of the law in these cases was less about protecting federal agents than about providing legal protection to cow protesters and immigrants into submission.

Shawn Hubler contributed reporting.

Jill Cowan is a Times reporter based in Los Angeles, covering the forces shaping life in Southern California and throughout the state.

Iran War Enters 6th Month and a Period of Greater Uncertainty

The New York Times July 27, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Here is a rundown of the major events of the war, as both sides consider their next moves.

By John Ismay

Reporting from Washington

Soon after the war began on Feb. 28, President Trump declared that Iran was “totally defeated and wants a deal.”

Then in March, Mr. Trump said the U. S. military would wrap up its campaign against Iran in two to three weeks. “We will be leaving very soon,” he said.

Now the conflict is entering its sixth month and a period of deep uncertainty. After nearly two weeks of attacks and counterattacks, Mr. Trump has held off a major escalation. But major issues between the two sides remain unsettled.

The cycles of fighting have resulted in staggering losses.

An estimated 1,700 Iranian civilians have been killed in airstrikes, which have devastated Iran’s infrastructure and deepened the country’s economic crisis.

Eighteen U. S. service members have died in the war, which the Pentagon estimates has cost $37.5 billion.

Here’s a rundown of the biggest moments of the war, and some of its deadliest incidents.

After the United States and Israel launch the war, Iran begins firing on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, effectively closing the waterway and sending oil prices skyrocketing around the world.

Feb. 28: In the opening barrage of the war, a salvo of Tomahawk cruise missiles launched from U. S. Navy warships kills 175 people at an elementary school in Minab, in southern Iran, most of whom are children.

A new type of American weapon called the Precision Strike Missile hits a sports hall, a school and two residential areas in southern Iran, killing 21 people.

The White House and Pentagon have not publicly acknowledged responsibility for either attack.

On March 1, the second day of combat, Iran attacks U. S. military facilities across the region with medium-range ballistic missiles and one-way attack drones. An Iranian attack drone kills six U. S. Army soldiers in Kuwait.

March 1: Three U. S. Air Force F-15 warplanes are shot down by Kuwaiti air defenses in an apparent friendly fire incident. All crew members are rescued.

March 4: A Navy submarine torpedoes an Iranian warship near Sri Lanka, likely killing more than 100 Iranian sailors. Iran calls it an “atrocity at sea.”

March 7: A U. S. Army soldier dies of wounds suffered in an attack on Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia.

March 12: Six U. S. airmen are killed when their KC-135 aerial refueling tanker crashes in western Iraq.

March 31: Mr. Trump says the United States will be out of Iran in two or three weeks.

The average price of a gallon of regular unleaded gasoline in the United States, which according to AAA had been $2.98 before the war, jumps to $3.98.

In early April, another F-15 is shot down — this time over Iran. The pilot is quickly rescued, but the jet’s weapons systems officer is rescued later. Multiple U. S. aircraft were destroyed in the second rescue operation, which involved hundreds of Special Operations troops and other military personnel. Another U. S. warplane, an A-10 Warthog, crashes and the pilot is rescued.

April 6: Central Command, which directs military operations in the Middle East, says the U. S. has hit more than 13,000 targets in Iran. It is the last update Centcom offers on the numbers of targets struck until airstrikes resume in earnest in July.

April 7: Mr. Trump announces a cease-fire.

April 11: Vice President JD Vance says the two sides have failed to reach a peace deal after 21 hours of talks in Pakistan.

April 12: The U. S. announces a blockade of Iranian ports.

April 19: A U. S. destroyer fires on an Iranian-flagged cargo ship in the Arabian Sea, and Marines seize the vessel. It is believed to be the first vessel that has tried to evade the U. S.-imposed blockade.

April 21: Mr. Trump extends the cease-fire.

The national average price for regular unleaded gasoline rises to $4.30 per gallon.

May 3: Mr. Trump announces “Project Freedom” to help stranded civilian merchant ships leave the Strait of Hormuz. The president is forced to pause the operation after less than 48 hours.

May 5: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, give a briefing to reporters on the Iran war. They have not given any since then.

May 7: Mr. Trump says his cease-fire is still in effect.

May 10: Mr. Trump rejects an offer from Iran to return to peace talks.

May 13: The Congressional Research Service says the U. S. military has suffered losses or damage to 42 warplanes, helicopters and drones in the war.

May 23: Mr. Trump says a peace deal is near.

In the three weeks leading up to the end of March, Centcom said it had guided around 70 commercial ships through the strait using a new route that hews tightly to the Omani coastline.

The national average for regular unleaded gasoline is $4.42 per gallon.

Mr. Trump began the month by saying peace negotiations with Iran are “very boring” and told a news outlet that he “couldn’t care less” if those talks with Iran break down.

June 11: The president again claims a peace deal is near.

June 14: The White House and Tehran reach a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, but leave the issue of Iran’s nuclear program unresolved. Mr. Trump says the strait will be “permanently toll-free.”

June 17: Text of the “memorandum of understanding” between the U. S. and Iran is released. But its language is vague, and the two sides have contradictory interpretations.

June 20: Mr. Vance departs Washington for more peace talks.

June 22: Mr. Trump eases U. S. economic sanctions on Iranian oil.

June 23: Iran attacks a commercial ship transiting the Strait of Hormuz. Over the next two days, U. S. forces launch airstrikes in response.

By the end of the month, the cost of a gallon of regular unleaded gasoline falls to $3.91.

July 1: The month begins with news that a U. S. Navy helicopter has made an emergency landing in the Arabian Sea. Days later, the senior aviator aboard is declared lost at sea.

July 4: The Pentagon launches an air show of warplanes, helicopters and parachutists over the National Mall in Washington. The event continues even after an evacuation is ordered because of the threat of extreme weather.

July 8: U. S. forces launch new airstrikes against Iran, hours after Mr. Trump said he thought a three-week-old cease-fire between the two countries was “over.”

July 9: Iran launches medium-range ballistic missiles at Jordan. U. S. Central Command says that it has struck 170 targets during the first 48 hours of renewed attacks.

July 11: Mr. Trump orders more airstrikes after Iran attacks a container ship in the Strait of Hormuz.

July 13: Mr. Trump threatens to impose fees on ships passing through the strait and reimposes a naval blockade on Iranian ports.

July 17: Three U. S. Army soldiers are killed by an Iranian attack on a military base in Jordan.

July 18: One U. S. Army soldier is killed during the disposal of an Iranian drone in northern Iraq.

July 26: The Pentagon changes the way it tallies casualties from the war, reporting a total of 624 U. S. service members wounded and 18 deaths.

Across the United States, the average price of a gallon of regular unleaded gas rises to $4.11.

After nearly two weeks of attacks by both sides, the war has remained on pause for several days.

John Ismay is a reporter covering the Pentagon for The Times. He served as an explosive ordnance disposal officer in the U. S. Navy.

Man Convicted in Idaho College Killings Seeks to Take Back Guilty Plea

The New York Times July 27, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

In an interview from prison, Bryan Kohberger said he had filed a petition to reopen the case. He blamed his guilty plea on “false promises” and wrong information.

By Mike Baker

Mike Baker began covering the Idaho murders on the day they happened. He is writing a book about the case.

The criminology student convicted last year of murdering four University of Idaho students in their home is seeking to abandon his guilty plea and obtain a trial, claiming he is innocent and was misled into confessing to the high-profile killings.

In an interview with The New York Times, Bryan Kohberger, who is currently serving four life sentences, said he had filed a petition challenging his conviction, citing concerns about how the plea deal came together.

“My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn,” Mr. Kohberger said in a statement provided to The Times on Sunday night. He reiterated in a phone call from prison in Idaho that he had an “absolute claim of innocence.”

Mr. Kohberger had not granted an interview or made public comments before speaking with The Times. He declined to discuss any evidence or other specific details related to his innocence claim, as well as the specific concerns he had about the plea process. It is rare for defendants to win post-conviction challenges.

The family of Kaylee Goncalves, one of the victims, said in a statement that Mr. Kohberger was like a “mosquito you just can’t seem to swat.”

“The real tragedy is this: If even a fraction of the energy spent trying to free a guilty man were directed toward honoring the victims, there would be statues of them on every corner, parks bearing their names, and days set aside to remember the lives they lost at the hands of a narcissist,” the statement read.

The Latah County Prosecutor’s Office did not return a call seeking comment. Idaho Attorney General Raul Labrador released a statement saying his heart went out to the victims’ families, noting they had “already endured unimaginable loss and now must face today’s deeply painful news.”

“My office stands ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out,” he said.

In November 2022, the four murders in Moscow, Idaho, a college town that had not seen a homicide in seven years, captivated the country for weeks as investigators struggled to identify a suspect. Mr. Kohberger’s arrest brought relief to the community but also stoked further mystery and speculation, as investigators never identified a motive or any previous relationship with the victims.

In court, law enforcement officials outlined the evidence against Mr. Kohberger. His DNA was found on a Ka-Bar knife sheath that had been left next to two of the victims. Amazon records showed he had purchased a Ka-Bar knife and sheath months prior. He drove a white Elantra, the type of car that investigators determined had been on surveillance video circling the crime scene and then speeding away from it. Mr. Kohberger’s phone showed he was out that night, with his phone turned off at the time of the murders.

Mr. Kohberger declined to discuss the evidence against him in his call with The Times. He said “the intention is for all of those questions to be investigated and answered appropriately in a trial setting.”

Mr. Kohberger, who had court-appointed representation throughout the case, ending with his guilty plea, said he prepared the documentation to challenge the case on his own. He requested to have a lawyer appointed to help him going forward.

In the handwritten filing made public by court officials on Monday, Mr. Kohberger focused on a claim of ineffective legal counsel. He said his lawyers failed to disclose or review exculpatory evidence and had made promises about what life in prison would look like, including details about visits and employment. These pledges, he said, had induced him to agree to the plea.

My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn.

Full document: Bryan Kohberger’s Statement About Abandoning His Guilty Plea

After he was arrested in December 2022, Mr. Kohberger’s initial lawyer said his client was eager to be exonerated. Court-appointed lawyers spent more than two years challenging the evidence collected against Mr. Kohberger, only for a surprise plea deal to come together a few weeks before a trial was to begin.

Mr. Kohberger accepted responsibility for the murders at a July 2025 hearing. He was not required to offer a motive for the killings — and never has. The lack of a detailed confession outraged some of the victims’ family members and even President Trump, who had called on the judge to demand an explanation from Mr. Kohberger.

In court, the judge asked Mr. Kohberger: “Are you pleading guilty because you are guilty?”

“Yes,” Mr. Kohberger responded. He later sat in silence at a sentencing hearing at which family members of the victims expressed their grief and anger.

In the early morning hours of Nov. 13, 2022, after a typical Saturday night out, the four victims were stabbed to death in an off-campus home. The bodies of Madison Mogen, 21, and Ms. Goncalves, 21, were found together in a bed on the home’s third floor. The bodies of Xana Kernodle, 20, and her boyfriend, Ethan Chapin, 20, were found in a bedroom on the second floor.

Two surviving roommates were in a bedroom on the home’s first floor. One of them reported seeing a shadowy figure in the middle of the night and hearing a commotion. But the roommates did not seek help until later in the morning, saying they had not realized what had transpired.

One of the experts who worked on Mr. Kohberger’s defense team has taken particular issue with the plea arrangement and the evidence. Brent Turvey, a forensic scientist who analyzed the crime scene for the defense, argued that the crime was committed by multiple perpetrators, criticized how investigators documented evidence and questioned why more testing was not done of a hair found with one of the victims.

The lawyers who served as Mr. Kohberger’s defense team have rebuked Mr. Turvey, telling The Idaho Statesman that he “is now speaking about topics that are still confidential, many of which are outside of his areas of expertise.” The lawyers did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday. Mr. Turvey’s concerns were included in a book about the case, “Broken Plea.”

Mr. Kohberger alluded to those issues in his statement, saying that “unanswered questions seem to multiply with each piece of discovery unsealed.” He said he was OK that a new trial would mean the prospect of a potential death penalty.

“Why am I breaking my silence?” Mr. Kohberger said Sunday in the interview from the Idaho Maximum Security Institution, just south of Boise. “A lot went wrong in those plea discussions. I really do want that to be heard.”

In the plea agreement that Mr. Kohberger signed, he acknowledged that he “knowingly, voluntarily, and intelligently waives all rights to appeal any and all issues in this case.” Still, defendants can make other claims about the legal process through post-conviction relief.

Mr. Kohberger was raised in Pennsylvania and had written online as a teenager that he felt “no emotion,” was suicidal and viewed himself as a “sickly, tired, useless and stupid man.” He later turned to heroin, friends said, but got sober and earned a master’s degree, growing enthralled with learning about serial killers and the minds of killers.

Then, in 2022, he moved to Pullman, Wash., to enter the Ph. D. program in criminal justice and criminology at Washington State University. He also applied for an internship with the local police department. But his term at the university was sullied after he clashed with a professor, and the university decided to fire him from his teaching assistant role.

Nicholas Bogel-Burroughs contributed reporting.

Mike Baker is a national investigative reporter for The Times, based in Seattle.

The New York Times July 27, 2026

Trump Administration

The filing focused on the question of whether a photograph of seashells arranged to read “86 47” constituted a true threat under federal law.

By Devlin Barrett

James B. Comey, the former F. B. I. director, asked a judge on Monday to throw out the indictment accusing him of threatening President Trump with a photograph of seashells arranged to read “86 47,” calling it a misuse of criminal law to punish free speech.

The charges, filed in North Carolina in April over an Instagram post Mr. Comey later deleted, say he “did knowingly and willfully make a threat to take the life of, and to inflict bodily harm upon, the president of the United States.”

Mr. Trump has argued that the term “86,” popular among restaurant workers, is mafia slang to kill someone, an accusation that many of his supporters have embraced. The other number, 47, is a reference to Mr. Trump, the 47th president.

“That claim,” Mr. Comey’s lawyers wrote in the new filing, “is contradicted by every possible source of meaning: dictionaries, context, precedent and common sense. ‘86’ simply means ‘get rid of’ or ‘eject’ and has no violent connotation except in the most uncommon usages.”

Mr. Comey’s lawyers are expected to file additional court papers on Tuesday, arguing that the case is part of a larger pattern of the Trump administration’s vindictive and selective prosecution of him.

Mr. Trump has publicly demanded that his Justice Department pursue criminal charges against Mr. Comey, whom the president blames for past investigations of his 2016 campaign and its possible ties to Russia as well as other conduct.

In September, Mr. Trump forced out a U. S. attorney in Virginia who concluded, along with career prosecutors, that the evidence did not support bringing charges against Mr. Comey over his testimony to Congress during a 2020 hearing. The president’s handpicked successor, Lindsey Halligan, a former insurance lawyer with no prior prosecutorial experience, then obtained an indictment against Mr. Comey, but the case was thrown out by a judge who determined that she had been unlawfully appointed.

Monday’s filing is focused on a narrower legal question, of whether the seashells photo constituted a true threat under federal law. Under a 2023 Supreme Court case, a true threat is a “serious expression” made by someone who intends to “commit an act of unlawful violence.”

The filing also notes that plenty of others, including protesters, right-wing activists and T-shirt vendors, have used the phrase “86” in reference to political figures, and have not been charged with threatening physical violence.

In a case involving demonstrators in Washington flying a flag reading “8647,” a federal judge concluded last month that “no reasonable observer could have viewed” the act as “a threat to the president’s life or physical safety.”

Devlin Barrett covers the Justice Department and the F. B. I. for The Times.

The Terrifying Housing Problem of Immigration Detention

The New York Times July 27, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

By Lauren-Brooke Eisen

Ms. Eisen is the senior director of the Justice Program at the Brennan Center for Justice at New York University Law.

In deep red Hanover County, Virginia, just north of Richmond, Donald Trump won 62 percent of the vote in 2024. It might have followed that the voters there supported his administration’s immigration agenda. And yet, in January, Hanover County’s board of supervisors opposed the Department of Homeland Security’s plan to purchase and retrofit a local 550,000-square-foot warehouse as an Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility. Protest was so vociferous that the Vancouver-based developer Jim Pattison Developments announced the sale would “not be proceeding.”

In the early months of the new Trump administration, D. H. S. spent some $1 billion on 11 warehouses, promising to turn those inhospitable spaces into 100,000 beds for immigrants on track to deportation. But, as in Hanover County, officials and communities across the country pushed back against warehouse expansion plans, citing humanitarian concerns, pressures on local infrastructure and services, and general revulsion at the notion of hosting detention centers in their hometowns. The agency is now planning to sell or offload seven of the 11 warehouses bought in that early spending spree.

But one solution created another problem: D. H. S. will now most likely increase its existing reliance on private for-profit firms to maintain or boost immigration detention capacity. That pivot comes with its own set of humanitarian worries, raises even greater transparency and oversight concerns and makes it harder for communities to resist the effort. At the start of Trump’s second term, the government was detaining around 40,000 immigrants. Today, there are more than 65,000 detainees housed across the country in for-profit and government-owned detention centers and county jails.

Whether privately run or operated by the government, immigration detention facilities have historically had a notoriously poor track record. Reports abound of detainees being placed in overcrowded and unsanitary facilities, deprived of medical care and served contaminated food. Thirty-three people died in ICE custody last year, the highest number in two decades. ICE has already recorded 20 deaths in detention so far this year.

Several of ICE’s newly purchased warehouse conversion projects were thwarted or delayed because of lawsuits arguing that the agency didn’t conduct the required environmental reviews. That worked for new spaces. Now, as ICE is working with both county jails and for-profit firms to expand detention capacity by drawing on empty beds in operating facilities, or reopening facilities that already existed, it will be harder for state and local governments to credibly argue that a town’s infrastructure can’t handle the influx of people.

Further, for-profit firms are generally not required to directly comply with the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). That means that when a family member or journalist is looking for information about a detainee, alive or dead, legal hurdles can stand in the way. FOIA applies specifically to federal government agencies. When it comes to information or communications that remain proprietary to a private company, the public cannot compel private prison corporations to provide those materials.

When journalists and others do receive documents through the federal government’s FOIA mechanism, the materials are often significantly redacted. It is already challenging for family members or private counsel to track down and even confirm the presence of a detainee, let alone his or her status, in this immigration detention system.

For-profit prison companies like GEO Group and CoreCivic — as well as local counties — have long contracted with the federal government to build and operate detention centers and transport detainees from one location to another. ICE is a significant source of revenue for these two companies: GEO Group reported that ICE made up 48 percent of its revenue for 2025; CoreCivic reported that ICE accounted for 35 percent of its total revenue that same year.

In February 2025, the federal government awarded a 15-year contract to GEO Group to house ICE detainees at its 1,000-bed Delaney Hall facility in New Jersey. Administration officials also contracted with CoreCivic to reopen a family detention facility in Dilley, Texas, that can hold 2,400 people. In March of this year, CoreCivic began receiving detainees at its newly opened Midwest Regional Reception Center in Leavenworth, Kan., which has the capacity to hold 1,033 people. Detainees at both the family detention facility in Texas and the facility in New Jersey have reported inhumane conditions and contaminated food. Both groups have disputed these claims, and have said that detainees have access to medical care and meals that adhere to religious diets, among other amenities.

“CoreCivic is committed to partnering with the federal government to help meet their goals and objectives,” CoreCivic’s senior director of public affairs, Ryan Gustin, wrote to me last month by email in response to questions about the federal government’s warehouse strategy and his perspective on the company’s ability to increase bed capacity to help meet the government’s demand. He noted that CoreCivic was not involved in the warehouse purchases and that the company has worked with the federal government for more than four decades. “We routinely engage with all our government partners on ways to deliver value to the taxpayer, and we welcome those conversations,” he said. GEO Group referred me to ICE for my questions.

There are some ways for a concerned public to address transparency and oversight issues. In 2017, the California legislature passed a law requiring the state’s Department of Justice to review and report on conditions of confinement at civil immigration detention facilities across the state. Other states should take California’s lead. This month, D. H. S. bought two California detention centers from CoreCivic for a combined $1.5 billion. CoreCivic will continue to manage the facilities, but now that the federal government owns the detention centers there could be legal challenges about state oversight.

At the national level, Congress should drastically expand the information that private prison companies must disclose, giving the public much better insight into the state of these facilities and the contracts behind them. The idea already exists in the Private Prison Information Act, a piece of legislation that has been introduced multiple times over the past two decades without success. The bill would require private prison companies to be subject to the same transparency requirements as the federal government when those companies are contracting with the federal government to hold federal prisoners or detainees.

Selling many of the recently purchased warehouses won’t dismantle the administration’s immigration detention agenda. And increasing reliance on for-profit firms comes with the dark possibility that we will know even less about what is happening to immigrants. But opening immigration detention practices to scrutiny is one of the most important ways to ensure that vulnerable people are being treated humanely.

Lauren-Brooke Eisen is the senior director of the Justice Program at the Brennan Center for Justice at N. Y. U. Law. She’s also the author of “Inside Private Prisons: An American Dilemma in the Age of Mass Incarceration.”
